title: Why there are still no non-WebKit browsers on iOS
body_text: Why there are still no non-WebKit browsers on iOS Why there are still no non-WebKit browsers on iOS | The Mozilla Blog Skip to content Mozilla Internet Culture Life Online Deep Dives Q&As Firefox Privacy & Security Firefox Features Tips and Tricks Firefox AI Mozilla VPN New Products Advertising Principles Our Work Internet Policy From the Team Download Firefox Search Search for: Internet Policy Why there are still no non-WebKit browsers on iOS November 20, 2026 Mozilla Firefox on iPhone is growing fast across the world. This is especially true in the EU since 2024, when the EU Digital Markets Act (DMA) started requiring Apple to let people choose their default browser; millions have picked Firefox, and daily use on iOS has doubled. People want to choose the browser on their phone. But there remains an important limitation to what is available on iPhones: Apple forces all browsers on iOS to be built on Apple’s own browser engine.  This has meant that companies like Mozilla cannot easily bring the full range of Firefox features and functionality to iPhone users because many of these are built within our browser engine , Gecko. iPhones and iPads are unique in having this restriction. On all other major operating systems, including Apple’s macOS, people can access the Gecko-powered version of Firefox. As a result of the DMA, Apple began allowing alternative browser engines on iOS in the EU. It published a set of conditions that companies like Mozilla must comply with to bring their own browser engine. At the time we said Apple’s rules made it “as painful as possible” for alternatives like Gecko. In the meantime, Japan also introduced new rules requiring alternative browser engines on iOS. Apple applied very similar conditions in Japan to those in the EU.     Nearly three years since Apple introduced these conditions in the EU and almost a year since Japan, not one developer has been able to launch a non-WebKit browser on iOS. The reason is simple: Apple’s conditions remain unworkable. The real test of any rule is whether it delivers the change it was meant to achieve in practice. Compliance on paper alone falls short of that test. Since the DMA came into effect we’ve been working behind the scenes to test and improve Apple’s conditions so that we can bring Gecko to iOS users. Those efforts have so far largely failed.  One of the conditions requires us not to disclose non-public information related to the project, but here’s an example of what we are up against: to use Gecko, we can’t simply update the Firefox app people already use and love. We’d have to build a whole separate app, a second Firefox. Then we’d have to ask every Firefox user to download it, move their bookmarks, passwords and history across, and manually switch over, step by confusing step. That’s a lot to ask of people who already made their choice. A significant proportion of people would understandably give up, including many who picked Firefox from the EU’s choice screen.   The conditions Apple imposes, including a level of user friction Apple would never accept for its own apps, mean that the open door feels more like a trap door.  Firefox users on iPhone chose an independent browser. They should get everything that comes with it, including Gecko, the last major browser engine not developed by a big tech company. We’ll keep pushing for a real level playing field, not an opening that drops independent browsers through the floor. Previous Post Has Microsoft wronged you? title: We promoted developers into architects without informing them
body_text: We promoted developers into architects without informing them Developer forever Home Posts About Contact Read my posts Read my posts All posts We promoted developers into architects without informing them Mani Doraisamy Nov 20, 2026 5 5 Yesterday, I was debugging a performance problem with our Google Forms addon. It turned out my colleague had vibe coded the logging part, so that he could monitor the new installs every week. Monitoring new customers is the most important part of running a business, so he is absolutely right in doing that. Except, he was logging the user’s email and Google has severely restricted how much detail you can get about the user since last December. So, AI had written a series of try/catch statements: First, try to get the email if the user gave consent to share it during installation. If it fails, it would try to fetch his user ID. If that fails, it would log an error saying the user has installed, but we don’t know his email or user ID. All of these are one line of code, but internally each of these makes multiple API calls to Google servers. Since logging was the first line to execute after installation, the welcome screen took 15 seconds to load. What is the right code for this? If you are a senior developer or architect who understands the number of API calls behind each method, you would have: Logged just the timestamp of the install instead of trying to fetch the email or user ID, and told the marketing team they won’t be able to send the follow-up email based on installation alone. Or, if marketing wants the user’s email on install, you would have shown the welcome screen first and logged the email or user ID asynchronously from the browser, while the user is looking at the welcome screen. But calling your server from the addon’s welcome screen might require your server to bypass security and log an unauthenticated payload. In other words, your job as an architect is to push back on requirements that can slow down the app. Or, find a way to work around the performance and security issues by making it async or accepting a reasonable hack. Why AI won’t push back AI is great at writing code. But it doesn’t know if you are launching the app or have millions of users, which it needs to make the right architecture call to log a timestamp vs email. It is also sycophantic and tries to execute your requirements exactly without pushing back, which means you end up with a slow app that takes 15 seconds to load a static welcome screen. Essentially, if you generate code by specifying your requirements instead of specifying your architecture, AI will decide the architecture on your behalf. It is so paranoid about security that it will never write code to accept an unauthenticated payload. Even if you write it yourself, it will rewrite it into an authenticated payload and screw up performance or force users to sign in again on your app. Your new job is to architect AI coding tools are tuned to implement your functional requirements and two non-functional requirements, i.e. security and backward compatibility to avoid breaking your app. This invariably leads to: Architecture that trades off performance for security and slows down the app. Multiple versions of datamodel design with redundant tables, columns and code. You can be the solution to this problem. You can understand the tradeoffs[1], define the architecture, design the datamodel first and ask AI to code within that constraint. Every time you give a requirement to coding tools that changes your architecture or design, they have to ask you before changing it, instead of changing it on their own. You have to tell it when it needs to be backward compatible, so it’s ok to keep multiple versions of logic or database tables, and when to delete the old logic and tables and keep a single version for maintainability. If you are an architect who is used to designing the datamodel, delegating the implementation to developers and then reviewing their code to see if they have implemented it correctly, this should be natural to you. But the problem is that today we have taken developers who were great at coding and moved them into an architect’s job. They see that the job they love, i.e. coding, is now completely done by AI. But nobody has told them about the new job of pushing back on requirements, designing the datamodel, constraining AI to their architecture and reviewing that it falls in line. This is the reason for all the confusion and hate among developers about vibe coding. Your future as a developer In our case, the right fix is simple. Log the timestamp, show the welcome screen first and tell marketing what they can’t get on install. But AI will never make that call for you, because it doesn’t know your users and it won’t push back on your requirements. That is the architect’s job. If you are a developer, the coding job is going away. But it doesn’t mean your job is going away. Non-developers who don’t understand architecture and design will end up with bad performance and unmaintainable database tables. So, stop missing the coding and become an architect[2]. Learn to push back on requirements, design the datamodel, constrain AI to it and review the code the way an architect reviews a developer’s code. You got promoted. Nobody told you, so I am telling you. Notes: [1] Ultimately, you have limited resources. Architecture is about trading off some requirements, so that your app can run with limited resources. Take CAP theorem as an example. You have to trade off consistency or availability or partition tolerance for your database. If you don't understand that tradeoff and ask AI to build a database that has all 3, it would reinvent Google Spanner++ and expect Google scale datacenter to run it. [2] This post is trending on HN . Some have correctly pointed out that good developers already do architecture and bad architects propose ivory tower architecture that falls apart during implementation. I have built ivory tower architecture whenever I am handsoff. This will become more common with AI, if we don't debug its code or don't hand code critical parts of the app from time to time. So, don't stop coding completely, but it's not a full time job anymore. 5 Like forum 5 share Share Comments · 5 Srinivasa Prasanna Nov 20, 2026 Mani - could adopting a method like spec-driven development have helped here ? title: Unforced Navier-Stokes Singularity and the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis
body_text: Unforced Euler singularity, unforced Navier-Stokes singularity, and the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis | What's new What's new Updates on my research and expository papers, discussion of open problems, and other maths-related topics. By Terence Tao Home About Career advice On writing Books Mastodon+ Applets Subscribe to feed Unforced Euler singularity, unforced Navier-Stokes singularity, and the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis 20 November, 2026 in math.AP , math.NT | Tags: AI , incompressible Euler equations , Levent Alpöge , Matei Coiculescu , Navier-Stokes equations , Riemann hypothesis , Tristan Buckmaster | by Terence Tao Obviously these results will be reported widely in other outlets, but I will note them here, in decreasing order of how “digested” the results currently are: Levent Alpöge, Tristan Buckmaster, and Matei Coiculescu, with heavy AI assistance, have written a human-readable proof of the finite time blowup for the unforced incompressible Euler equations in three dimensions , which is formalized in Lean here . Levent Alpöge and Tristan Buckmaster, again with heavy AI usage, have generated a proof of the finite time blowup for the unforced incompressible Navier Stokes equations in three dimensions, again with a Lean formalization . Here, the paper is technically human-readable and the general strategy of proof is broadly clear (following one of the expected paths to this result, namely to numerically build an approximate discretely self-similar solution and then use rigorous perturbation theory to convert this to an exact solution); but more work needs to be done to create a proper, professionally written proof. Levent Alpöge, using an internal AI model, has generated an (enormous) Lean-only proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis. This Lean Zulip thread is probably the best place to follow the efforts to verify the proof and extract the strategy of proof (which, from very initial analysis, appears to use the full power of modern developments on the Langlands program and arithmetic geometry). (UPDATE: the moderators of the Lean thread are now focusing the discussion on the Lean-related aspects of the proof only.) I imagine the digestion process will take some time, though in this case at least we have a human author to communicate with to assist with this task. See also Buckmaster’s Mastodon post regarding the first two results. As with the Landau-Siegel problem (the resolution of which is a corollary of GRH), the main promising routes have been automorphic methods, algebraic number theory methods, or arithmetic geometry methods; the latter were the key for instance to Deligne’s resolution of the function field analogue of RH (the Weil conjectures). Reply 21 November, 2026 at 1:57 am JWS There’s a report that reverse-engineers the Lean proof to reclaim attributions : https://www.ihes.fr/~rzhang/files/GRH%20note.pdf Reply 21 November, 2026 at 3:29 am Anonymous I’m a bit disappointed to see the general reactions of the community concerning the proof of GRH. I think the fact that a proof is even possible is incredible and just goes to show the power of the tools developed during the last century, and especially the last 50 years. As far as I’m concerned the “right proof” (as in a theoretical framework in which a proof of GRH is “easy”, “clear” or “natural”) is still very much elusive, and will likely remain so for a long time. If anything I’m hopeful that the recent LLM-assisted results will finally make us rethink the kind of mathematical work we appreciate most, and foundational (or more “philosophical”) work can take center stage. Reply 21 November, 2026 at 2:39 pm Anonymous I think people are being pulled in different directions. I think what is missing is the personal side of things. Before, we would celebrate the result and the people responsible. But now, any result proven with powerful AI models is more accurately attributed to the entirety of human mathematical endeavour than it is to any one person. This is not to say that the human author(s) of such results are not deeply involved, but the credit is nevertheless spread very thin. In my opinion, credit in mathematical research is not meaningful anymore from 2026 onwards. It’s not a bad thing, it’s just different and we need to adjust to it. Yet I am still hopeful about mathematics and research. We just need to find a better way to evaluate contributions and to get excited about new results and theories and better proofs of existing results, rather than who proved them. Although RH isn’t particularly meaningful in my corner of mathematics, so I don’t have any personal attachment to it, we can celebrate that it has a formal proof in Lean and is almost certainly true in the corresponding model/foundation. Reply 21 November, 2026 at 3:58 am Anonymous Perhaps the greatest achievement of artificial intelligence is not that it can outthink humans. It is that it can make humans celebrate something they do not even understand. Reply 21 November, 2026 at 5:53 am pascoej Were there any leaks of the other proof beforehand? Reply 21 November, 2026 at 6:18 am thoughtfully9f6ecf67dd After Alessandro released his human proofs,many people decided to take a hit on it and use AI to find all the possible gaps.it was formally expressed that this was an hurried draft, and that many gaps were still existed in the paper. ​One of the more serious issues was the failure of the uniform bound on the Archimedean integral, which diverges logarithmically close to t = 1 due to the jump discontinuity.But this is still clearly fixable,and viables adaptations exist. One possible way to replace the current φ function could be φ(t) = (ln t)tˆ(-z) for t > 1 and 0 for t ≤ 1.Continuity at t = 1 would work and cancels the 1/(t-1) singularity, as ln t/(t – 1) converge to 1 like needed and making the integral holomorphic for Re(z) > -1/2 By doing this,Montel’s theorem probably wouldn’t be neeeded to and instead use the identity theorem since the trace is established for Re(z) > 1/2. The boundedness of the biorthogonal vectors is a trickier issue,but placing the zeros inside boxes instead of one by one using the heights of Thm 7.1.4.2 can potentially help without changing the core of the argument. Reply 21 November, 2026 at 1:03 pm Anonymous Why on earth is everybody not saying anything about how absurd this is… The Lean proof dump accomplishes mainly two things: A “ok” one: Alpöge provided a Lean-guaranteed certificate that RH is true. To me, the certificate on its own is neutral, because in my opinion, although such a certificate (at least nowadays) is as important as the natural language / digested proof, the importance of such a certificate only rises AFTER the existence of the natural language / digested proof. Its existence by itself doesn’t do much if you only care about the problem and the techniques developed to solve it. If you only care about using it as a black-box result, I think only the certificate is fine, but my bet is that, once we understand the argument, the ideas that went into it will let us prove things far stronger than what we knew how to deduce from RH alone… A bad one: from Vakil’s account, it seems pretty clear that Alpöge’s announcement rushed the release of Masullo’s unfinished proposed proof (in natural language!!!) of GRH. The hope, according to Vakil, was to spend a year polishing the writing and running it by other people before announcing it, and (at least in principle) the author of the paper DOES UNDERSTAND in principle everything he did. Why didn’t Alpöge, after getting the result, wait and try to understand and simplify it to something that is at least readable and whose ideas are clear? He even claims himself in that strange remark note that he believes simplifications will follow rapidly… But no. In the meantime, he’s left the mathematical community to do this work for him. [To be fair, he did say he would now try to make the argument more understandable, but why didn’t he do that from the outset? If he expected substantial simplifications so soon, why announce the result before he could present a readable proof, whether on his own or with collaborators?] Had he and any other AI company not published this earlier, not only would that have been NOT a problem (since we are talking about a pure math result, not a desperately needed cure for some disease), but that would have allowed Masullo to spend the year Vakil said they had hoped to spend polishing the proof, and maybe we would not be needing to see the problems people are reporting in the draft of the work he rushedly submitted. (Needless to say, had Alpöge himself spent some time polishing the proof alone or with others, that would also have been fine.) Actually that would have been much better, since understanding would have been prioritized. And isn’t that what we have been claiming we should do? To understand? Why should a mathematician who waits until they can properly explain a discovery be placed at a disadvantage for doing part of the mathematical work before announcing it? And we certainly should not support Alpöge’s method of sharing the discovery. After all, he is incentivizing a race-model of mathematics (and ok, it has always been like this, but he has a HUGE amount of resources on his side and simply didn’t publish a human-readable proof…) that does not add much to the understanding aspect that is what science should focus on. After these points, I ask us to do the following thought experiment. Suppose, for instance, that Alpöge’s proof was the only one that appeared on 11/20/26 and that no other (realistic) attempt to prove RH/GRH was happening backstage. We know now that such a non-robotic and lengthy approach exists (we still do not know whether it is correct or not, but still). Then, Alpöge’s proof might discourage people from looking for a proof they could understand from the very start (even if not the 250,000 pages, then maybe “only” 10,000 pages?) and induce us to believe that no such understandable proof could exist, and that the future now is only for us to bow down to the great LLMs and hear what they shall say to us, and only digest what they have to say. Moreover, in this scenario, why wouldn’t he have waited to publish until he had made it into something readable? Why do you want to win a race with a supermachine? [Something that is very upsetting is the nitid anthropomorphization of LLMs that Alpöge constantly performs when saying “Claude and I”. Claude is not a person! It is a tool, for God’s sake. There is no “Claude and you”. There is only you – why are you taking some of the responsibility of being the human party off your shoulders?] The purpose of science is human understanding. We do not have access to every fine detail of reality and so we must produce a compressed but beautiful abstraction of reality to be able to understand it as humans. Had we the capacity to access every single instance of reality, we would not need science, for anyone could simply look and say “oh indeed there are no non-trivial zeros outside the critical line” and also know why it happens like that (if one only knew the former, but not the later, then it would not have access to every component of reality, which is a contradiction). As finite beings, though, we need abstractions that let us see a pattern we would miss even if someone put every detail in front of us. Finding an abstraction like that is itself an act of discovery. Machines do not every instance of reality either, but they can perform an approximation of that due to the sheer amount of computational power they have. But we must believe that we can understand and that we will understand. That is the basic underlying principle of the sciences. If we start giving up on that and believing that only a huge amount of bytes can explain why something is true, then we have stopped doing science, and maybe just have become oracle listeners. Anyways, this is just my opinion. I might be wrong. Feel free to criticize the points I brought up. AI disclosure: I wrote this comment and used ChatGPT 6.2 Astra to check the grammar and help me soften some wording, especially where I discuss the authors’ motives. Another thing to keep in mind is that Masullo took pride in not using AI. It certainly wouldn’t have taken Alpöge another year to distill the long-form proof into a more human-friendly form, so he would have scooped Masullo anyway in your scenario. There was no upside to waiting, once the proof was complete. Reply 21 November, 2026 at 2:25 pm Una Competing with AI on existing conjectures is a dead end. Even if AI produces a vast number of math results, who will the readers be? Can an author declare they are the best in the world without evaluation from readers or critics? title: Hurried Announcement: Alessandro Masullo GRH
body_text: Hurried Announcement: Alessandro Masullo GRH | Math 216: Foundations of Algebraic Geometry Home About AGITTOC 2020 2011-12 course 2014 course 2015-16 course 2017-18 course Math 216: Foundations of Algebraic Geometry November 20, 2026 Hurried Announcement: Alessandro Masullo GRH Posted by ravivakil under Uncategorized Leave a Comment   Hi everyone, I am at the American Mathematical Society Executive Committee and Board of Trustees meeting now, and about to chair an hours-long meeting, but this is urgent, so I will try to get this out quickly. Alessandro Maria Masullo has a proposed proof of GRH, and Brian Conrad has been looking closely at it for months and gave extensive feedback which is being incorporated, and it is so far looking good to him. It is all human, with no AI. The hope was to have Brian work with Alessandro for a year to polish the writing and then announce it after running it by enough people. Now it seems best to put out the current draft. I hope people quickly check it, formalize, fill any small gaps if they occur. I really hope it works. I have great faith in Brian’s judgement, and Brian has put a lot of thought into checking what Alessandro has done. There is a long story to tell, but right now I want to get the file out. Here it is. Update about 8 hours later: I’m out of the meetings, and now catching up! Several people have contacted me to report problems in the proposed proof, identified with the assistance of different AI models. (Thanks to several mathematicians in particular who were first to let me know.) As is usual, all issues need to be resolved to the satisfaction of the community before this proof would be accepted as true. (I make no claim as to the correctness of the proof strategy.) Photograph: Leonardo Muñoz/AFP/Getty Images Stock markets Nasdaq erases all 2026 gains as AI sell-off dampens Anthropic’s second day of trading The Nasdaq lost trillions in value, with the AI startup’s IPO failing to buoy it as investors question huge sums being poured into AI buildout Who are Anthropic’s seven co-founders, now worth $180bn? Lauren Almeida and Graeme Wearden Fri 20 Nov 2026 16.38 EST First published on Fri 20 Nov 2026 05.02 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google As Anthropic’s stock dropped during its second day of trading, the wider stock market dipped with it. On Friday, the Nasdaq Composite erased all its gains for 2026 and closed down 5% from its value on 1 January. The Dow Jones Industrial Average and S&P 500 closed in correction territory. Anthropic’s record-breaking IPO failed to stem a global sell-off in AI-linked companies, and the tech-heavy Nasdaq erased some $4tn in market value this week, according to the Wall Street Journal. Shares in the frontier AI company behind the Claude chatbot, which floated in the US on Thursday, fell by 9% on Friday, ceding most of the gains from the biggest initial public offering in history. They dropped to $88.30, towards the $83 level at which Anthropic priced its stock market debut. Anthropic’s first two days as a listed company have been volatile. Its shares jumped by 17% on Thursday, after briefly surging by almost 40% when trading in the firm began. 11:06 Is Claude creator Anthropic really worth $1.3 trillion? - The Latest US technology stocks followed Anthropic down on Friday, with the memory chipmaker SanDisk falling 14% and rival Micron down 12%. Nvidia fell 14%, eliminating hundreds of billions of dollars in market cap. Who are Anthropic’s seven co-founders, now worth $180bn? Read more Neil Wilson, a UK investor strategist at Saxo, said there was “just relentless selling in tech”. He warned: “Anthropic shares tumbled to take an $85 handle as the post-IPO euphoria gives way to the reality of a steep sell-off across the tech and AI space that shows no sign of easing just yet.” Global markets slumped on Friday too; Asian stock markets recorded their worst week since 2020, as shares in big chip companies fell. In Taiwan, stocks dropped 6.7% to hit their lowest point since mid-April, with the chip maker TSMC down about 6%. The scale of the decline in Taiwan prompted the chair of its stock exchange to pledge to ensure the stable operation ⁠of capital markets, and reassure investors they should remain confident in the fundamentals of Taiwanese companies. In Japan, the Nikkei index fell 5%, while South Korea’s tech-heavy Kospi index lost 5.5%. Shares in the tech investor SoftBank had their worst day in more than two years, down 14.5% in Tokyo, amid worries around its aggressive bets on AI. European stock markets posted their biggest weekly loss since March 2025, with the pan-European Stoxx 600 dropping 1.9% on Friday. London’s blue-chip stock index hit a five-month low. The sell-off followed losses on Wall Street on Thursday, where the main indices all fell by more than 2% on a day dominated by Anthropic’s IPO . View image in fullscreen South Korea’s Kospi index lost 5.5% at end of trading. Photograph: Yonhap/EPA Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said Anthropic could be “draining market liquidity”, as investors sell shares in other companies to raise funds to pay for stock in the newly floated AI firm. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Business Today Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion “The slide from yesterday’s highs sends a message that there might be more at work here than investors realise, and while brokers are scrambling to buy more, that liquidity has to come from somewhere, and the other tech names may be the first ones to feel the pressure,” Beauchamp said. Anthropic’s flotation has failed to ease worries around the AI trade, as investors increasingly question whether companies can deliver the returns necessary to justify the billions of dollars being poured into the AI buildout. Daniela Hathorn, a senior market analyst at Capital.com, said: “The IPO demonstrated that demand for AI exposure remains strong, but it has not been enough to overcome concerns about elevated valuations, profitability and the sustainability of investment spending. “The broader market mood has shifted from buying the dip towards questioning whether the correction has further to run. The weakness in equal-weighted indices suggests that selling pressure is no longer confined to a handful of technology giants, while Europe’s recent outperformance has also faded.” Nvidia shares fell byafter California served the chip company with a subpoena as part of an investigation into whether its advanced semiconductors ended up in China. Britain’s FTSE 100 share index dropped by 5.1% this week, its biggest weekly fall since the start of the Iran war. Fears that US central bankers may raise interest rates to fight inflation have lifted the dollar to a 19-month high, and pushed down the gold price – with gold on track for its worst week since March. Bitcoin hit its lowest level in four months, dropping below the $60,000 point for the first time since early July. title: Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights
body_text: [2611.21885] Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights Skip to main content Search Submit Donate Log in Search arXiv Press Enter to search · Advanced search --> Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2611.21885 (cs) [Submitted on 16 Nov 2026 ( v1 ), last revised 18 Nov 2026 (this version, v2)] Title: Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights Authors: Jiajun Fan , Neil He , Changyi Yang , Andy Mao , Xi Zhu , Chaoran Cheng , Kaiqu Liang , Shuaike Shen , Zetian Li , Ruihan Guo , Ge Liu View a PDF of the paper titled Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights, by Jiajun Fan and 10 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: A language model is trained once and frozen. Making it better takes another training run, or a prompt, a harness or extra computation at inference that is gone once the task ends. We show a third way: to our knowledge for the first time, a language model rewrites its own weights by its own reasoning and becomes better, with no gradients and no training. We call this self-rewriting: the model is its own optimizer. In earlier work, a frontier model edited a much smaller one; here an open 27B model, given its weights, its graded answers and the ability to run itself, diagnoses its own failure and rewrites the weights behind it. It surpasses itself: its own edit makes it 6.6 points more accurate on problems it never saw. It keeps getting better: it tests its edits on practice problems and submits only what works, each edit improving on the last, and over eight consecutive sessions its accuracy only rises. It repairs a damaged copy of itself, like a broken robot that fixes itself without being rebuilt: the copy solves almost nothing, yet with no retraining and without ever reading the original weights, the model brings it back to over 80% of the original accuracy on image tasks it never saw. And the ability emerges with scale: in one model family, the smaller models make no edit or break themselves, and only the largest improves and repairs itself. Unlike test-time scaling, self-rewriting writes its gain into the weights, at no cost per answer; unlike training, it runs only forward passes, as serving does. The wall between training and inference is a limit of our tools, not a property of intelligence. We believe self-rewriting is a necessary step toward recursive self-improvement: a model that, like a human, does not separate training from inference could keep upgrading itself for life, with no larger model, no harness or prompt engineering, and no pre- or post-training. Alpöge and T. Buckmaster and the Lean 4 formalization that accompanies it. Contents paper/finite-time-blow-up-navier-stokes.pdf : the paper (79 pages, version of 20 November 2026). lean/ : the Lean package (Lean v4.33.1 with Mathlib, at the revision pinned in lean/lakefile.toml ). lean/README.md explains how the formal statements relate to Theorem 1.1, Theorem 7.1, Corollary 7.2 and Appendix B of the paper, and where the formal proofs differ from the proofs of the paper. lean/NOTICE says in words what each statement file contains and what is proved. The Lean package The statement files at the top of lean/ give the definitions and state the theorems with sorry in place of their proofs; Solution.lean proves them from the library lean/Breakdown/ . Each comparator*.json pairs a statement file with Solution.lean , names the theorems whose statements must agree, and permits only the axioms propext , Quot.sound and Classical.choice . To build, from lean/ : lake exe cache get lake build The library is large (about 2,270 files and 600,000 lines), and a full build needs a great deal of memory and time. What is and is not here The formalization contains no data. The certificate whose hash the paper gives is not in this repository; the paper says that it will be released. That the certificate satisfies the conditions of Appendix B is verified by a rigorous computation, involving interval arithmetic (128 bits of precision, with the Arb library through FLINT), which is not part of the formalization and is not in this repository either. The source of the paper is not in this repository. State of the Lean text The package is the one of the paper's working repository, with one patch of 20 November 2026 applied to the cell-layer statements and to the library proofs that depend on them: the weight of one bound becomes $(|m|+\tfrac12)^2$ in place of $m^2+\tfrac14$ , one constant of a cell may be zero, and the set of the harmonics of the model in a cell is restricted to those that do not vanish there. Appendix B of the paper states the conditions in this patched form. The patched package was not rebuilt when this repository was assembled. About No description, website, or topics provided. title: DreamCoder: Coding harness and IDE from the author of Mastering Emacs
body_text: Announcing DreamCoder - Mastering Emacs Close Try Mastering Emacs for free! Are you struggling with the basics? Have you mastered movement and editing yet? When you have read Mastering Emacs you will understand Emacs. Learn Emacs Open main menu Mastering Emacs About Article Index Reading Guide My Emacs Packages Log in → --> Close menu Mastering Emacs About Article Index Reading Guide My Emacs Packages From the author of Mastering Emacs Announcing DreamCoder I talk about DreamCoder, a frontier coding harness and IDE I have been working on for quite a long time. I also talk about the history of AI, LISP and Emacs, and how it all fits together. Download  DreamCoder Read on By Mickey Petersen 20 November 2026 8 comments It’s been a little bit quiet around these parts; sorry about that. I’ve been really busy for the past fifteen months with a major project that I am finally ready to formally release. So I’d like to talk about that project, and also a potted history of AI and Emacs. It’s called DreamCoder , an AI coding harness that is very different from the ones you’re probably familiar with already. I installed Claude Code a few days after its first release some time in May 2025. I put some coins in the slot machine and I put it to work building a complex piece of enterprise middleware I’d built several times in my career. Wow.. watching this thing chomp its way through the project with that chaotic, early Sonnet energy. It was far, far from perfect; it required a lot of human steering, input and correction, but the speed advantage was undeniable, and seeing it jump between disparate programming languages, frameworks and theoretical and practical programming from one turn to the next was just such a sight to behold. One thing that struck me with Claude Code is that it was the first terminal application I’d used in a long time. I found it an odd choice for a coding agent; then everyone else copied them and made their own terminal coding agents. Why on earth do I have to stare at a shoe rack-sized terminal window to do this? Sure there are GUI versions also; but the terminal interface remains the primary modality for most of these tools. Most GUIs, and most harnesses now have them also, are second-class citizens. And they all look the same. A boring sidebar with chat headings and a chat pane is what most of them look like. But a serious coder needs more than that. Even a casual user will bristle when they try to copy and paste multi-line text in a terminal. So in May 2025 I decreed that I would build a better harness, and surely now that I have AI this should not take more than 2 or 3 months to build. And so, after 15 months of work, and endless UI and backend iterations, culminating in a successful beta test, I am now ready to release DreamCoder, which is I think the acme of what a coding harness should be. DreamCoder is a frontier coding harness with a tiling window manager that runs in your browser on all 3 platforms. Before I get into the meat and potatoes of all of that, I want to talk about AI history and Emacs’s role in it. Let’s roll back time to the 1950s. Past Emacs and LISP, if you did not know, both have a special place in the annals of AI history. John McCarthy was an AI researcher at MIT, and in the 1950s he set out to create the Advice Taker , a piece of software that envelops a framework for what a basic human should know that he called commonsense reasoning using “mathematical logic”. His postulation was that if we can express with symbolic precision all the aspects of what constitutes humanity like ordinary facts about life, that we can set in motion the rudiments of AI. In the 50s there was little in the way of computer software that could do this. To formalize such a system you need a lot of data, rigorously formatted, and a method of manipulating the data. The data and code itself may intertwine recursively , and so an ordinary programming language would not work. To help him achieve this, McCarthy created the LISt Processing (LISP) language made up of two facets: M-expressions, a functional language in the vein of Algol; and S-expressions, designed for symbolic data representation, and never intended as a method of writing code. S-expressions were dolled up with parentheses. M-expressions meanwhile used square brackets to visually separate the two. Uniquely, the language specification had an eval feature that would prove that the language is also a universal Turing machine… if only McCarthy had the means to do so. It was theoretical because McCarthy lacked, in time, staff and money, what he needed build this recursive evaluator that can take as input its own world state and evaluate it alongside new expressions, a fact made even more apparent by the sheer complexity of his M-expression language and the limited resources he had at the time. Steve Russell who worked with him proved him wrong the way most young people do: by just doing it. Russell wrote the first LISP Interpreter with a working eval function, but M-expressions got sidelined; the imperative, procedural nature of programming got squished into S-expressions instead. They had to hand roll the language on paper then punch it into cards and then batch run them. Eliding M-expressions was a simple matter of pragmatism. And so LISP was born. And through several accidents of history, M-expressions never gained traction. M-expressions live on in Wolfram’s Mathematica, but few other places. Much later, McCarthy eventually conceded that, “One can even conjecture that LISP owes its survival specifically to the fact that its programs are lists, which everyone, including me, has regarded as a disadvantage.” S-expressions were always intended as the storage format with a bridge language to manipulate them. But by pushing evaluation into the same symbolic representation format as the data, we have what we call LISP today. That is why LISP is so unique. Consider a simple calculator. (+ 2 2) can simultaneously represent an expression that we want to compute, two plus two , or perhaps a ledger of record of a calculation we have already done. McCarthy never built the Advice Taker in its purest form. He and his team ran into many philosophical, mathematical and computational walls that kept them occupied for a long time. The idea behind the Advice Taker was simple. If you want to go somewhere in your car, you can symbolically express this by building a chain of narrative facts – kinda like a flowchart, but as small snippets of rules and facts, not as one grand design. The system would automatically resolve ambiguities, and all the logician had to do was capture the microcosm of the world he wished to represent: (at me home) (walkable home car) (walkable home driveway) (drivable car shop) And so on. If you’re a student of Computer Science you’ll see echoes of Prolog here. The intent was simple: if we can symbolically express the world around us, we can advise that symbolic world with real-life facts, and have the automaton that uses this reified symbolic world change with it. But the axiomatic complexity of a world model would never survive an encounter with a 3-year-old child. Every axiom you write begets a new one — so you can walk to your front door? Well what if the door is locked? Or what if your car is parked on the street and not in your drive way? A rules-based order of the world is a tender, beautiful one; but it is hard to build. It’s a fractal of ever-more specific and pedantic rules that conspire against you, just as you think you have a soluble world, typed and ready. Anyone who has ever written Prolog knows exactly what that feels like! I have my own personal story to add to this. In the 90s as a teenager I got a summer internship at a business that built banking software. They clearly didn’t know what to do with us teenaged interns, so on our first day they crammed us in a room and split us into teams and told us to build a flow chart for assembling a bike. Team exercise or something. Best one wins. We were told to be as specific and explicit as possible and account for as many conditions as we could think of, and the poor employees who had to mind us did their best to help. I distinctly recall losing because in my flowchart I forgot to open the box the disassembled bike came in. McCarthy meanwhile eventually moved on and set up his own AI lab at Stanford, but the idea of the Advice Taker lived on. In the late 70s Stallman and Steele create EMACS (Editing MACroS), also at MIT’s AI Lab, a set of building blocks on top of TECO, a famously inscrutable text editor. TECO did not update the screen by default; you had to toggle that on and hope your edits worked. You typed out terse keyboard commands, crossed your fingers and hoped you got it right, and then you patiently waited for your text manipulation to take effect. Rinse and repeat until you got what you wanted. Stallman and Steele wanted more: they wanted macros so they could automate tedium of typing all that line noise. This strand of augmentation and later on self-modification is of course a unifying theme in Emacs today. The history of Emacs is long; but its outcome is known to us. I am typing this very article in Richard Stallman’s Emacs. McCarthy’s Advice Taker left its mark in a subtle but indelible way. Warren Teitelman built the ADVISE system in his thesis with a cool title that reads like something out of a pulpy 1970s sci-fi novella: PILOT: A Step Toward Man-Computer Symbiosis . Teitelman, he later said, was deeply inspired by McCarthy’s original idea of advising systems . In his thesis, he describes a method of arresting a function call and inserting code before or after it is run. He was tired of editing other people’s LISP code by hand, and wanted a way of modifying their code without touching it directly. He built and rebuilt his system several times over the years, culminating in his ADVISE system in Interlisp, a structured editor and language runtime for manipulating LISP code and data. Interlisp eschewed plain text files; instead, you manipulated the tree at a high level of abstraction with explicit instructions like “move X list to Y position”. You can see my own attempts at merging structured editing with plaintext editing in Combobulate . MIT AI hackers eventually implemented Teitelman’s ADVISE system from his PILOT thesis in their own versions of Emacs. Later, it was canonized in Chalupsky’s own 1992 re-implementation in Emacs Lisp that lives on ( M-x find-library advice.el ) as one of Emacs’s advice systems to this day. What began as an idea for expressing automata using symbolism in an as-yet theoretical language in the 1950s culminated in a system for dynamically altering functions in GNU Emacs in the 1990s. What an unlikely lineage and history. A cast-iron system made of stern rules cannot spawn general intelligence. Symbolism and AI did not end with advising functions. There were many attempts at symbolic intelligence. Terry Winograd’s SHRDLU ; Marvin Minsky’s Frame Systems ; and even Emacs’s ELIZA-style M-x doctor all make use of symbolic “AI”. None of them brought us closer to the AI that proponents of symbolic AI hoped they would. In hindsight that seems obvious. Writing a LISP macro just so will not produce artificial intelligence; nor will a carefully crafted web of rules and symbolic algebra suddenly spark intelligence. We know that today, but for a generation of computer scientists it felt like the future we have all read about in science fiction novels: a perfect, logical intelligence. A positronic brain . Robby the Robot; HAL 9000; C-3PO; Data; or the Speedies and Cuties from I, Robot. The unifying theme of these science fiction stories is they are automatons that follow strict rules — they obey Asimov’s three Laws of Robotics. Every turn of hardware and software brought them ever closer to one day realizing the vision of an artificial intelligence, captured in neat axioms and LISP S-expressions, and modified in tools like Emacs. It is surprising that symbolic AI, the vanguard movement for artificial intelligence, would instead dissipate into the wider body of Computer Science and programming as tools, languages and concepts, but not survive as a viable method of achieving AI. Perhaps we always knew. Because at some point – even if we never really fully internalized it – we discovered that a ductile system that is shaped by its master’s desires is a tool that survives the ages because it remains eternally useful. A cast-iron system made of stern rules cannot spawn general intelligence. For all the mathematical purity, beauty even, of the idea of a clockwork mind that is introspectable and malleable and its behavior expressed as S-expressions and interpreted by elegant algorithms and honed macros, we can, through the benefit of hindsight – now that we do have AI through other means – see that it was not to be. The argument in favor of ductility is especially poignant when you learn of the Connectionists , which sounds like a bad 1960s band, but was in fact a loose coalition of people who believed firmly that neural networks, not symbolic AI, were the path to success. The Connectionist viewpoint was deeply unpopular in AI academia of that era, and funding for it was scarce. Frank Rosenblatt invented the Perceptron, a foundational concept in neural networks, in 1957. Before Rosenblatt died in 1971, Marvin Minsky, an authority in the AI movement at MIT and a leading proponent of Symbolism, knifed the idea of Perceptrons and neural networks in a book he co-authored with Seymour Papert. They named the book, which they also dedicated to Rosenblatt, Perceptrons . The book deftly explains the mathematics of Perceptrons but undercuts their possible utility by showing that a single-layer Perceptron cannot represent an XOR gate. It was a deliberately obtuse reading of what neural networks could and could not do. With one additional hidden layer, a network can represent an XOR gate. It was a sneaky thrust of the stiletto: Minsky’s claims were overstated. A fact that was not lost on anybody in the Symbolic or Connectionist camps. It’s disputed if the Perceptrons book led to the first AI winter in the 1970s. It certainly did not help. But funding for many AI research paths dried up in the 1970s. The Connectionist movement was vindicated in the long run. They lost the battle then, but they won the war, and the fruits of their research eventually gave us AI. The ductility we so prize in our software and tools today is antithetical to a strict, symbolic world model spun of axioms and facts that we hoped would one day birth AI. Yet to try and give birth to this world they had to build the most ductile tools of them all: LISP and, from that, also software like Emacs. The ultimate hacker’s tool. It is ironic then that a neural network, a crude facsimile of how a brain works, a construct that is by its nature ductile and malleable, won out in the end. So I feel a profound sadness that I started out programming DreamCoder in Emacs, the most extensible editor in the world, by hand back in May 2025, only to see DreamCoder write itself… in DreamCoder today. Future I am still sad, but I also know that our industry completely reinvents itself every decade or two. This is my second career upheaval. Most programmers today have not been around long enough to go through it themselves. So I feel for them that this especially massive quake is their first encounter with how unsentimental our industry is. But for all the sadness, I wake up every day with a feeling of optimism that I have not felt in a very long time. I finally get to build again, no longer weighed down by my decades of knowledge and experience that held my ambition in check. I truly have not felt this liberated since I was a teenager programming in Delphi, blissfully unaware that the things I was busy building were impossible for a self-taught teenager to ever realize. I see this reflection in others: the best programmers I know also love AI. Amateurs also revel in AI’s capabilities, happy that they can finally solve problems they could never afford to pay a programmer to do for them. I must admit that building software has, over the years, gotten a lot more complex, with an ever-larger share of that work being repetitive tedium. This is more so with hobby software – as I do not get paid to do it, so I do not have a moral duty to see it through – where I’d do all the fun bits leaving just the enervating, boring and soul-crushing parts behind. Do you have a projects folder full of sad, abandoned projects like I do? Now I can craft in abundance. AI has freed up a lot of toil but I somehow still find myself busy all day doing real work. Building a coding harness is perhaps the closest I will get to the optimism all those researchers and scientists must have felt in the 1970s and 1980s. They hoped that with a little bit more work, their logical rules would kindle a new intelligence. Fifty years on, and I can simply tell DreamCoder to improve itself and watch as it changes before me. I can ask the AI running inside it to analyze the changes I have made to its tools and prompt and have it adjust them accordingly. It feels like science fiction; the very thing the researchers of yesterday strove to build. Yet we really do live in this reality now. Taste is a scarce, human resource. So. DreamCoder . Let me address the 900 lb gnu in the room: DreamCoder is not an Emacs-related application. The reason is unfortunately one of economics and access: I want to build an AI coding harness for everyone. But don’t worry: I have some cool plans for DreamCoder + Emacs, and AI + Emacs more generally going forward. So stay tuned. But what about all those other coding harnesses? Well, most of those harnesses all suffer from the same mistakes. It is a problem that is not unique to coding harnesses or the people who make them, but a constraint we all labor under, and one that is not easily replaced by AI: Taste is a scarce, human resource. And for all the bounty of AI, it still requires a human to persevere and to see things through. One thing intensive use of AI coding has taught me is that we’re going to need a lot of computer programmers who know what they’re doing going forward. I believe this is so, because let us be honest, most people do not want to program computers, even if that computer can actually do the bulk of the work for them. It requires a steady hand to build reliable software; that has not changed. Therefore, if we programmers have to spend a lot of our time interacting with AI, then the tool we do it with should be ‘human-centric’ in its design, and it should take advantage of all the modern features we have at our disposal. Back in May 2025 I took a look at all the tooling and said “no, thank you.” Today I look at the landscape and I feel pretty much the same. And I think I am not the only one who feels that way. Most of these coding harnesses, to me, feel bristly. They shouldn’t be; but they are like that because we are at an important inflection point where no one really knows what the future looks like. We’re all just… fumbling around a bit. It’s an exciting time to build software, even if we don’t quite know what the world will look like a few years hence. One thing I am adamant about is that DreamCoder must be a powerful, frontier-class coding harness. That means it should have all the features you’d expect from that: backgroundable sub agents, MCP servers, cache efficiency, and all that stuff. Check. Sub-agents MCP servers Your own agents Terminals beside chats The frontier-harness basics. Click any of them to see it full size. But that stuff quickly recedes into the background because, you know, it just works. Day to day you will dart between chats and terminals and whatnot, and you need an interface that accommodates that. Emacs is a tiling window manager; so is DreamCoder. DreamCoder’s window manager is a little bit cleverer than most window managers as every pane has a minimum, comfortable and maximum size. The window manager will therefore ensure windows always fit snugly on your screen, and you’ll never end up in a situation where windows are tiny and unreadable. It has a sophisticated constraint satisfaction solver that tries to balance your demand for a new window (“open a terminal”) with the challenge of keeping your visible panes roughly the same size. If DreamCoder can’t wedge in a new pane, it’ll punt one to the hidden window bar. Just click it to resurface it, or hover it to see what it’s doing; it’s a live view. Panes are made to fit; if a new pane must evict an old one, it is pushed to the hidden window box. Avy-style selection and embark-style actions. Because of my Emacs roots, I think a good tool must be keyboard-friendly. Because it runs on a browser you get the mouse for free of course. But smacking the tab button over and over is a frustrating user experience in complex webapps, and doubly so a tiling window manager: where exactly are you going to end up when you tab from one window to the next? To combat that, I built an avy-style window and “point of interest” selector for chats. Tap a key and pick from a selection of “embark”-like actions such as clicking links or opening pictures. It’s a work in progress, but I think it works well. Familiar type-to-complete mechanics Most high-volume operations like opening and creating panes is done through a Helm-like interface with search-as-you-type. It’s really efficient, of course. And it works with a mouse also; which is sort of the point. The keyboard’s there for those who want it, and the mouse for regular folk who are just getting started. One unique feature of the design, which admittedly I am still exploring privately, is that everything is stored as Javascript objects (on account of running in your browser) so it’s not too much of a leap to build “macros” that prefill most of these dialog windows, leaving behind just the fields you want to edit. But yeah. With DreamCoder I want to take the best of Emacs and its coterie of third-party packages and bring some of that with me. The world is still not ready for an Emacs-shaped future, sadly, so that is why DreamCoder is a standalone application and a web frontend. Another thing that drives me wild: I see people with tmux running 10 claude codes (or codex, or…) cycling between them like a duck gallery at a carnival to see if one of them is done working, or if it needs human intervention. So there’s two things to unpack here: one is running lots of things in parallel, and the other is observability. You need insight into what is going on: is an AI jammed because it’s awaiting an answer or a tool safety prompt? Perhaps you’ve parked a bunch of chats pending some conversations with coworkers or other work that must finish first. In DreamCoder you have workspaces. They’re like virtual desktops (or window configurations in Emacs lingo): a snapshot view of panes as you want em. As you can see from the screenshots, panes expand to fill all the space. So if you want more space, you can: resize them (with the mouse or keyboard); shuffle them to a named workspace; or float them so they sit on top of the other windows. The event graph Objectives Image panes On your phone More than a chat window, already. But if you’ve got a lot of things happening in multiple workspaces, it’s hard to keep tabs on that. That’s why DreamCoder has a big, honking minimap in the top-right corner. One for each workspace. The minimap is a miniature of your actual layout. Each pane in the map gently pulses when it’s working, and it makes it abundantly clear when it’s blocked. When there’s nothing to do, it’s green. Because workspaces and panes are distinct things you interact with, it must be easy to navigate between them. I also wanted full-on, optional Emacs key bindings, but that is… pretty much impossible to properly build. Browsers lock you out of some rather important Emacs button combinations. Sadly that feature is parked until I can solve it on all major browsers without breaking your normal browser keys. That’s not to say it doesn’t have Emacs-inspired key bindings. Most global actions are reachable with Alt+x , akin to M-x ; local, pane-specific ones with Alt+c . Alt+m activates keyboard mode: you can now type the number of the named pane to jump to it; or WASD to switch the active pane in that cardinal direction. Support for open weight models like Qwen, Gemma, Deepseek, GLM, etc. is also very important to me. They work so well. I’m really surprised, here in late 2026, just how capable small models are at local-only development compared to just one year ago. Qwen 3.8 27B, for example, is fantastically good for its size. You can do a lot of good software development with it if you’re a capable hand yourself. Bigger models equal more auto piloting; but that Qwen model? Wow. So local models work great. In fact I think the future is local for a lot of use cases. Intelligence is fast approaching a cost where it will be too cheap to meter. If you remember the personal computer revolution in the 1980s and 1990s, then there are definitely echoes of that here. If you’ve been holding off on local models then I do recommend you reconsider. Small ones like Qwen 3.8 27B (or its cousin, Flash Next) can run well on a high-end gaming rig or Mac, or with a little investment if you do not have that. If you have a dinky old computer and you’re cash starved, then not all hope is lost. Turn to the potato agronomists on twitter: give twitter’s AI, Grok, what you have and what you can reasonably spend and tell it to track down the cutting edge setup for your rig. This is no lie the fastest, easiest way to catch up to the cutting edge of self-hosted inference today. Five minutes. Coding harnesses are the IDEs of the future As I’ve been building DreamCoder, I have come to the belief I’m not just building a coding harness. Coding harnesses are an IDE for the future; it will do more than just display a chat window for coding agent work. DreamCoder does more than that already. It’s going the way of Emacs in that it’ll consume a wide range of adjacent workflows and tools. But I have only just gotten started. I am brimming with ideas I’m building in parallel, but they take time because as I said it’s not about the code; it’s just one small facet of building something that works well. But you know that already: it’s always the last mile. DreamCoder is the most ambitious, technically complex and advanced software project I have ever built in my life. And that’s just the beginning. I’m not done. I’ve barely started. I will be blogging about this going forward, in addition to my usual Emacs scribblings. In fact, the thing I’m currently grinding away at is a world-class pentest and cybersecurity suite in DreamCoder. Every single bit of software we have ever written is vulnerable; we have many rough years ahead of us. Just look at the crippling vulnerabilities coming out every day now almost. Even the most security conscious person is going to find themselves on the wrong side for no other reason than we depend on packages that were mature and stable and assumed to be secure. DreamCoder can do its bit to help catch many of most obvious weaknesses, especially as new software is minted every day that also needs thorough testing. Pentested endpoints and their states Findings and how exploits were traced Screenshot of DreamCoder's upcoming, awesome pentesting and cybersecurity suite. It's built for humans . The AI does the work, and you and your team assess its results and impact. The graph overview is AI-generated from its explorations and findings. Do not worry: no human will ever have to suffer the indignity of writing flow charts like that. (If you're interested in/have questions about the pentesting stuff, please e-mail me.) To round it off, I would like to formally invite you to join me in making DreamCoder better by trying it out . It’s great. It’s not a toy; it’s not a demo; and it’s not a weekend prototype. It’s a frontier coding harness that has most of what you’d expect: MCP, backgroundable sub agents and shell commands, terminal windows, skills, hooks, 99% cache hit, it runs for days, and an interactive UI for all of it. There’s a handy dandy importer for your Pi, OpenCode or Codex configs also to help you get started. A couple of clicks and your model settings are set up in DreamCoder. Ready to go. Please do e-mail me your thoughts ( (rot13 "zvpxrl@znfgrevatrznpf.bet") ) on AI, coding harnesses, what you’ve built with it, and what you think more generally about where our world is heading. I’m keen to hear from you. And if you want to hear more from me on the technical aspects of AI, building coding harnesses, and more, then do sign up for the DreamCoder newsletter below. Try DreamCoder Download  DreamCoder macOS Windows Linux Docker The DreamCoder newsletter An occasional e-mail when there's DreamCoder news: new releases, and new writing on AI and coding harnesses. Very interesting software, I've always felt there's something wrong with the current design of harnesses. I will give this a try in the next few days. I am curious about two things. First, would it be possible to make use of existing harnesses kernels ? Second, are you planning to release the source code ? — heiwiper · reply DreamCoder has its own internal tool loop system; it does not use other harnesses' kernels. That might be a thing in the future if there is enough demand for that. — ⭐ Mickey Petersen · reply so sad that browser is the best way to get cross platform gui, i generally hate applications that reinvent the window manager but this one is worth it. embark actions are an amazing solution i never found, i will be using those vehemently in my shithole projects. the "graph/visualization first" ui shape is i think the future of HITL harnesses. — Paths · reply I adore the slight skeumorphism in the UI design. One nitpick: The download page misdetects the operating system, though, it detects Arch as Debian and tries to give me the Debian package.
