Yes Geolocation Data: For example, information that can be used to determine a device’s physical location. Yes Sensory or Surveillance Data: For example, call recordings or other audio, electronic, or visual monitoring or surveillance. No ‍ Note: We do not collect Biometric Information, Inferences and Profile Data, Professional or Employment-Related Information, or Education Information in the consumer context. ‍ Sensitive Personal Information Categories of Sensitive Personal Information Purposes for Collection, Use, or Processing Sold or Shared for Targeted Advertising Social Security Number, Driver’s License, State Identification Card, or Passport Number To enable secure account access; authenticate users; provide and maintain services; prevent unauthorized access, fraud, and security incidents; and ensure system integrity. To process transactions, subscriptions, and payments; manage billing and collections; fulfill contractual obligations; detect and prevent fraud; and comply with financial and legal requirements. To support service functionality; enhance user experience; conduct analytics and business intelligence; and support security, fraud detection, and operational purposes. No Account log-in, financial account, debit card, or credit card number in combination with any required security or access code, password, or credentials allowing access to an account, or other financial information as defined under applicable state law No Financial information (e.g., payment card data, billing information) No Precise geolocation No Status as a victim of a crime We may collect this information in limited circumstances, such as in connection with a law enforcement subpoena or similar legal process. No ‍ Note: We do not collect other sensitive personal information under applicable state laws. ‍ Retention Periods The period of time for which we retain personal information depends on the purposes for which we collect and use it. We will delete or de-identify personal information when it is no longer needed to fulfill the purposes listed for each category, unless a longer retention period is required or permitted to: (a) comply with applicable laws, including tax, accounting, and recordkeeping laws; (b) establish, exercise, or defend legal claims; (c) prevent fraud and ensure the security of our services; or (d) fulfill another legitimate business purpose permitted by applicable state law. Where technical or operational limitations prevent complete deletion or de-identification, we will take reasonable measures to prevent further processing. ‍ Notice of Sale and/or Share Our use of tracking technologies may be considered a “sale” or “sharing” of personal information with third parties for cross-context behavioral advertising (e.g., targeted advertising) under applicable state law. You can opt out of such tracking by clicking the “ Your Privacy Choices ” link in the footer of our website, which will allow you to access our cookie and tracking preference center and select or modify your preferences. Please note that this mechanism provides opt-out rights under applicable state privacy laws. You may also opt out by enabling a recognized opt-out preference signal, such as the Global Privacy Control (“GPC”), on your browser or device. See “Making Requests to Opt-Out; Opt-Out Preference Signals and Universal Opt-Out Mechanisms” below for additional details. ‍ ‍ Privacy Policy The purpose of this Privacy Policy is to provide you with a comprehensive description of our online and offline practices regarding our Information Practices. You have certain rights to control the use of your personal information. This privacy policy describes your rights as it relates to our Information Practices as to your personal information and how you can exercise those rights. ‍ The following table includes disclosures for the preceding 12 months of: categories of personal information we have collected about consumers, the categories we have disclosed for a business purpose, and categories of third parties with whom we shared the personal information during that period. ‍ General Personal Information Category Business or Commercial Purpose for Collection & Disclosure Categories of Service Providers / Contractors to Whom Disclosed Identifiers Providing, operating, and maintaining products and services Managing accounts, transactions, billing, and customer relationships Communicating with users regarding services, support, and updates Ensuring security, integrity, and fraud prevention Debugging and maintaining system functionality Performing analytics, research, and business intelligence Improving, developing, and enhancing products and services Personalizing user experience and content Supporting advertising and marketing activities Complying with legal, regulatory, and contractual obligations Supporting internal business operations and administration Evaluating or conducting mergers, acquisitions, or other corporate transactions Affiliates Cloud hosting and storage providers Payment processors and billing providers Customer support and communications providers Website and application service providers Analytics and performance monitoring providers Advertising and marketing partners Security and fraud prevention providers Compliance, legal, and audit support providers Personal Information Categories from Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.80(e) Characteristics of CA or Federal Protected Classifications Commercial Information Internet or Other Similar Network Activity Geolocation Data Sensory Data ‍ Sensitive Personal Information Unless otherwise allowed by applicable state law, we will only collect certain types of sensitive personal information with your consent. We will only collect, process, or disclose sensitive personal data where it is strictly necessary to provide or maintain a specific product or service you have requested, and we will not sell sensitive personal data. We do not use or disclose the below sensitive personal information for purposes other than those business purposes specifically enumerated under applicable state law. ‍ Category Business or Commercial Purpose for Collection & Disclosure Categories of Service Providers / Contractors to Whom Disclosed Social Security Number, Driver’s License, State Identification Card, or Passport Number Identity verification Legal and regulatory compliance Account authentication and access Payment processing and billing Fraud prevention and security Service delivery and account management Compliance and legal support providers; cloud hosting providers. Account log-in, financial account, debit card, or credit card number in combination with any required security or access code, password, or credentials allowing access to an account, or other financial information as defined under applicable state law Payment processors; billing providers; cloud hosting providers; security and fraud prevention providers. Precise geolocation Analytics providers; cloud hosting providers; security providers. Status as a victim of a crime We may collect this information in limited circumstances, such as in connection with a law enforcement subpoena or similar legal process. None. ‍ In the previous 12 months, we did not collect any other sensitive personal information under applicable state laws. ‍ For each category of personal information identified above, we also disclose such personal information to the following categories of third parties: At Your Direction. We may disclose your personal information to any third party with your consent or at your direction, including where you choose to interact with third-party services or integrations. Business Transfers or Assignments. We may disclose or transfer your personal information to a buyer, successor, or other entity as reasonably necessary to facilitate a merger, divestiture, restructuring, reorganization, dissolution, joint venture, collaboration, assignment, sale, transfer, or other disposition of all or any portion of our business, assets, or stock (including as a going concern or in connection with any bankruptcy, liquidation, or similar proceeding), in which personal information is among the assets transferred. Legal, Regulatory, and Safety. We may disclose your personal information to government authorities, regulatory agencies, law enforcement, courts, and other parties as reasonably necessary to: (i) comply with any law, rule, regulation, court order, subpoena, or other legal process; (ii) respond to any government, regulatory, or law enforcement inquiry, investigation, or request; (iii) establish, exercise, prepare for, or defend legal claims; (iv) enforce or apply our Terms and Conditions and other agreements, including for billing and collection purposes; (v) prevent, detect, protect against, or respond to security incidents, identity theft, fraud, harassment, or other malicious, deceptive, or illegal activity, including by exchanging information with other companies and organizations for fraud-prevention and security purposes; (vi) protect the rights, property, or safety of Company, our personnel, our customers, or others, including to protect an interest essential for the life or physical safety of any individual; and (vii) otherwise as permitted or required by law. In limited circumstances, information we receive or process in connection with legal process, law enforcement requests, security investigations, or similar matters may include information that is sensitive or otherwise subject to special legal protections. We process such information only as reasonably necessary for the applicable legal, regulatory, safety, security, or claims-related purpose. Mobile information. We do not share mobile information with third parties or affiliates for marketing or promotional purposes. Text messaging originator opt-in data and consent are excluded from all categories of information we disclose and will not be shared with any third parties, excluding aggregators and providers of the Text Message services. ‍ De-identified and aggregated information. We may disclose aggregated information about our users and de-identified data or information that does not identify an individual, without restriction. ‍ Where we maintain de-identified data (data that cannot reasonably be used to infer information about, or otherwise be linked to, an identified or identifiable individual), we commit to the following: (1) we take reasonable measures to ensure the data cannot be associated with an individual; (2) we publicly commit to maintaining and using the data in de-identified form and will not attempt to re-identify the data, except for the purpose of determining whether our de-identification processes comply with applicable law; and (3) we contractually obligate any recipients of the de-identified data to comply with all applicable requirements regarding de-identified data. Data used for usage analytics and business intelligence may be anonymized or aggregated so that resulting insights do not constitute Personal Information. ‍ Sources of Personal Information. The categories of personal information identified above were collected from the following categories of sources: you directly; your devices when you interact with our websites, platforms, and applications; service providers acting on our behalf; third parties such as data aggregators, social media companies, and publicly available sources; your employer or organization in connection with business customer relationships; and business partners, such as event or conference organizers. ‍ AI Processing Disclosure: We may employ artificial intelligence (AI) technologies to support and enhance our operations; any such processing is conducted in compliance with applicable laws and governed by data processing agreements. ‍ What We Sell to Third Parties or Share with Third Parties for Cross-Context Behavioral Advertising and Right to Opt-Out We have sold or shared with third parties for cross-context behavioral advertising (e.g., targeted advertising) the following categories of personal information to advertising networks and analytics providers in the preceding 12 months: Identifiers; Internet or Other Similar Network Activity; Commercial Information; Geolocation Data. We do not sell or share sensitive personal information. ‍ Right to Opt-Out of Sale/Sharing or Targeted Advertising You have the right to direct us to stop selling or sharing your personal information for cross-context behavioral advertising (the “Right to Opt-Out”). You may exercise this right by: (1) Clicking the “Your Privacy Choices” link to manage your preferences; or (2) Submitting your request through an Opt-Out Preference Signal/Universal Opt-Out Mechanism, such as the Global Privacy Control (“GPC”), as described further below. ‍ We do not have actual knowledge that we sell the personal information of minors under 18 years of age. ‍ Right to Opt-Out of Marketing Communications You may opt out of marketing communications at any time: Email marketing: Use the unsubscribe link in the footer of any marketing email. SMS/text marketing: Reply “STOP” to any marketing text message. Telemarketing calls: Inform the sales representative who calls you, or email privacyrequest@backblaze.com with your request. Third Party Links The Platform may contain links to other websites or applications. Please be aware that we are not responsible for the content or privacy practices of such other websites or applications. We encourage our users to be aware when they leave our Platform and to read the privacy statements of any other website or application that collects personal information. ‍ ‍ Your State Law Privacy Rights Right to Know/Access : Certain states provide the right to request our disclosure of any of the following: The categories of personal information we have collected about you (which may include any inferences). The categories of sources from which the personal information is collected. The business or commercial purpose for collecting, selling, or sharing with third parties for cross-context behavioral advertising ( e.g. , targeted advertising). The categories of third parties to whom we disclose personal information. The specific third parties to whom we disclose personal information. The specific pieces of personal information we have collected about you. Right to Correct: You have the right to request that we correct inaccurate personal information we maintain about you, taking into account the nature of the personal information and the purposes of our processing. We may request documentation from you to help assess accuracy. If we determine the contested information is more likely than not accurate based on the totality of circumstances, we may deny the request and will explain the basis for our decision. ‍ Right to Delete: You have the right to request that we delete personal information we have collected from or about you, subject to certain exceptions permitted by law. If we cannot fully comply with a deletion request, we will explain why and delete the information that is not subject to an exception. ‍ Right to Opt-Out of Sale/Sharing; Targeted Advertising: You may have the right to “opt out” of the “sale” or “sharing” of your personal information for cross-context behavioral advertising, or processing of your personal data for purposes of targeted advertising (as those terms are defined by applicable state law). ‍ Right to Withdraw Consent: Where we have collected or used your personal information based on your consent, you have the right to withdraw your consent at any time. ‍ Right to Appeal: If we deny your request to exercise any of the rights described above, you may have the right to appeal that decision by submitting a request to appeal to us. ‍ Right to Non-Discrimination: We will not discriminate against you for exercising any of your state privacy rights. However, we may still offer you certain financial incentives permitted under applicable state law, such as discounts, rewards, premium features, loyalty accounts, or club card programs that can result in different prices, rates, or quality levels. ‍ How to Exercise Your Rights Making Requests to Know/Access, Delete, or Correct : You may exercise your rights, as applicable by state law, by submitting a verified consumer request to know information (and to receive your personal information in a portable format), to correct information, or for deletion. ‍ The response to a request to know will provide the personal information we have collected and maintained about you, in a portable format, unless an exception under applicable state law applies. Please note that, depending on the applicable state law, we may not be required to provide personal information to you if you make multiple requests in a certain time period. ‍ You may submit a request by using our Privacy Rights Request Form available here , or by contacting us at privacyrequest@backblaze.com . We will verify your request using the information you provide through the request form or in your communication. If you submit a request that is not through one of the above designated methods or is deficient in some manner unrelated to verification, we will provide you with information on how to submit the request or remedy any deficiencies with your request. We cannot respond to your request or provide you with personal information if we cannot verify your identity or authority to make the request. We will only use personal information provided in a verifiable consumer request to verify the requestor’s identity or authority to make the request. ‍ Once we receive your verifiable consumer request, we will confirm receipt within 10 business days, or as allowed under applicable law, and describe our verification process. We will confirm receipt of your request and respond, consistent with applicable law, if we can verify your identity. Requests for deletion will require separate confirmation that you want your information deleted. We do not knowingly collect information of minors under the age of 18. ‍ Making Requests to Opt-Out; Opt-Out Preference Signals and Universal Opt-Out Mechanisms: Our use of tracking technologies may be considered a sale or sharing for targeted advertising under applicable state law. You may exercise your right to opt out of sale, sharing, or processing for targeted advertising by (1) clicking the “Your Privacy Choices” link at the bottom of our website and selecting your preferences, or (2) broadcasting an opt-out preference signal or universal opt-out mechanism (“UOOM”) that we recognize, including the Global Privacy Control (GPC) (on browsers and/or browser extensions that support such a signal). We recognize and process opt-out preference signals and UOOMs as valid opt-out requests as required by applicable state law. If you do not have a Backblaze account or are not logged into your account, your request to opt out will be linked to your browser identifier only and not linked to any account information. Because the signal is browser-specific, you will need to broadcast subsequent signals if you access our website through different devices (e.g., computers, smartphones, or tablets). You may return to the preference center at any time to review or update your cookie and tracking selections by clicking the "Your Privacy Choices" link in the footer of our website. ‍ Withdrawing Consent : Where we have collected or used your personal information based on your consent, you may withdraw your consent at any time. If your request relates to cookies, online tracking, targeted advertising, or similar technologies, you may withdraw or modify your consent by clicking the “Your Privacy Choices” link in the footer of our website and updating your preferences through the Cookie Settings link. ‍ Appealing a Denial of a Request : If we deny or decline to take action on your verified consumer request, you have the right to appeal. To submit an appeal, please email us at privacyrequest@backblaze.com within 90 days of receiving our denial. Within 45 days after receipt of your appeal, we will inform you in writing of the action taken or not taken and provide a written explanation of the reasons for our decision. If we deny your appeal, we will also provide an online mechanism or other method through which you may contact your state Attorney General or applicable regulatory authority to submit a complaint. ‍ Using an Authorized Agent to Submit a Verified Consumer Request California: Only you, or a natural person or a business entity registered with the Secretary of State to conduct business in California that you have authorized to act on your behalf, may make a verifiable consumer request related to your personal information, to opt-out of sale or sharing, or to limit the use or disclosure of your sensitive personal information. If you use an authorized agent, you may provide a power of attorney executed pursuant to California Probate Code sections 4000 to 4465. If a power of attorney that meets those provisions is not submitted, you will be required to provide the authorized agent signed permission to submit a request, verify your identity directly by submitting a verified consumer request according to the procedures in the section “How to Exercise Your Rights,” and directly confirm with us that you provided the authorized agent permission to submit the request. To submit authorized agent documentation, contact us at privacyrequest@backblaze.com . ‍ Other States: If you use an authorized agent, you may provide a power of attorney executed pursuant to applicable state law. If a power of attorney is not submitted, you may be required to provide commercially reasonable identification of your identity and evidence of your authorized agent’s authority to act on your behalf. For example, you may need to provide the authorized agent signed permission to submit a request, verify your identity directly by submitting a verified consumer request according to the procedures in the section “How to Exercise Your Rights,” and directly confirm with us that you provided the authorized agent permission to submit the request, by contacting us at privacyrequest@backblaze.com . ‍ ‍ Privacy Disclosure for Residents of the European Economic Area and the United Kingdom This section of the Privacy Policy applies if you are in the European Economic Area ( EEA ) or the United Kingdom ( U.K. ) and supplements the Privacy Policy. ‍ The Legal Basis for Processing Your Personal Information Under the General Data Protection Regulation (“GDPR”) and/or the United Kingdom General Data Protection Regulation (“UK GDPR”), we are required to have a valid legal basis for processing your personal information, and we must inform you of that legal basis. Our legal basis for collecting and using the personal information described above will depend on the specific personal information concerned and the context in which it is collected. Generally, we will collect personal information from you only when you have consented to such collection, when we need the personal information to perform our obligations under a contract with you (for example, when you create an account or use our services), or where the processing is in our legitimate business interests (for example, to detect and prevent fraud and to analyze usage for analytics, modeling, and business intelligence). In some cases, we may also have a legal obligation to collect personal information from you (for example, to verify your identity when accessing your account or services). ‍ Where we rely on legitimate interests, we balance our interests against your interests, rights, and freedoms and apply appropriate safeguards to protect your personal data. ‍ If we ask you to provide personal information to comply with a legal requirement or to enter into a contract with us, we will make this clear at the time we request that personal information. We will also tell you whether providing that personal information is mandatory or not (as well as the possible consequences if you do not provide your personal information). Similarly, if we collect and use your personal information, we will provide you with our legitimate business interests for such collection and use. ‍ If you have questions about or need further information concerning the legal basis for which we collect and use your personal information, please contact us as provided in the Contact for More Information section below. ‍ Data Storage, Transfers, and Security We use industry-standard methods of securing electronic databases of personal information. However, you should know that no company can fully eliminate security risks associated with personal information. To help protect yourself, please use a strong password, do not use the same password to access your Backblaze account that you use with other accounts or services, and protect your usernames and passwords to help prevent others from accessing your accounts and services. ‍ Your personal information may be transferred to and processed in the United States and other countries where Backblaze and its service providers operate, which may have data protection laws that differ from those in your jurisdiction. ‍ Where required by law, we implement appropriate safeguards for such transfers, including contractual protections and other legally recognized mechanisms. While your information is outside of your country of residence, it is subject to the laws of the jurisdiction in which it is held and may be subject to disclosure to governments, courts, law enforcement, or regulatory agencies pursuant to applicable law. ‍ Your Data Protection and Privacy Rights and Choices If you reside within the EEA or in the U.K., you have the following rights under applicable law, which you can exercise at any time: Right of access: You can access your personal information that we collect. Right to rectification: You can correct, update, or delete your personal information and associated data by logging into your account or contacting us as provided in the “Contact for More Information” section below. Right to erasure: You can request deletion of your personal information, subject to certain exceptions. Right to restrict processing: You can ask us to restrict the processing of your personal information where, for example, you contest the accuracy of the data or object to our processing. Right to data portability: Where applicable and technically possible, you can request that we provide your personal information in a structured, commonly used, and machine-readable format. Right to object: You can object to the processing of your personal information where we rely on legitimate interests as our legal basis. Right to withdraw consent: Where we have collected and processed your personal information with your consent, you can withdraw your consent at any time. Withdrawing your consent will not affect the lawfulness of any processing we conducted prior to your withdrawal, nor will it affect the processing of your personal information conducted in reliance on lawful processing grounds other than consent. Right to opt out of marketing: You have the right to opt out of marketing communications we send you at any time. You can exercise this right by using the unsubscribe link provided in each email. Please note that even after you opt out, you will still receive service and transactional communications from us. Right to lodge a complaint: You have the right to complain to a data protection authority about our collection and use of your personal information. See the Data Protection Authorities section below for contact details. Please see the Exercising Your Privacy Rights section below to exercise your privacy rights. ‍ We will respond to your request within 30 days of receipt. Where a request is complex, or we have received a large number of requests, we may extend this period by a further two months, as permitted under applicable law. If we extend the response period, we will inform you within 30 days of receiving your request and explain the reason for the delay. We will not charge a fee for responding to your request unless the request is manifestly unfounded or excessive, in which case we may charge a reasonable fee or decline to respond. ‍ Accessing Your Data If you have an account, you may log in to access, update, or delete your personal information and associated data. If you are unable to access your account, you may contact us using the information provided in the Contact for More Information section below. ‍ Object or Restrict Data Processing In cases where we rely on your consent to process personal information, you can revoke your consent by contacting us. Revoking your consent does not affect the lawfulness of any processing conducted prior to your withdrawal. ‍ You may manage your cookie and tracking preferences through the cookie and tracking preference center, which may be accessed by clicking the Cookie Settings link in the footer of our website or through any other cookie settings mechanism made available on the Platform. Please note that cookie and tracking preferences are generally browser- and device-specific, and data collected before we can identify or authenticate you may not be able to be associated with your account. ‍ Profiling and Automated Decision-Making Backblaze does not make decisions about you that produce legal effects or similarly significant effects based solely on automated processing, including profiling. In particular, we do not use automated decision-making to make decisions about your eligibility for services, pricing, or access to functionality. This does not prevent us from using personal information for ordinary business purposes, such as analytics, lead management, marketing segmentation, customer relationship management, fraud prevention, security, or service improvement, where such processing does not produce legal or similarly significant effects concerning you. ‍ Data Protection Authorities If you are not satisfied with how we handle your personal information, or with our response to a request you have made, you have the right to lodge a complaint with the relevant data protection authority in your jurisdiction. You may contact the applicable authority by clicking below: European Economic Area (EU DPAs) United Kingdom (Information Commissioner’s Office) Switzerland (Federal Data Protection and Information Commissioner) We encourage you to contact us first using the information in the Contact for More Information section below, so that we may address your concerns directly. ‍ Cookies and Similar Technologies Please read our Cookie Notice to learn about our practices regarding cookies and similar technologies. ‍ You may access or modify your cookie and tracking preferences at any time by clicking the Cookie Settings link in the footer of our website. The exact choices available to you may depend on your location and the laws that apply to you. ‍ Cookies: Cookies are small data files stored on your device when you visit. Cookies allow us to recognize your device during subsequent visits and personalize your experience based on your preferences. title: Garage Door Spam
body_text: Garage Door Spam – Harrison Was Here Harrison Was Here About Posts RSS Harrison Photography Garage Door Spam 16 Nov, 2026 In the beginning, my garage door opener worked fine. When the door opened or closed, I would get a notification. If I'm away from home and the door opens, something weird is going down. The "myQ" app generally worked although it was encrusted with ads: I continued using it because I trusted that notifications were meaningful... ...until recently (October 2026): This is un-fucking-acceptable. As in, absolutely fucking not. The manufacturer (Chamberlain) cut off third-party access to its APIs (via myQ) in late 2023. In response, I purchased a pair of ratgdo32 devices to opt out of the bullshit. ratgdo is a WiFi control board for your garage door opener that works over your local network using ESP Home or HomeKit The device is a ~$62 board from ratcloud llc running open-source firmware that wires to the opener's existing terminals and speaks LiftMaster's Security+ 2.0 protocol locally. These were easy enough to hook up. I won't reproduce the instructions here. The bundle included six black wires, an auxiliary harness I didn’t need. My router hands each board a fixed address at 192.168.0.192 and 192.168.0.245. Apple's HomeKit just worked and I'm able to control them with voice commands: “Hey Siri, open Door 1” When I was growing up, my father wired a mercury switch onto our garage door that lit up a light in the hallway when we'd left the garage door open. This was a valuable signal that helped our family avoid accidentally leaving the door open overnight. Since the ratgdo32 has a JSON status endpoint, I was able to rebuild Dad's solution in software with Slack: The script runs at night checking for an open door: */10 21 -23,0-5 * * * garage-watch The repo maintainer made my day when I submitted a tiny pull request : "Simple and useful. Happy to merge this. Thank you." Both boards are now reachable over my Tailscale network, so my monitoring software can load /healthcheck. This required a custom route: /Applications/Tailscale.app/Contents/MacOS/Tailscale set \ --advertise-routes = 192 .168.0.192/32,192.168.0.245/32 After approving the route, my monitoring software can verify the hardware is working. Everything runs locally with no cloud, and notifications now say who opened the door which myQ never did. To anyone at Chamberlain responsible for myQ, I offer my sincerest Fuck You. title: If you stop writing code, you also get worse at reviewing it
body_text: If you stop writing code, you also get worse at reviewing it · cekrem.github.io cekrem.github.io learnelm.dev Jesus!? About Recommended Books Podcast (🇳🇴) Blog If you stop writing code, you also get worse at reviewing it November 20, 2026 4-minute read AI • Software Craftsmanship • Coding-as-Craft Whatever skill you’re learning, it won’t take long before someone with experience in that particular field tells you to get your hands dirty. It’s fine to read “Born to Run”, but you won’t be running an ultra marathon any time soon if you don’t start running. Whether it’s muscle memory, technique, physical fitness or problem solving you need to work on to reach your goals, you need to practice . This isn’t a controversial statement in any field at all , and has never really been. Except in software engineering, somehow. When it comes to software engineering, we somehow lost our way, thinking that our skills won’t stop improving if we stop practicing . Making such a claim in any other field would be sneered at at best. Imagine John Scofield 1 saying he stopped practicing his guitar because “he was at a good enough level, musically, to maintain (and even improve!) his expertise” simply by 1) instructing others on how to play (either in vibe general terms, or with a strict spec musical notation), and then 2) listening to what they played and iterating until it sounded good enough for his next record. “My music is better”, he would claim, and moreover “actually playing the guitar was never the point anyway, there’s more to making music.” Mind you, my point in this post is not to discuss the short term quality of code output (or recorded guitar playing, to continue the proverbial thread), but rather the skill of the craftsman practicing his craft vs the one who doesn’t practice at all. To make another comparison that’s arguably closer to software engineering, or at least the “writing and reasoning about code” part of it, let’s look at authors in other fields. I have no doubt that reading great prose has the potential to nudge a writer towards better writing of his/her own; in fact it’s super important to have creative references to draw upon - no doubt at all. But, imagine an author who 1) stopped writing, and only pursued reading and giving feedback to other writers, and worse yet 2) mostly read AI generated prose !? To be perfectly honest, I would expect a quite steady (if not exponential) decline of this author’s writing skills. “There’s more to software engineering than writing code” Link to heading Sure. But if we can at least agree that the code that runs our software is a non-trivial part of it (though, granted, not all of it by far: The other parts of developing and maintaining software speak even louder against using generative AI as a significant tool service! ), we should aspire to be proficient in understanding how code works, what good code looks like, what to watch out for and how software architecture plays a vital part in making code Easy To Change. Simply “reviewing all the code Claude produced” won’t quite cut it. And who are you trying to fool, after all; at this point you’re not really reading half of it, are you? So I propose something that used to be a no-brainer: Keep practicing! Which brings me to my next point: All engineers(!) need to be good at solving problems Link to heading if || while you can argue that the need for being hands-on on your software’s code varies, I propose you can’t argue that we’re still solving problems . And the moment you stop practicing solving problems is the moment you stop getting better at it, just like everything else. Simple as that. This is hardly new, btw: you could always tell who beat Doom using cheat codes and who finished the game the real way! If the end goal is to “beat the game”, then by all means cheat; if the end goal is getting good at it , then I’d advice you not to. Some lessons are only learned the hard way (trial and error ), and very few are learned without effort at all . Repeated LLM usage for problem solving pounds the following premise into our brain’s wiring: If something is hard, tricky or requires effort, you shouldn’t even try. And right there goes our learning, craft and joy, right out the window. In a world where people are using AI to summarise books instead of reading them and turning to AI for therapy , I don’t want to keep using it. It feels like such a slippery slope. As literacy and numeracy rates decline , I can’t help but question whether encouraging us to rely on AI so heavily is a good idea . It makes me wonder: are we still thinking for ourselves at all? — Em’s blog 2 , emphasis mine. Please, John Scofield, don’t stop playing your guitar!   ↩︎ I’m not sure who Em is, but their blog is great!  ↩︎ © 2021 - 2026 Christian Ekrem

title: Unauthenticated remote code execution in Nginx
body_text: Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution in NGINX: CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007 | Wiz Blog Wiz Platform Solutions Pricing Resources Customers Company Sign in Under attack? Get a demo Blog Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution in NGINX: CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007 Two critical HTTP/2 flaws can allow attackers to compromise NGINX servers, putting the websites, APIs, and sensitive data they handle at risk. Watch the Threat Briefing Webinar Nir Ohfeld , Tomer Schwartz November 18, 2026 | Executive Summary Wiz Research, Ikotas Labs, Metnir, Rapid7, and Xint independently uncovered two critical remote code execution vulnerabilities in NGINX, software used to receive and route traffic to production applications and APIs. NGINX is a common default for the front door of modern web architectures, where it handles HTTPS and routes incoming traffic to the right application or API. As the world's most widely used open-source web server , it powers more than 225 million websites . Successful exploitation could let attackers take control of affected NGINX servers, steal sensitive data, tamper with websites, or disrupt services. The vulnerabilities, tracked as CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007, are both rated Critical, with a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2. The flaws are in NGINX itself. Websites and APIs can be exposed even when their own application code is secure. Both vulnerabilities require HTTP/2 to be enabled on the affected NGINX server. Additional conditions are described below. CVE-2026-123007 affects versions dating back to NGINX 1.9.5 in 2015. We reported our findings to F5, the company behind NGINX, and collaborated with its security team on remediation and coordinated disclosure. Organizations should identify affected deployments and apply the security updates when released. We recommend updating affected NGINX deployments to the latest release which includes multiple security fixes. Responsible disclosure timeline October 21, 2026: Wiz reports the HTTP/2 use-after-free vulnerability, later assigned CVE-2026-123633, to F5, including confirmed remote code execution with an ASLR bypass and a proposed fix. F5 confirms that another research team had previously reported the same vulnerability. November 10, 2026: F5 supplies a patch for CVE-2026-123633 for review. November 16, 2026 : Wiz reports the second HTTP/2 vulnerability, later assigned CVE-2026-123007, to F5. November 17, 2026 : F5 confirms that the second report matches CVE-2026-123007 and is included in the planned November 18 security release. November 18, 2026: F5 security release and coordinated public disclosure. Overview Wiz Research, Ikotas Labs, Metnir, Rapid7, and Xint independently uncovered CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007, two critical unauthenticated remote code execution vulnerabilities in NGINX, and reported them to F5, the company behind NGINX. Successful exploitation can compromise the server running NGINX, allowing attackers to execute code, steal sensitive data, tamper with websites, or disrupt services. NGINX often handles traffic for several applications, so a single affected deployment can put multiple services at risk. The flaws are in NGINX itself and can affect websites even when their own application code is secure. Both vulnerabilities require HTTP/2 to be enabled on the affected NGINX server. Our testing of CVE-2026-123007 demonstrated code execution on NGINX serving ordinary static files, without a backend application or third-party modules. Wiz Research used Wiz Atlas , the harness powering Wiz’s AI Code scanning solution , to discover both vulnerabilities. Our researchers used Gemini 4 Carbon and ChatGPT 5.6 Sol to validate the impact of both vulnerabilities, confirming that each could allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute code on the server. We reported our findings to F5 and worked with its security team on remediation and coordinated disclosure. The integer underflow vulnerability dates back to NGINX 1.9.5 in 2015, meaning it had been hiding in the code for more than a decade. The use-after-free vulnerability had been there for nearly six years. Like the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities we reported last month and Java4Shell , disclosed yesterday by Calif, these are memory-safety flaws that have historically been extremely difficult to discover and exploit. Finding them often requires tracing subtle interactions between memory operations and multiple code paths. For years, that complexity itself created a practical barrier. AI is fundamentally dissolving that barrier. As AI models get better at following those interactions, both researchers and attackers can uncover longstanding flaws in software that powers the internet and modern applications. The fact that multiple independent research teams uncovered the same vulnerabilities in both PHP and NGINX, after they had remained in the code for years, makes this shift particularly striking. And as AI capabilities advance, each new generation of models may uncover even more complex vulnerabilities that were previously beyond practical reach. Complexity can no longer be relied upon as a barrier to discovery or exploitation. This changes not only which vulnerabilities can be found, but how quickly longstanding risks can become real threats. Over time, finding and fixing these flaws can harden the software we all depend on. In the near term, faster discovery and a shorter window between disclosure and exploitation add to an already demanding workload for security teams. Turning a published fix into protection in production still takes substantial manual work, from validating patches to coordinating rollouts with service owners. We recommend focusing on how quickly you can reduce exposure in production. Identify deployments running the affected version and configuration, prioritize those an attacker can reach, and apply mitigations while patches are tested and rolled out. In this post, we explain the vulnerabilities and their impact, and provide mitigation and detection guidance. Organizations should identify affected deployments and apply the security updates as soon as they are available. If upgrading is not immediately possible, temporarily disable HTTP/2. What is NGINX? NGINX is the world's most widely used open-source web server , powering more than 225 million websites . It is commonly used as a reverse proxy in front of websites and APIs. In this role, NGINX accepts incoming requests, forwards them to the appropriate application server based on its configuration, and returns the response to the user. NGINX can also serve web content directly and act as a load balancer , distributing traffic across multiple servers. A single NGINX deployment can serve several applications, making it a shared entry point for the websites and APIs behind it. The Vulnerabilities Both vulnerabilities are memory-safety issues in how NGINX handles HTTP/2 traffic. In CVE-2026-123633, a connection's memory is freed while a request still needs it, creating a use-after-free. In CVE-2026-123007, incorrect flow-control accounting leads to an invalid memory copy. Each can lead to unauthenticated remote code execution on the NGINX server. Tracking ID The bug What an attacker can achieve CVE-2026-123633 HTTP/2 connection use-after-free Execute arbitrary code on the NGINX server without authentication. CVE-2026-123007 HTTP/2 send_window integer underflow Execute arbitrary code on the NGINX server without authentication. Both vulnerabilities require HTTP/2 to be enabled, but their additional requirements differ. CVE-2026-123633 affects reverse-proxy processing when available connection slots run low. CVE-2026-123007 can also affect NGINX serving content directly, as demonstrated in our testing over HTTPS on 64-bit systems. Typical memory safety mitigations such as ASLR do not protect against these issues, as attackers can use either vulnerabilities for memory read access prior to code execution. Impact On affected NGINX versions with HTTP/2 enabled, these vulnerabilities can allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary code on the server. The flaws are in NGINX itself. Exploitation does not depend on a bug in the website or API behind it, so applications with secure code can still be exposed. For CVE-2026-123007, we demonstrated remote code execution on a server serving ordinary static files, without a backend application or third-party module. An attacker could use this access to run commands, steal sensitive data, tamper with websites, or disrupt services. Because one NGINX deployment can serve several applications, the impact could extend across multiple websites and APIs. Illustrative deployment: an attacker exploits NGINX to run code on the server, putting the applications and data it serves at risk. Coordinated disclosure We reported both vulnerabilities to F5 and collaborated with its security team on remediation and coordinated disclosure. We also shared proposed fixes. Ikotas Labs, Metnir, Rapid7, and Xint also independently discovered and reported these issues to F5. We thank the F5 and NGINX teams for their work on the fixes. Vulnerabilities Addressed in the Release F5's security release addresses several other vulnerabilities in NGINX. Below is a summary of these additional CVEs, as well as the two critical HTTP/2 remote code execution flaws detailed in this post (captured in the first two rows of the table): CVE Description Impact CVSS Affected Versions CVE-2026-123007 Memory corruption in HTTP/2 flow control Exploitable in default configurations with HTTP/2 enabled 9.2 1.9.5-1.31.8 CVE-2026-123633 UAF in HTTP/2 Exploitable configured with HTTP/2 as a proxy server 9.2 1.19.7-1.31.8 CVE-2026-121810 UAF in HTTP/3 Exploitable configured with HTTP/3 as a proxy server 9.2 1.25.0-1.31.8 CVE-2026-123634 UAF during response processing in DNS resolver RCE when attacker controls upstream host name 9.2 0.6.18-1.31.8 CVE-2026-113425 UAF in mail proxy module RCE when configured as a mail server proxy with auth_http 9.2 0.5.33-1.31.8 CVE-2026-118899 Infinite loop while reading client request body Potential denial-of-service when server supports TLS 1.3 8.7 1.13.0-1.31.8 CVE-2026-120993 NULL pointer dereference Denial-of-service when configured with proxy_protocol v2 6.9 1.31.4-1.31.8 CVE-2026-125283 Buffer overflow when using alias with try_files Theoretical RCE in uncommon nginx.conf configuration 6.9 0.9.6-1.31.8 CVE-2026-123640 Insufficient validation in stream ssl_preread SSRF-like access when configured with ssl_preread 6.9 1.15.2-1.31.8 CVE-2026-120967 Client certificate bypass Client certificate bypass in specific SNI configurations 6.3 1.25.5-1.31.8 Mitigation and detection Identify affected NGINX deployments with HTTP/2 enabled and upgrade to a release that fixes both vulnerabilities as soon as it is available. Product CVE and first affected version or branch Fixed releases NGINX OSS CVE-2026-123633: 1.19.7 1.30.7 stable; 1.31.9 mainline NGINX Plus CVE-2026-123633: R33; 37.0.0 37.0.7.1; 37.2.0.1 NGINX OSS CVE-2026-123007: 1.9.5 1.30.7 stable; 1.31.9 mainline NGINX Plus CVE-2026-123007: R33; 37.0.0 37.0.8.1; 37.3.0.1 If you cannot upgrade immediately, temporarily disable HTTP/2 on affected NGINX instances: Set http2 off; in affected server blocks on NGINX 1.25.1 or later, and remove the http2 parameter from any listen directives . Test application compatibility, reload NGINX , and confirm the old workers have exited. Re-enable HTTP/2 after upgrading. Investigate unexpected NGINX worker crashes or commands launched by NGINX; these are general warning signs, not confirmed indicators of these vulnerabilities. Technical deep dive CVE-2026-123633: An active connection marked as reusable NGINX keeps a list of connections that it can close when it needs room for new ones. An HTTP/2 connection can join this list when it has no active requests, but must leave it when a request starts. We start by sending only part of a HEADERS frame, which carries an HTTP/2 request's headers. With no active request streams, ngx_http_v2_handle_connection() marks the connection as reusable while waiting for the rest: ngx_reusable_connection(c, 1); if (h2c->state.incomplete) { return; } When we send the rest of the frame, ngx_http_v2_create_stream() creates a request stream and increments h2c->processing . However, it does not remove the connection from the reusable list. We now have a request being processed on a connection that NGINX still considers safe to close. Triggering the use-after-free Next, we need NGINX to close this connection while the request is still running. Forwarding the request to an application server can trigger this. Opening an upstream connection calls ngx_get_connection() . When free connection slots run low, ngx_drain_connections() selects reusable connections to close. Our HTTP/2 connection is still on that list, so NGINX can select it while processing its own request. Before closing it, NGINX tries to send a GOAWAY frame to notify the client. Even creating this frame can fail, for example, if NGINX has reached its internal frame limit for the connection and has no frame available for reuse. In that case, the error path closes the connection and frees the memory associated with it. Processing then resumes in the original request, which still uses that memory. We have reached the use-after-free. From use-after-free to remote code execution The freed memory can now be reused for other data. The request-processing code still follows its old pointers, treating the new contents as the original request or connection. This use-after-free can lead to unauthenticated remote code execution on the NGINX server. CVE-2026-123007: HTTP/2 send_window integer underflow Returning credit for unsent data HTTP/2 allows several requests, called streams, to share one connection. Flow control limits how much response data NGINX can send before the client is ready to receive more. NGINX tracks the connection's remaining allowance in a counter called h2c->send_window . When NGINX queues response data, it subtracts that data's size from the counter before sending it. If a stream is canceled while its data is still queued, ngx_http_v2_filter_cleanup() removes the unsent data and returns the unused allowance: h2c->send_window += window; This refund does not check HTTP/2's maximum allowed window. If the client has already increased the allowance while data was waiting to be sent, the refund can push the counter above that maximum. NGINX is now tracking a value the rest of its HTTP/2 code assumes cannot occur. A bounds check that no longer works The next problem is in ngx_http_v2_state_window_update() , which checks whether an increase would exceed the limit: if (window > NGX_HTTP_V2_MAX_WINDOW - h2c->send_window) The check subtracts the current allowance from the maximum to calculate how much room remains. But the refund has already pushed the allowance past that maximum. Because the calculation uses an unsigned integer, which cannot represent a negative number, the subtraction wraps around and underflows to a very large positive value. The check now treats an invalid counter as though it has plenty of room left and allows further increases. From an invalid length to remote code execution The invalid counter eventually reaches ngx_http_v2_send_chain() , where it is converted to the signed integer type off_t to calculate how much data to send. A sufficiently large value becomes negative. That negative length then reaches the code that describes a portion of a response buffer, leaving its end pointer before its start pointer. When the TLS send path in ngx_ssl_send_chain() processes this malformed buffer, further signed and unsigned conversions turn the invalid length into an out-of-bounds memory copy. An attacker can use this to disclose memory, corrupt the heap, and lead to unauthenticated remote code execution on the NGINX server. We confirmed remote code execution with an ASLR bypass on official NGINX 1.31.7 and 1.31.8 builds. The tested path used HTTP/2 over TLS on 64-bit systems serving response data from memory. Ordinary static files can reach this path through standard TLS processing, without a backend application or third-party module. Exploitation To confirm these vulnerabilities, Wiz Research built proof-of-concept exploits and managed to run them in multiple lab settings against servers running common NGINX configurations we’ve seen in customer environments. In the interest of customer protection, we will not be releasing these exploits at this time. Like other memory-safety issues, such vulnerabilities are difficult to exploit remotely and require the attacker to disclose memory addresses, groom and shape the heap correctly, and handle different NGINX versions, builds, and configurations. In reality, attackers may not need to target every single configuration, and we have seen in PHP2Shell that widespread attacks initially start against packaged products where many customers use the exact same build and configuration. Motivated attackers may tailor exploits for specific targets. Any exploit assumes the attacker is able to communicate directly with the affected NGINX server. CDNs and WAFs that terminate HTTP/2 may mitigate parts of the exploit by not reflecting the exact payload back to the underlying NGINX server. This depends on implementation. Specifically, CVE-2026-123007 requires the attacker to send a large number of WINDOW_UPDATE records to increase it to an arbitrary value. Detection rules covering long standing HTTP/2 connections sending large amounts of data may hint at an attack associated with this vulnerability. CVE-2026-123633 has different exploitation constraints and is more likely to be exploited when NGINX is configured in proxy configuration. How Can Wiz Help? Wiz customers can use the pre-built query and advisory in the Wiz Threat Center to search for vulnerable instances in their environment. Conclusion With NGINX handling traffic for critical websites and applications, the impact of flaws in its core extends far beyond a single service. This research is another example of AI uncovering critical vulnerabilities in widely deployed infrastructure. The flaws were already there; AI helped us find them. As we saw with PHP2Shell , AI is changing the economics of vulnerability research. The same capabilities that help defenders uncover flaws can also help attackers investigate them. Software that has been used and reviewed for years still needs to be examined as these tools improve. The opportunity is to make this work routine: finding vulnerabilities in the software organizations depend on and working with maintainers to fix them. Our collaboration with F5 brings that approach to NGINX, helping protect the applications and services behind it. Stay in touch Hi there! We are Nir Ohfeld and Tomer Schwartz from the Wiz Research Team ( @wiz_io ). We are a group of veteran white-hat hackers with a single goal: to make the cloud a safer place for everyone. We focus on finding new attack vectors in cloud software and uncovering isolation issues in the systems organizations depend on. We would love to hear from you on X or at research@wiz.io . The Vulnerabilities Impact Coordinated disclosure Vulnerabilities Addressed in the Release Mitigation and detection Technical deep dive CVE-2026-123633: An active connection marked as reusable Triggering the use-after-free From use-after-free to remote code execution CVE-2026-123007: HTTP/2 send_window integer underflow Returning credit for unsent data A bounds check that no longer works From an invalid length to remote code execution Exploitation How Can Wiz Help? Conclusion Stay in touch Critical NGINX and Java4Shell: Technical Threat Briefing with Wiz Research Join us for a 20-minute technical briefing on the critical NGINX and Java4Shell vulnerabilities disclosed over the past 24 hours. Watch the Webinar Continue reading CVE-2026-114938 OpenJDK RCE (Java4Shell): Everything You Need to Know Tomer Schwartz , Merav Bar November 17, 2026 Detect and mitigate Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), a critical 9.2 RCE vulnerability affecting OpenJDK and major Java-based applications. The package gets almost 200k downloads a month. The malicious versions have since been quarantined.
