title: PostgreSQL 19
body_text: PostgreSQL: Release Notes Home About Download Documentation Community Developers Support Donate Your account November 19, 2026: PostgreSQL 19 Released! Quick Links Documentation Manuals Archive Release Notes Books Tutorials & Other Resources FAQ Wiki Release Notes PostgreSQL 19.0 E.1. Release 19 Prev   Up Appendix E. Release Notes Home   Next E.1. Release 19 # E.1.1. Overview E.1.2. Migration to Version 19 E.1.3. Changes E.1.4. Acknowledgments Release date:  2026-11-19 E.1.1. Overview # PostgreSQL 19 contains many new features and enhancements, including: New REPACK command that reclaims disk space and reorganizes table contents, which can improve query performance. REPACK (CONCURRENTLY) allows repacking without blocking reads and writes to the table. pg_plan_advice extension for controlling query planner decisions and pg_stash_advice extension that applies plan advice automatically based on the query. Better performance in many areas, including automatic scaling of the number of I/O worker processes, quicker foreign-key checks, and further planning and execution optimizations. Logical replication can now be enabled without a server restart when wal_level is set to replica . Logical replication of sequence values . Support for “ read-your-writes ” consistency on standbys via the new WAIT command. Parallel autovacuum of table indexes and autovacuum prioritization through a new scoring system. The above items and other new features of PostgreSQL 19 are explained in more detail in the sections below. E.1.2. Migration to Version 19 # A dump/restore using pg_dumpall or use of pg_upgrade or logical replication is required for those wishing to migrate data from any previous release. See Section 18.6 for general information on migrating to new major releases. Version 19 contains a number of changes that may affect compatibility with previous releases. Observe the following incompatibilities: Add server variable password_expiration_warning_threshold to warn about password expiration (Gilles Darold, Nathan Bossart) § The default warning period is seven days. Issue a warning after successful MD5 password authentication (Nathan Bossart) § The warning can be disabled via server variable md5_password_warnings . MD5 passwords were marked as deprecated in PostgreSQL 18. Remove RADIUS support (Thomas Munro) § PostgreSQL only supported RADIUS over UDP , which is unfixably insecure. Force standard_conforming_strings to always be on in the database server (Tom Lane) § Dumps created using pre- PostgreSQL 19 versions of pg_dump or pg_dumpall , and using standard_conforming_strings = off , will not properly load into PostgreSQL 19 and later servers. Users should create dumps using PostgreSQL 19 or later versions of these applications, or use standard_conforming_strings = on . Client applications still support operations with servers having standard_conforming_strings = off , for compatibility with old servers. The server variable escape_string_warning has been removed as unnecessary. Disallow carriage returns and line feeds in database, role, and tablespace names (Mahendra Singh Thalor) § pg_upgrade will also disallow upgrading of clusters that use such names. This was changed to avoid security problems. Change the default index opclasses for inet and cidr data types from btree_gist to GiST (Tom Lane) § § The btree_gist inet / cidr opclasses are broken because they can exclude rows that should be returned. pg_upgrade will disallow upgrading of clusters with btree_gist inet / cidr indexes. Disallow system columns from being used in COPY FROM ... WHERE (Tom Lane) § The values of such columns were not well-defined. Change a json_array() call which returns no rows to return an empty JSON array (Richard Guo) § This previously returned NULL . Cause transactions to pass their READ ONLY and DEFERRABLE status to postgres_fdw sessions (Etsuro Fujita) § This means READ ONLY transactions can no longer modify rows processed by postgres_fdw sessions. Change default of max_locks_per_transaction from 64 to 128 (Heikki Linnakangas) § Lock size allocation has changed, so effectively settings must now be doubled to match their capacity in previous releases. Remove server variable io_workers (Thomas Munro) § This has been replaced by four new variables; see Section E.1.3.1.2 . Change JIT to be disabled by default (Jelte Fennema-Nio) § Previously JIT was enabled by default, and activated based on optimizer costs, but this costing has been determined to be unreliable. This change requires sites that are doing many large analytical queries to manually enable JIT . Change parallel vacuum leaders and workers to share the cost-based vacuum delay limit (Bharath Rupireddy) § Previously each worker process slept based only on the cost it incurred itself, so a parallel vacuum could consume several times the budget set by vacuum_cost_limit . With this change, VACUUM with parallel workers and cost-based delay enabled might run slower than in previous releases. Rename column sync_error_count to sync_table_error_count in system view pg_stat_subscription_stats (Vignesh C) § This is necessary since sequence errors are now tracked separately. Rename wait event type BUFFERPIN to BUFFER and rename wait event BufferPin to BufferCleanup (Andres Freund) § Remove wait event BufferContent and add more precise wait events BufferShared , BufferShareExclusive , and BufferExclusive (Andres Freund) § Change index access method handlers to use a static IndexAmRoutines structure, rather than dynamically allocated ones (Matthias van de Meent) § Remove optimizer hook get_relation_info_hook and add better-placed hook build_simple_rel_hook (Robert Haas) § Change psql 's \crosstabview command to honor the \pset null setting (Chao Li) § Change full text search and pg_trgm to use the database's locale provider for character classification when parsing text (Jeff Davis) § Previously, characters were classified using libc, regardless of the locale provider. In databases with a locale provider other than libc (e.g., ICU , builtin ) and where the locale configured through that locale provider behaves differently from the LC_CTYPE setting configured for the database, particularly a LC_CTYPE of C , the output of some full text search and pg_trgm functions could change. When upgrading such databases using pg_upgrade , it is recommended to reindex all indexes which use full text search and pg_trgm after the upgrade, and to recompute any stored tsvector values. Change how fuzzystrmatch functions handle non- ASCII characters (Peter Eisentraut, Jeff Davis) § § dmetaphone() and dmetaphone_alt() now upper-case their input using the database's default collation rather than always using libc, and soundex() , metaphone() , and difference() now treat only ASCII letters as letters. When upgrading with pg_upgrade , it is recommended to reindex any indexes that use these functions after the upgrade. Remove MULE_INTERNAL encoding (Thomas Munro) § This encoding was complex and rarely used. Databases using it will need to be dumped and restored with a different encoding. E.1.3. Changes # Below you will find a detailed account of the changes between PostgreSQL 19 and the previous major release. E.1.3.1. Server # E.1.3.1.1. Optimizer # Allow NOT IN clauses to be converted to more efficient ANTI JOIN s when NULLs are not present (Richard Guo) § Allow more LEFT JOIN s to be converted to ANTI JOIN s (Tender Wang, Richard Guo) § Allow use of Memoize for ANTI JOIN s with unique inner sides (Richard Guo) § Allow some aggregate processing to be performed before joins (Richard Guo, Antonin Houska) § § § This can reduce the number of rows needed to be processed. Improve hash join's handling of tuples with NULL join keys (Tom Lane) § Improve the planning of semijoins (Richard Guo) § Allow Append and MergeAppend to consider explicit incremental sorts (Richard Guo) § Convert IS [NOT] DISTINCT FROM NULL to IS [NOT] NULL during constant folding (Richard Guo) § The latter form is more easily optimized. Simplify IS [NOT] DISTINCT FROM to equality/inequality operators when inputs are proven non-nullable (Richard Guo) § Perform earlier constant folding of var IS [NOT] NULL in the optimizer (Richard Guo) § This allows for later optimizations. Simplify COALESCE() and ROW(...) IS [NOT] NULL to avoid evaluating unnecessary arguments (Richard Guo) § § Simplify IS [NOT] TRUE/FALSE/UNKNOWN to plain boolean expressions when the input is proven non-nullable (Richard Guo) § Speed up join selectivity computations for large optimizer statistics targets (Ilia Evdokimov, David Geier) § Add proper optimizer statistics for functions returning boolean values (Tom Lane) § Allow extended statistics on virtual generated columns (Yugo Nagata) § Allow function pg_restore_extended_stats() to restore optimizer extended statistics (Corey Huinker, Michael Paquier, Chao Li) § § § § Add function pg_clear_extended_stats() to remove extended statistics (Corey Huinker, Michael Paquier) § Adjust the optimizer to consider startup costs of partial paths (Robert Haas, Tomas Vondra) § Allow negative values of pg_aggregate . aggtransspace to indicate unbounded memory usage (Richard Guo) § This information is used by the optimizer in planning memory usage. E.1.3.1.2. General Performance # Improve performance of foreign key constraint checks (Junwang Zhao, Amit Langote, Chao Li) § § Improve asynchronous I/O read-ahead scheduling for large requests (Andres Freund) § § § Allow io_method method worker to automatically control needed background workers (Thomas Munro) § The new server variables are io_min_workers , io_max_workers , io_worker_idle_timeout , and io_worker_launch_interval . Allow query table scans to mark pages as all-visible in the visibility map (Melanie Plageman) § Previously only VACUUM and COPY ... FREEZE could do this. Allow autovacuum to use parallel autovacuum workers (Daniil Davydov) § § The maximum number of workers is controlled by server variable autovacuum_max_parallel_workers and per-table storage parameter autovacuum_parallel_workers . Allow TID Range Scans to be parallelized (Cary Huang, David Rowley) § Improve COPY FROM performance for text and CSV input using SIMD CPU instructions (Nazir Bilal Yavuz, Shinya Kato) § Improve NOTIFY to only wake up backends that are listening to specified notifications (Joel Jacobson) § Previously most backends were woken by NOTIFY . Change wal_compression equals on to use the best WAL compression method available (wenhui qiu) § Previously this always used pglz . Change the default TOAST compression method from pglz to the more efficient lz4 (Euler Taveira) § This is done by changing the default for server variable default_toast_compression . Improve performance of internal row deformation (David Rowley) § Improve performance of repeated UTF-8 case-folding operations (Andreas Karlsson) § Improve performance of hash index bulk-deletion and GIN index vacuuming using streaming reads (Xuneng Zhou) § § Improve sort performance using radix sort (John Naylor) § Improve timing performance measurements (Lukas Fittl, Andres Freund, David Geier) § § This benefits EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, TIMING) and pg_test_timing , and is controlled via server variable timing_clock_source . Optimize plpgsql syntax SELECT simple-expression INTO var (Tom Lane) § E.1.3.1.3. System Views # Add system view pg_stat_lock and function pg_stat_get_lock() to report per-lock-type statistics (Bertrand Drouvot) § Add system view pg_stat_recovery to report recovery status (Xuneng Zhou, Shinya Kato) § § Add system view pg_stat_progress_repack to report the progress of REPACK , CLUSTER , and VACUUM FULL (Álvaro Herrera) § Add system view pg_stat_autovacuum_scores to report per-table autovacuum details (Sami Imseih) § Add vacuum initiation details to system view pg_stat_progress_vacuum (Shinya Kato) § The new started_by column reports the initiator of the vacuum, and mode indicates its aggressiveness. Add analyze initiation details to system view pg_stat_progress_analyze (Shinya Kato) § The new started_by column reports the initiator of the analyze. Add system view pg_dsm_registry_allocations to report dynamic shared memory details (Florents Tselai, Nathan Bossart) § § Add mem_exceeded_count column to system view pg_stat_replication_slots (Bertrand Drouvot) § This reports the number of times that logical_decoding_work_mem was exceeded. Add slot synchronization skip information to pg_stat_replication_slots and pg_replication_slots (Shlok Kyal) § § § The new columns are slotsync_skip_count , slotsync_last_skip , and slotsync_skip_reason . Add update_deleted column to system view pg_stat_subscription_stats (Zhijie Hou) § This reports the number of rows where updates were ignored due to concurrent deletes. This requires the subscriber have retain_dead_tuples enabled. Add sync_seq_error_count column to system view pg_stat_subscription_stats to report sequence synchronization errors (Vignesh C) § § Add stats_reset column to system views pg_stat_all_tables , pg_stat_all_indexes , and pg_statio_all_sequences (Bertrand Drouvot, Sami Imseih, Shihao Zhong) § It also appears in the sys and user view variants. Add stats_reset column to system views pg_stat_user_functions and pg_stat_database_conflicts (Bertrand Drouvot, Shihao Zhong) § § Add location column to system views pg_available_extensions and pg_available_extension_versions to report the file system directory of extensions (Matheus Alcantara) § Add backup_type column to system view pg_stat_progress_basebackup to report the type of backup (Shinya Kato) § Possible values are full or incremental . Add connecting value to system view column pg_stat_wal_receiver . status (Xuneng Zhou) § Add reporting of the bytes written to WAL for full page images (Shinya Kato) § This is accessible via system view pg_stat_wal and function pg_stat_get_backend_wal() . Add columns to system views pg_stats , pg_stats_ext , and pg_stats_ext_exprs (Corey Huinker) § Adds table OID and attribute number columns to pg_stats , and table OID and statistics object OID columns to the other two. Add information about range type extended statistics to system view pg_stats_ext_exprs (Corey Huinker, Michael Paquier) § E.1.3.1.4. Monitoring # Allow log_min_messages log levels to be specified by process type (Euler Taveira) § The new format is type : level . A value without a colon controls all process types, allowing backward compatibility. Add server variable log_autoanalyze_min_duration to log long-running analyze operations by autovacuum operations (Shinya Kato) § Server variable log_autovacuum_min_duration now only controls logging of vacuum operations by autovacuum. Enable server variable log_lock_waits by default (Laurenz Albe) § Add server variable debug_print_raw_parse to log raw parse trees (Chao Li) § This is also enabled when the server is started with debug level three and higher. Make messages coming from remote servers appear in the server logs in the same format as local server messages (Vignesh C) § These include replication, postgres_fdw , and dblink servers. Add reporting of WAL full-page write bytes to VACUUM and ANALYZE logging (Shinya Kato) § Add IO wait events for COPY FROM/TO on a pipe, file, or program (Nikolay Samokhvalov) § Add wait events for commit_delay and for WAL write and flush LSN s (Xuneng Zhou) § § Have pg_get_sequence_data() return the sequence page LSN (Vignesh C) § Add function pg_get_multixact_stats() to report multixact activity (Naga Appani) § Issue warnings when the wraparound of transaction IDs or multixacts is less than 100 million away (Nathan Bossart) § The previous warning was 40 million. Warnings are issued to clients and in the server log. E.1.3.1.5. Server Configuration # Add scoring system to control the order that tables are processed by autovacuum (Nathan Bossart) § The new server variables are autovacuum_freeze_score_weight , autovacuum_multixact_freeze_score_weight , autovacuum_vacuum_score_weight , autovacuum_vacuum_insert_score_weight , and autovacuum_analyze_score_weight . Add server-side support for SNI (Server Name Indication) (Daniel Gustafsson, Jacob Champion) § New configuration file PGDATA/pg_hosts.conf specifies hostname/key pairs. Allow OAuth validators to register custom pg_hba.conf authentication options (Jacob Champion, Zsolt Parragi) § Allow roles pg_read_all_data and pg_write_all_data to read/write large objects (Nitin Motiani, Nathan Bossart) § These roles are designed to allow non-super users to run pg_dump . Allow background workers to be configured to terminate before database-level operations (Aya Iwata) § This allows database-level operations to complete more quickly since blocking background workers can now be terminated. Allow server variables that represent lists to be emptied by setting the value to NULL (Tom Lane) § Update GB18030 encoding from version 2000 to 2022 (Chao Li, Zheng Tao) § See the commit message for compatibility details. E.1.3.1.6.  Streaming Replication and Recovery # Add WAIT command to allow standbys to wait for LSN values to be written, flushed, or replayed (Kartyshov Ivan, Alexander Korotkov, Xuneng Zhou) § § Improve function pg_sync_replication_slots() to wait for replication synchronization completion (Ajin Cherian, Zhijie Hou) § Previously, certain synchronization failures would not be reported. Add server variable wal_sender_shutdown_timeout to limit replica synchronization waits during shutdown (Andrey Silitskiy, Hayato Kuroda) § By default, senders still wait forever for synchronization. E.1.3.1.7.  Logical Replication # Allow sequence values stored in subscribers to match the publisher (Vignesh C) § § § This occurs during ALTER SUBSCRIPTION ... [ADD|SET|REFRESH|DROP] PUBLICATION . Function pg_get_sequence_data() allows inspection of sequence synchronization. Allow CREATE / ALTER PUBLICATION to publish all sequences (Vignesh C, Tomas Vondra) § This is enabled with the ALL SEQUENCES clause. Allow ALTER SUBSCRIPTION on publications to synchronize the existence of sequences on subscribers to match the publisher (Vignesh C) § This is enabled with the REFRESH SEQUENCES clause. Allow CREATE / ALTER PUBLICATION to exclude some tables (Vignesh C, Shlok Kyal) § § § § This is controlled with the EXCEPT clause, and is useful when specifying ALL TABLES . Add CREATE / ALTER SUBSCRIPTION setting retain_dead_tuples to retain information needed for conflict detection (Zhijie Hou) § § § Also add setting max_retention_duration to limit retain_dead_tuples retention. Allow CREATE SUBSCRIPTION to use postgres_fdw foreign data wrapper connection parameters (Jeff Davis) § The connection parameters are referenced via CREATE SUBSCRIPTION ... SERVER . When server variable wal_level is replica , allow automatic enablement of logical replication when needed (Masahiko Sawada) § New server variable effective_wal_level , application pg_controldata , and function pg_control_checkpoint() report the effective WAL level. Allow wal_receiver_timeout to be set per-subscription and user (Fujii Masao) § § This allows subscribers to use different wal_receiver_timeout values. Add optional pid parameter to pg_replication_origin_session_setup() to allow parallelization of SQL -level replication solutions (Doruk Yilmaz, Hayato Kuroda) § E.1.3.2. Query Commands # Allow GROUP BY to process target list subqueries that have expressions referencing non-subquery columns (Tom Lane) § Also fix a bug in how GROUPING() handles target list subquery aliases. Allow window functions to ignore NULLs with the IGNORE NULLS / RESPECT NULLS clause (Oliver Ford, Tatsuo Ishii) § Supported window functions are lead() , lag() , first_value() , last_value() , and nth_value() . Add support for INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO SELECT ... RETURNING (Andreas Karlsson, Marko Tiikkaja, Viktor Holmberg) § This allows conflicting rows to be returned, and optionally locked with FOR UPDATE / SHARE . E.1.3.3. Utility Commands # Add REPACK command which replaces VACUUM FULL and CLUSTER (Antonin Houska) § The two former commands did similar things, but with confusing names, so unify them as REPACK . The old commands have been retained for compatibility. Allow REPACK to rebuild tables without access-exclusive locking (Antonin Houska, Mihail Nikalayeu, Álvaro Herrera) § § § This is enabled via the CONCURRENTLY option. Server variable max_repack_replication_slots was also added. Allow GRANT / REVOKE to specify the effective role performing the privileges adjustment (Nathan Bossart, Tom Lane) § The GRANTED BY clause controls this. Support forward references in FOREIGN KEY constraint clauses within CREATE SCHEMA (Jian He, Tom Lane) § Allow CHECKPOINT to accept a list of options (Christoph Berg) § § § Supported options are MODE and FLUSH_UNLOGGED . Add CONNECTION clause to CREATE FOREIGN DATA WRAPPER to specify a function to be called for subscription connection parameters (Jeff Davis, Noriyoshi Shinoda) § § Add SUPPORT clause to CREATE AGGREGATE so extensions can specify support functions to optimize aggregate calls (Tom Lane) § Add memory usage and parallelism reporting to VACUUM (VERBOSE) and autovacuum logs (Tatsuya Kawata, Daniil Davydov) § § E.1.3.3.1.  Constraints # Allow ALTER TABLE ALTER CONSTRAINT ... [NOT] ENFORCED for CHECK constraints (Jian He) § Previously enforcement changes were only supported for foreign key constraints. Allow ALTER TABLE ... COLUMN SET EXPRESSION to succeed on virtual columns with CHECK constraints (Jian He) § This was previously prohibited. E.1.3.3.2.  COPY # Allow multiple headers lines to be skipped by COPY FROM (Shinya Kato, Fujii Masao) § Previously only a single header line could be skipped. Allow COPY FROM to set invalid input values to NULL (Jian He, Kirill Reshke) § This is done using the COPY option ON_ERROR SET_NULL . Allow COPY TO to output JSON format (Joe Conway, Jian He, Andrew Dunstan) § § JSON output can also be a single JSON array using the COPY option FORCE_ARRAY . Allow COPY TO to process partitioned tables (Jian He, Ajin Cherian) § § Previously COPY (SELECT ...) had to be used to output partitioned tables. This also improves logical replication table synchronization. E.1.3.3.3.  EXPLAIN # Add EXPLAIN ANALYZE option IO to report asynchronous IO activity (Tomas Vondra) § § § Add reporting of WAL full-page write bytes to EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, WAL) output (Shinya Kato) § Add Memoize cache and lookup estimates to EXPLAIN output (Ilia Evdokimov, Lukas Fittl) § This can show why Memoize was chosen. E.1.3.4. Data Types # Add the 64-bit unsigned data type oid8 (Michael Paquier) § Add more jsonpath string methods (Florents Tselai, David E. Wheeler) § They are ltrim() , rtrim() , btrim() , lower() , upper() , initcap() , replace() , and split_part() . These are immutable like their non- JSON string variants. Allow casts between bytea and uuid data types (Dagfinn Ilmari Mannsåker, Aleksander Alekseev) § Add ability to cast between database names and oid s using regdatabase (Ian Lawrence Barwick) § Add functions tid_block() and tid_offset() to extract block numbers and offsets from tid values (Ayush Tiwari) § E.1.3.5. Functions # Add date , timestamp , and timestamptz versions of random(min, max) (Damien Clochard, Dean Rasheed) § § Allow encode() and decode() to process data in base64url and base32hex formats (Andrey Borodin, Aleksander Alekseev, Florents Tselai) § § § This format retains ordering, unlike base32 . Add functions to return a set of ranges resulting from range subtraction (Paul A. Jungwirth) § The functions are range_minus_multi() and multirange_minus_multi() . This is useful to represent range subtraction results with gaps. Add function error_on_null() to return the supplied parameter, or error on NULL input (Joel Jacobson) § Allow IS JSON to work on domains defined over supported base types (Jian He) § The supported base types are TEXT , JSON , JSONB , and BYTEA . Add full text stemmers for Polish and Esperanto (Tom Lane) § The Dutch stemmer now uses a different algorithm, which changes the stems of many words; the previous algorithm is available via dutch_porter . The English, French, German, Lithuanian, Norwegian, Spanish, Swedish, and Turkish stemmers have also been updated and produce different stems for some words. Allow event triggers to be written using PL/Python (Euler Taveira, Dimitri Fontaine) § E.1.3.6.  Libpq # Add special libpq protocol parameters for compatibility testing (Jelte Fennema-Nio, Jacob Champion) § Otherwise known as protocol grease , which was active during the 19 beta period. These will no longer be sent as of the PostgreSQL 19 official release, but the parameter reservations will remain for potential use in the future. Add libpq connection parameter oauth_ca_file to specify an alternate certificate authority when communicating with OAuth providers (Jonathan Gonzalez V., Jacob Champion) § This can also be set via the PGOAUTHCAFILE environment variable. The default is to use curl 's built-in certificates. Allow libpq environment variable PGOAUTHDEBUG to specify particular debug options (Zsolt Parragi, Jacob Champion) § The UNSAFE option still generates all debugging output. Improve custom OAuth client flows (Jacob Champion) § § Previously, libpq reported only a generic error message during custom flow failures, and each flow implementation was required to calculate the issuer identifier independently. Add a new authdata hook type PQAUTHDATA_OAUTH_BEARER_TOKEN_V2 that precomputes the issuer ID and lets hooks provide error details. Add libpq function PQgetThreadLock() to retrieve the current locking callback (Jacob Champion) § E.1.3.7.  psql # Allow the search path to appear in the psql prompt via %S (Florents Tselai) § This works when psql is connected to PostgreSQL 18 or later. Dismiss alert {{ message }} openssl openssl Repository navigation Code Issues 1k ( 1k ) Pull requests 689 ( 689 ) Discussions Actions Projects Wiki Security and quality Insights More items [NSF] [CVE-2026-121481] Buffer overflow in EVP_EncodeBlock() - # 33652 # 33652 Open nmouha wants to merge 6 commits into openssl:master openssl/openssl:master from nmouha:cve-2026-121481 nmouha/openssl:cve-2026-121481 Copy head branch name to clipboard Conversation Commits 6 ( 6 ) Checks Files changed Open [NSF] [CVE-2026-121481] Buffer overflow in EVP_EncodeBlock() # 33652 nmouha wants to merge 6 commits into openssl:master openssl/openssl:master from nmouha:cve-2026-121481 nmouha/openssl:cve-2026-121481 Copy head branch name to clipboard Conversation nmouha commented Nov 10, 2026 Copy link Copy Markdown Contributor This fixes "Buffer overflow in EVP_EncodeBlock()" ( CVE-2026-121481 ) by returning -1 for invalid inputs to EVP_EncodeBlock() : NULL input or output buffers, negative lengths, and lengths for which the encoded size does not fit in an int . The OpenSSL SRT has asked for it to be fixed publicly; the advisory is still pending. Returning -1 for invalid inputs is the most straightforward fix, and matches what happens in wolfSSL's compatibility layer for OpenSSL's EVP_EncodeBlock() . I'm suggesting a similar guard for EVP_DecodeBlock() . No length limit is needed here because the decoded length always fits in an int , but it is a good idea to reject NULL buffers and negative lengths. Moreover, I propose to fix the incorrect length check in the base64encode() function of http_client.c , which rejected only len > INT_MAX . I am adding tests in test/base64_dec_avx2_test.c to cover the new behavior, and documenting the -1 returns in doc/man3/EVP_EncodeInit.pod . Exploiting this vulnerability from the command line is possible by passing a large -proxy_pass to openssl s_client . I confirmed that GOST accepts these large passwords out of the box. However, the password has to be supplied through an environment variable ( env:VAR ), otherwise the command line will be too long. Note: the pattern of CVE-2026-121481 is similar to that of CVE-2021-23840 . Checklist documentation is added or updated tests are added or updated --> Sorry, something went wrong. Uh oh! Both EVP_EncodeBlock() and EVP_DecodeBlock() can legitimately return 0, so 0 is not an error for either function. EVP_EncodeBlock() returns 0 when dlen == 0, and EVP_DecodeBlock() returns 0 when the input is empty after trimming. Also, for EVP_DecodeBlock(), the current failure paths (e.g., trimmed length not a multiple of invalid base64 characters) all return -1. So, I wanted to make sure that both EVP_EncodeBlock() and EVP_DecodeBlock() consistently return -1 on any error. As I mentioned before, returning -1 is also what WolfSSL does in its OpenSSL compatibility layer. I understand the concern that third-party callers may cast the return to size_t without checking. But are we not making things more difficult for third-party calls if both 0 and -1 can indicate errors, or if the existing EVP_DecodeBlock() errors will be changed from -1 to 0? software engineering, knowledge work, and science workflows. Koray Kavukcuoglu SVP, Google DeepMind and Chief AI Architect, Google Share x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link In this article Gemini 4 Neon is available Delivers across enterprise, analytical, and scientific work Built for production-ready code Brings efficiency and control to production-grade workflows Built for fast, low cost, frontier-level cyber defense Designed for safe, dependable execution Built for deeper analysis Start building with Gemini 4 Neon today Today, we’re introducing Gemini 4 Neon — bringing frontier-level intelligence with fast end-to-end task completion across complex software engineering, knowledge work, and science workflows. Neon ranks ahead of comparable models and #3 overall with a score of 61 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at its xhigh thinking level, landing just behind larger, slower models. On the Vals Index , Neon ranks #2 and lands on the Pareto frontier. Beyond just pushing on raw model capability, we’re continuing to make our models better to work with, Neon ranks #2 on steerability (adapting cleanly to mid-task user corrections) on the new Agent Arena Index . Neon also excels at multi-step instruction following and builds on our ongoing progress to curb fabrication, recording our lowest fabrication rate yet in internal Google Antigravity testing. The model is priced at $3 per million input tokens ($0.15 per million cached input tokens, a 95% discount) and $15 per million output tokens, with a 1 million-token context window. Gemini 4 Neon is rolling out today in the Gemini API in Google AI Studio , Gemini for business (via API and model dropdown), for paid Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in Google Antigravity , and for Pro and Ultra subscribers in the Gemini app . Delivers across enterprise, analytical, and scientific work Enterprise work lives in spreadsheets, PDFs, charts, audio, and video. Neon can synthesize across all of these inputs in a single 1 million-token context window and turns inputs into structured deliverables. Independent evaluations rank Neon as one of the top models and on benchmarks like the Vals Index , it ranks #2 (70.9%), and reaches #1 on both the Legal Research Bench and Tax Agent Bench . Neon also shows strong wins across categories on Surge AI , ranking #1 on most benchmarks across finance, accounting, spreadsheet modeling, and complex constraint following. It also scores 73.5% on Chartography for reading dense professional charts and performs on par with leading models on Agents' Last Exam v1.1 (75.8%). It achieves #1 overall on both Zapier’s AutomationBench (56.3%) and Andon Labs' Vending-Bench 2 ($16,843), a long-horizon simulation of running a business. Finally, it debuts #2 globally with a score of 1336 on Arena's new Agent Arena Index across 4,200+ real-world agent sessions. On scientific and mathematical reasoning, spanning quantitative analysis, mathematics, and technical research problems, Neon is best in class on Terminal-Bench Science (70.5%), RiemannBench (84.0%), and HLE-Diamond (71.3%). Built for production-ready code Engineered for long-running agent workflows, Neon sustains performance through complex, tool-heavy tasks end-to-end — whether running standalone or acting as a fast, high-judgment Orchestrator directing parallel Hydrogen subagents in Google Antigravity. It cuts down on redundant file reads, shares progress as it works, and handles context compaction reliably in long sessions. Across core developer and researcher workflows, Neon achieves frontier performance and is competitive with the leading models in its class, ranking #1 overall on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index (58.6), with a score of 65.2% on Terminal-Bench 4.1 and 46.2% (at its default high setting) on FrontierCode 2.0 . For production-ready code, Neon handles multi-file debugging and refactoring across repositories with targeted, surgical edits. On SWE-sweep, it already leads on the mini-SWE harness (12.8%) and more than triples to a state-of-the-art 39.0% in Google Antigravity showing what the Antigravity harness unlocks. Driving Blender MCP in Google Antigravity, Gemini 4 Neon used /swarm to build a photorealistic 3D lab bench visualizing the model names with elemental accuracy pairing Bunsen flames for Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Hydrogen with high-voltage gas discharge tubes for Gemini 4 Argon and Neon. In Google Antigravity, Gemini 4 Neon wrote a first-person WebGL2 freeride ski simulator from scratch on real Mont Blanc and Chamonix elevation terrain — combining 10,200 lines of custom shaders, 120 Hz ski physics across six alpine lines, dynamic carved tracks, slab avalanches, and spatial Web Audio with zero pre-made assets. Using /swarm in Google Antigravity, Gemini 4 Neon pulled archival photos to recreate Alan Turing’s 1936 study at King’s College, Cambridge in interactive 3D — from King’s Chapel outside to Room X.8 inside, complete with a working Universal Turing Machine running on his desk. In Google Antigravity, a Gemini 4 Neon agent swarm turned a single image into a 100,000-cell Google Sheet with zero embedded images and zero Apps Script — using over 500,000 live spreadsheet formulas to run edge detection, map 3D depth, and relight the scene across six interactive modes. Brings efficiency and control to production-grade workflows We’re refining thinking levels with each new model release to give teams finer control and a smoother progression from one tier to the next. Neon’s four levels scale steadily, letting teams dial intelligence and token spend to what each workload needs. Neon delivers high performance at a lower cost per task across third-party benchmarks. At its default high thinking level, it pairs a high Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index score with a 32% lower cost per task than Carbon. It also sits on the Pareto frontier on both the Vals index and Agent Arena at high, with roughly 50% to 80% lower cost per task than top competing frontier models. xhigh thinking adds deeper, multi-step reasoning for the hardest engineering, analytical, and scientific workloads. Neon shows its highest intelligence score here, while still costing 36%+ less per task than competing models at their highest setting. Built for fast, low cost, frontier-level cyber defense As agentic coding scales, generating secure code from the start is critical. Gemini 4 Neon produces more secure code than Carbon across all easy, medium, and hard challenges on AutoBaxBench , achieving state-of-the-art on the hard tier (76%). Securing systems also means proactively finding flaws before attackers do. Penetration testing has served as a cornerstone of enterprise cybersecurity. On WebExploitBench v1.2 , Neon is state-of-the-art (51.26%) at half the cost of competing large models. To fortify existing code, Neon for cyber delivers frontier-level performance across the code hardening lifecycle — vulnerability finding, validating, and patching — all while being faster and more cost efficient than large frontier models. Finding code vulnerabilities: Neon achieves state-of-the-art performance on SEC-bench Pro (90.5%), while costing roughly half as much per challenge. Validating risk through exploitation: To prioritize which vulnerabilities to remediate, defenders rely on models to check which vulnerabilities are exploitable. On ExploitGym, it achieves frontier-level performance using half the tokens of Carbon. Patching vulnerabilities: Fixing the root cause of vulnerabilities is a critical step in the cybersecurity defense lifecycle. Neon reaches 70.7% on Collinear’s CWE-bench v2 , driving a 3.4% uplift over Carbon. Gemini 4 Neon for cyber is rolling out to trusted defenders in the coming days as part of the Fairwind Program . Designed for safe, dependable execution Gemini 4 Neon builds on improvements from our Gemini 4 safety and security stack — maintaining Gemini 4 Carbon-level protections against severe misuse and prompt injection while advancing further on model alignment and agentic behavior. For a model meant to carry demanding, long-running work in production, we concentrated on: Mitigating frontier misuse safety risks: Because Neon brings frontier-level capabilities to a faster, lower-cost model, we paired it with strong real-time safeguards against cyber and biosecurity misuse comparable to our Carbon protections, while declining far less legitimate work in these areas, refusing for instance just 1.98% of tasks on Terminal-Bench 4.0 and 0% on Terminal-Bench-Science. Advancing alignment and disciplined model behavior: In internal coding use, alert rates from our chain-of-thought and action misalignment monitor remained below the already low baselines set by Carbon, suggesting improved alignment propensity for Neon — and that same monitor is deployed to protect Neon across external surfaces. Neon is trained to complete multi-step work without cutting corners, fabricating results, or overstepping user boundaries — continuing to improve the balance between following through on requests and staying within scope. It matched Carbon with 0.0% cheating on Terminal-Bench 4.0 and took shortcuts on just 2.45% of tasks on our coding cheating evaluation (the lowest rate of any Gemini 4 model). It also achieved a 0.09% misaligned action rate on our agentic safety suite and a 99.2% pass rate on our agent honesty evaluation. On our agentic behavior evaluation, Neon builds on Carbon’s strong baseline by further reducing under-service by 43%–56% and overreach by 15%–35% across different effort levels. Protecting users from indirect prompt injection attacks: On Gray Swan's IPI benchmark, Neon is more resilient than other models in its class when malicious instructions are planted in the web pages, emails, documents, or code it accesses. We found that with real-time safeguards at its highest thinking level, Neon resisted every attack within this Gray Swan benchmark, matching the 0.0% attack success rate reached only by other Gemini models. For more details, see the Gemini 4 Neon model card . Built for deeper analysis In the Gemini app, Gemini 4 Neon excels at work that requires frontier-level reasoning and fast responses. Higher-quality writing and knowledge work: Neon writes clearly, with well-structured responses and a natural, direct tone. It reads uploads like spreadsheets, PDFs, and photos more precisely, turns dense material into helpful reports and summaries, and pulls in relevant details from Google apps like Gmail and Docs. Reliable research and analysis: Neon frequently incorporates details from sources across the web to keep responses current for fast-moving topics like comparing pricing across vendors before a major purchase or pulling together a complex brief with the latest market data. Faster help for tougher tasks: Tasks in Gemini can now run on Neon, working through complex, multi-step jobs more quickly and efficiently than with larger models. Get more done while stretching usage limits further when handing off tedious to-dos, like analyzing billing statements to spot why a utility charge spiked or cross-checking multiple receipts and documents to negotiate a refund. Where Neon sits in the Gemini 4 family Neon is built for complex coding, analytical reasoning, and production-grade enterprise workflows. While Carbon tackles your hardest, long-horizon projects and Hydrogen handles fast everyday execution, Neon balances depth and efficiency. Neon delivers frontier-level reasoning for complex, high-frequency workflows faster and more cost efficiently. Start building with Gemini 4 Neon today Gemini 4 Neon begins rolling out today: For developers: Build with the Gemini API paid tier in Google AI Studio and Android Studio , if you’re a paid Google AI Pro or Ultra subscriber, you can try Neon in Google Antigravity and all Pro and Ultra subscribers can try it in AI Studio. For enterprises: Use Gemini 4 Neon in Gemini for business (via the API or model drop-down) and Google Antigravity. For consumers: If you’re a Google AI Pro or Ultra subscriber, you can select Gemini 4 Neon from the model drop-down in the Gemini app . For cybersecurity defenders: Eligible Fairwind Program members will begin receiving access over the next few days. To request access to the Fairwind Program, contact your Cloud account team. title: "I can tell you wrote this yourself"
body_text: "I can tell you wrote this yourself" – Em's Blog Em's Blog Home Blog What I'm Doing Now Photo Guestbook "I can tell you wrote this yourself" 19 Nov, 2026 Those were some of the first words my honours project supervisor said to me last week when we met to discuss a progress report I had written to mark the midway point of the project. It's a roughly 10-page report on the control of flapping-wing micro aerial vehicles - which is probably very boring unless you're particularly interested in that. I accidentally set the due date for the report a week early in my calendar, so after spending 48 hours stressed and pumping out 5,000 words, citing references and adding diagrams 1 , I was pleasantly relieved to find I'd tricked myself into being quite productive. I had a lot of time to get my supervisor to review the report and action his feedback. When he told me he could tell I wrote it myself, I wasn't sure how to take it. A compliment? An insult? Then he followed it up with: "I've been sent a lot of reports written by AI." At first this shocked me. Our reports are limited to 10 pages - so the appendices are getting a big workout around here - how hard is it to write 10 pages yourself? But then I thought about what the last year of my engineering degree has been like. Assignment documents that start with "you are strongly encouraged to explore the use of AI" which quickly turns into the clear understanding that you aren't just encouraged but expected to use it. That you're disadvantaged by not using it. The hardest class of my degree was spent in a brick-walled windowless computer lab prompting an AI for eight hours a day. The reason why we've been pushed to use it? Apparently it's the way the industry is going. Apparently actually knowing things doesn't matter nearly so much as knowing how to prompt a machine to do the thing. Apparently the future of engineering - at least in my field - is to become a glorified babysitter. The AI isn't going anywhere, they say, so it's best we learn how to manage it well. But sitting in a room telling an AI "ignore the approaching deadline, we still have 8 hours, keep working" isn't exactly filling me with enthusiasm for the rest of my career. It's soul crushing, and I don't want to outsource so much of my thinking to it. In a world where people are using AI to summarise books instead of reading them and turning to AI for therapy , I don't want to keep using it. It feels like such a slippery slope. As literacy and numeracy rates decline , I can't help but question whether encouraging us to rely on AI so heavily is a good idea. It makes me wonder: are we still thinking for ourselves at all? Because I worry that it starts with using it for an assignment when you're encouraged to, but then it turns into relying on it to write a 10-page report on a project you should know back-to-front. A project that you'll have to present and defend in person when it finishes. And then you're asking it for advice, using it to summarise books, turning to it for anything you would normally look up or ask a friend. The internet is riddled with AI content that is making it increasingly more difficult to tell fact from fiction. In a world where everything is so polarised and deliberately provoking, the ability to identify bias or motivation in the content we consume has perhaps never been more important. Being able to think for ourselves has perhaps never been more important. As the tech world continues to offer us increasingly more opportunities to automate things, I'm practically begging you to please not automate your thinking. Read the books. Write the papers. Search for answers instead of asking AI. Ask a friend. Ask your mum about the mystery illness you're convinced you're developing and then take her advice and try drinking a glass of water. Think about what the creators of the content you consume want you to think 2 . Treat the things you consume like the Year 7 English class where you were taught how to identify persuasive techniques. Think about things as much as possible. Please just don't get the AI do it for you. On a more positive note, here's some recent good things: Got to see a tawny frogmouth up close recently - in the middle of the day! One has nested in a tree near the university's engineering precinct. Finished my final assessment for the semester today! Officially only one semester to go! Went and saw 'You Can See Everything' with Han last week and I can't stop talking and thinking about it. If you've seen it, please talk to me about it. If you haven't seen it, please go and see it! Felt homesick the other day and made Mum's scalloped potatoes recipe! SO good. The weather has been beautiful lately. Morning runs and walks have been extra fun. The other morning I ran past a guy walking barefoot through the park with a CAT in his backpack. Made plans with Bec & Han to see 'Sunrise On The Reaping' next Monday - no spoilers if you've already seen it! Keen to talk about it after then. Anyhow, happy almost-weekend! -- Em Subscribe via RSS or email below! LaTeX is painful. ↩ I think what I want you to think here is probably pretty obvious. ↩ Toast this post   Powered by Bear ʕ•ᴥ•ʔ

How about making an animation of a LEGO house building itself? Or making a realistic render â¦ Show more Have you ever wondered how objects from our daily lives are designed? How can we generate a computer 3D model of a mug, a bottle of Diet Coke, or a Saturn V rocket? What about designing the blades of a jet engine? A test dummy? How about making an animation of a LEGO house building itself? Or making a realistic render of a bowl of fruit? In this workshop, you will learn skills to design all these and much more! How to CAD Almost Anything introduces students to CAD (Computer-Aided Design) through various fun examples focused on reverse engineering. In contrast to traditional mechanical design courses, this workshop emphasizes the design process itself, understanding how to plan and best leverage our available tools to arrive at our desired result. Thus, the sessions are less about following the instructions on an engineering drawing and more about independent thinking and strategizing, such as reverse engineering an object into a 3D model. Come and learn how to CAD almost anything! title: Java4Shell: RCE in OpenJDK when processing Base64
body_text: Java4Shell: Write once, RCE everywhere Skip to content calif .io Calif Research ↗ CVE-2026-114938 Java4Shell Write once, RCE everywhere Story by the New York Times A memory-corruption vulnerability in OpenJDK's Base64 decoder. A remote attacker with no credentials can overwrite heap memory, read it in the style of Heartbleed, and reach remote code execution. Begin ↓ Technical write-up ↘ Check your servers ↘ Recommendations ↘ The Story 01 Overview 02 Write once, RCE everywhere 03 Wait, Java has a memory-corruption vulnerability, in Base64?! 04 Era of the centaur hacker 05 The tragedy of the commons 06 A call for vibe-uncoding After we disclosed PHP2Shell , we realized many people didn't know what PHP was. So we decided to go after something a little more familiar: Java. Today, we are disclosing Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), a memory-corruption vulnerability in OpenJDK's Base64 decoder. OpenJDK is the most popular Java runtime. Under CVSS 4.0, this vulnerability scores 9.2 out of 10 (CRITICAL). While PHP is a high-level web technology, Java sits much deeper. Java is the world's third most popular programming language , powering 90% of Fortune 500 companies . It is the beating heart of the modern economy. Banking, aviation, telecommunications, nearly every critical sector runs on Java, including national security systems. Base64 is a very common way of representing binary data as text. It is used in authentication protocols, to encode file uploads, and to deliver network messages. To decode Base64 faster, OpenJDK uses specialized x86-64 CPU instructions to process many bytes at once. We discovered a bug in that optimized machine-level code that lets malformed input overwrite neighboring memory. With careful exploitation, the corruption can reveal sensitive memory, as Heartbleed did, or lead to remote code execution. The corruption itself can be triggered by just 64 A characters followed by a single = : Copy AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA= In older OpenJDK 17, the trigger input is 128 of A followed by = . Write once, RCE everywhere Our initial testing demonstrated remote code execution in the following widely deployed Java applications, in their default configs. Pre-auth RCE: Keycloak Atlassian Jira Atlassian Confluence JFrog Artifactory Jenkins PingFederate Post-auth RCE: Apache Kafka Broker Apache Solr Elasticsearch Gerrit Spinnaker The lists are non-exhaustive. We also demonstrated RCE in sample applications built on widely used frameworks, including Apache Struts and Spring Boot. Ordinary features such as authentication and file uploads can expose the vulnerable Base64 decoder, extending the potential impact far beyond the products we tested. samczsun also shared a client-side exploit with us. A Java program that opens a TLS connection to a malicious server can be compromised, even if it exposes no service of its own. Here is a demo video of the exploits running: Wait, Java has a memory-corruption vulnerability, in Base64?! Yes. First time? Memory corruption is the most common class of vulnerability on the Internet. But one of Java's biggest selling points is memory safety. Java manages memory on developers' behalf and checks memory accesses, protecting applications from the memory-corruption bugs common in other software. But like PHP and many other technologies, much of Java itself is written in low-level languages like C, C++, and, in this case, assembly, where memory corruption is still a part of life. To speed up Base64 decoding, OpenJDK uses specialized AVX-512 VBMI instructions on supported x86-64 processors. The bug sits in the hand-rolled assembly code that handles the final few characters. For the 65-character input above, OpenJDK allocates a 50-byte result array. After decoding the first 64 characters, the routine mishandles the stray = and calculates a negative output length. That invalid length becomes a full 64-byte write, sending 62 bytes past the end of the array. Java eventually rejects the input, but by then neighboring objects may already be corrupted. Era of the centaur hacker As with PHP2Shell, Calif used AI to find and weaponize Java4Shell. AI brings the horsepower. Our researchers bring the context. The best hacker today is neither AI nor human. It is the centaur hacker , part human, part AI. It took our own Quang Luong an hour to discover the vulnerability, and two more hours to develop the first working exploit. The total token cost was less than $200. One thing to note about this vulnerability is that there is no universal exploit. Depending on how Base64 is used and how the application works, different steps may be required for exploitation. Calif was able to accelerate the exploit development by spending initial effort building pipelines and strategies, then directing AI agents to use those for initial exploitation. Afterwards, most of the later chains are built almost autonomously with AI. The tragedy of the commons Java is one of many shared software stacks we all rely on. Over the years, it has grown to serve many different needs. Each feature request may make sense on its own, but everyone inherits the added complexity. Those who need a feature get the benefit. Everyone else carries the code and its risks, even if they never use it. Java4Shell is a concrete example. The Base64 optimization helps applications that decode enormous amounts of data. But the code ships to everyone else too, including applications that gain little from it. On affected systems, an optimization few applications needed became a serious security risk. Features can be useful, and most bugs can be fixed. But why do we have to worry about code we never needed in the first place? A call for vibe-uncoding If you don't need something, there is little reason to keep it running in your systems. Do you need that hand-rolled assembly Base64 decoder to process a few hundred bytes? Probably not. Earlier this year we found Squidbleed , an older cousin of Heartbleed, hiding in the Squid proxy since 1997. The bug was in Squid's FTP module. But who uses FTP anymore? It's a dead protocol and should be removed. Removing code is harder than it sounds. An apparently unused feature may have hidden dependencies. Someone has to understand what can be removed, make the change, and test what remains. This is where AI can help to make that work practical at a scale we could not previously afford. The same centaur hacker that discovered PHP2Shell and Java4Shell can comb a large codebase and flag dead code, bloated features, and needless optimizations. We call this vibe-uncoding : identify the parts a system actually needs, then remove everything else to reduce its attack surface. With AI, everyone is asking, “What can we build?” But maybe the right question for security is, “What can we delete?” The Write-up 01 The Tail of Base64 02 Discovery 03 The vulnerability 04 Exploitation strategy 05 Heap Feng Shui (Grooming) 06 Remote Heap Feng Shui 07 Warm-up, rehearsal, and retries 08 Limitations 09 PoC 10 Affected products 11 Recommendations 12 Disclosure timeline 13 Credits The Tail of Base64 By Quang Luong On affected OpenJDK builds, malformed Base64 data can cause a constant-value overwrite of allocated heap memory. Through remote Heap Feng Shui, we turn that overwrite into a heap leak and remote code execution. Discovery A few months back, I was developing a 0-click exploit on a certain phone vendor. The bug was constrained: it is a linear out-of-bounds write and we have no way to bypass ASLR. I almost considered it unexploitable until I audited the Android Runtime. Turns out, it has some predictable memory allocation pattern and if you align the registers from the starting memory corruption just right you can make the runtime interpret attacker's bytecode. Lesson learned Complicated system interactions are hard, and this complexity can make exploiting hard bugs easy. After completing that exploit chain, inspired (and bored), I decided to look into something completely different. So I pulled the official JVM implementation (OpenJDK HotSpot) and started auditing. Java is a mature platform, so I was aware that having a "good" bug here would be hard, but I wanted to give it my best attempt anyway. Recalling my earlier lesson that complex systems and code crossing multiple boundaries are difficult to get right, I focused the audit on the JIT compiler, intrinsics, widely accessible APIs, and cryptography. Well, more precisely, I told Codex to look at those areas like any serious security researcher in 2026. To be honest, I didn't expect to find anything trivially exploitable, perhaps only some logic flaws or side-channel issues. Most early results Codex brought me were slops, either unreachable or the requirement of exploitation is not realistic at all. This looks like a gamble I am going to lose. But you know what, fortune favors the bold. So I just prompted harder... Eventually, Codex brought me a finding for a memory corruption in the Base64 decoder itself. I came looking for copper and found gold, through sheer persistence. But wait, is it really gold, or just fool's gold? Note That sheer persistence is prompting AI and ignoring slops for around 20 minutes, by the way. The vulnerability The issue lies in OpenJDK HotSpot's x86-64 Base64 intrinsic. C2 is the most aggressive JIT compiler in the Java Virtual Machine. Specifically, if you trigger a function repeatedly, then it will compile that function into native code. Even then, ordinary native code itself is not fast enough. Modern CPUs have specialized instructions that allow processing data even faster. HotSpot uses them in optimized routines called intrinsics. The x86-64 Base64 intrinsic miscalculated the padded tail's store mask, causing an out-of-bounds write. The x86-64 Base64 intrinsic iterates through the input in 256-byte blocks; if it is less than 256, then it will do so in 64-byte blocks. When the input is less than 64 bytes, it uses evmovdqub , the intrinsic for the VMOVDQU8 instruction. This instruction takes a 64-bit mask that decides which bytes are read from or written to memory. The mask is first calculated from the input and output length, then updated to reflect the number of padding bytes ( '=' ) in the Base64-encoded string. This is shown in the following (pseudocode): Copy // Zero High Bits Starting with Specified Bit Position input_mask := bzhiq(-1, input_length) output_len := (input_length / 4) * 3 // handle padding if input[input_length - 1] == '=': output_len -= 1 input_mask >>= 1 if input[input_length - 2] == '=': output_len -= 1 input_mask >>= 1 output_mask := bzhiq(-1, output_len) In the above code, if the remaining input is of the form =, ==, X=, X==, XY= , or === , then output_len will be computed as zero. However, since there is padding, output_len is decremented, resulting in an underflowed value of -1 or -2 . Since bzhiq(-1, output_len) doesn’t change any bits if output_len >= 64 , this results in output_mask == -1u64 . Later the code uses evmovdqub to read and write multiple bytes at a time. For a write, if the mask bit is 1 , the byte at that index in the vector register is written to memory. So when output_mask == -1u64 , all 64 bytes are written during the following operation: Copy evmovdqub( Address(dest, dp) /* Address: destination address addr */, k1 /* k1 == output_mask */, tmp /* XMMRegister src register/value to write */, true, Assembler::AVX_512bit /* vector length */ ); The generated stub returns the number of bytes it successfully decoded, and returns early when it detects invalid input. The remaining bytes are handled by the Java code, which throws IllegalArgumentException if the input is invalid. At runtime, the decoded buffer length is calculated as (ceil(inp_len / 4) * 3) - padding . When the bug is triggered, with 65 bytes ( [64 bytes] + '=' ) as input, that calculation allocates a 50 -byte buffer. During decoding the bug makes output_mask == -1 for evmovdqub , so 64 bytes are written starting at offset 48 , an out-of-bounds write past the end of the buffer. On OpenJDK 17, the trigger input is 'A' * 128 + '=' instead of 'A' * 64 + '=' , because the length threshold to reach the code path is higher. Exploitation strategy The Base64 bug was gold, but not the type that sits on the riverbed waiting to be panned out. It was the type that was deep, dark, and hard to access. While we had memory corruption, exploiting it looked difficult, perhaps even borderline unexploitable, since it only wrote fixed bytes to the heap. Only the landing position of the out-of-bounds write is controllable. We get the following 64 bytes write starting from the position in buffer where the remaining sets of Base64 decoded bytes would have been written to: Fully controlled write to byte 0 (in bound) 4-bit controlled write to byte 1 (in bound) Uncontrolled write to bytes [2, 63]. For bytes 48..63 , the value will always be 0x9a . The uncontrolled out-of-bounds write turned out not to be a big problem. We reused a common JavaScript engine exploitation primitive, the classic technique of overwriting a buffer length. We call the buffer whose length we overwrite the writer . Once its length is corrupted, it keeps accepting our chosen bytes, so if we place another array or object after it, we can corrupt that neighbor with all of our chosen values. That upgrades the fixed write into a bounded, chosen-value linear write. If we then corrupt another array's length and its data is copied back into the response, we have built a heap disclosure primitive, the reader , from the out-of-bounds read. At this point, before any code execution, we already had JavaBleed, the ability to leak contents from the Java heap, which may hold PII, private keys, other secret keys, and tokens. From the writer and reader , the rest of this write-up builds the full attack. We repair the objects the linear write damaged to keep the JVM running, mount data-only attacks on application logic, and escalate the bounded write into arbitrary writes that reach the Code Cache and JVM hooks for code execution. But first things first, we need to align the heap to our advantage. Alternative strategy Other alignments conceptually exist (e.g. type confusion, registers control from GC itself). Due to time constraints, we have not researched them deeply, and this strategy generalized well enough for our cases. Give us a shout if you invent something new. Heap Feng Shui (Grooming) G1 divides the heap into fixed-size regions . Before the region arithmetic matters, the critical arrays have to leave their threads' private allocation ranges. HotSpot normally gives each Java thread a thread-local allocation buffer (TLAB) , a private slice of Eden. Objects created by different request threads advance different cursors, which gives us no useful order between a Base64 decoder in one TLAB and a writer in another. The first grooming layer controls the allocation route. The critical array's size and the space left in the worker's TLAB decide whether HotSpot refills that TLAB or takes the attacker-preferred outside-TLAB allocation path . The second layer controls the layout. However, we do not choose how G1 allocates memory, and we don't know the current heap state. To approach this limitation, Calif used the tried and tested method of Spray and Pray. Object sizes and padding fix offsets inside region-sized spans. We spray several live writer and reader pairs to give the decoder output several possible neighbors. When its region lands immediately below a writer region, the widened reader produces a larger application response. We discard misses and retry until successful. One early challenge during exploit development was that the AI would get stuck during heap grooming primitive development. In order to save tokens and time, Calif wrote a small heap tracer and visualizer to give the agent information about the heap state, combined with our expertise on specific cases. Remote Heap Feng Shui In order to perform remote grooming, each request data would be sent up until the critical heap allocation would occur. By ensuring the data that was previously sent had a TCP acknowledgement, the exploit would have control over the allocations up to date. Once we were confident our data so far is buffered on the target, we then sent the rest, completing the http request. This allows both heap allocation control and more precise schedule as delivering small network packets is more stable than big ones. 01 / PARK THE REQUESTS PREFIX DELIVERED SHORT ENDING PARSER PADDING DELIVERED HELD WAITS WRITER DELIVERED HELD WAITS READER DELIVERED HELD WAITS DECODER DELIVERED HELD WAITS 02 / RELEASE THE SHORT ENDINGS PAD WRITER READER PAD DECODER CONTROLS ALLOCATION TIME G1 STILL CHOOSES THE ADDRESS The exact allocation and free order schedule belongs to the targeted application profile, while we are able to control the adding, writer, reader, and decoder pieces. The current attack is sensitive to network conditions, like RTT and jitter. Low, stable round-trip times are preferred for a more reliable attack. In our controlled environment, we performed this attack over the internet through public IP addresses instead of just assuming perfect laboratory conditions. For the current attack path to achieve optimal stability and reliability in exploitation, Calif turned to physics and utilized money to solve the problem, rather than experimenting with TCP/IP stack configuration. In other words, Calif rented another VM in the same region as our target. Warm-up, rehearsal, and retries To summarize the chain so far, we will warm up the Base64 decoder to C2 tier. We can rehearse the exploit run to calibrate timing and responses against the target before causing corruption to occur. Once the required information has been obtained, we can trigger the vulnerability. Incorrect placement could cause the JVM to crash, but in many instances, we can simply try again. WARM Run valid decodes until the JIT selects the affected fast path. No memory is corrupted. REHEARSE Optional safe round for calibration. TRIGGER Send the malformed tail. If the objects line up, the fixed spill enlarges the writer. DISCLOSE Continue the writer so chosen bytes enlarge the reader, then collect the response-derived heap bytes. REPAIR Use the disclosed originals to restore temporary headers and untouched neighbors when the chain has a repair path. FINISH Make the application-specific change and verify it through a live request. Limitations Request streaming. Some current grooming profiles need partial request bodies to reach the application. A proxy that waits for the complete body removes their release timing. nginx buffers request bodies by default . Request buffering is not a general mitigation. Elasticsearch runs from one complete request, so this setting does not stop that chain. After a configured WebSocket upgrade , later frames pass through a tunnel and request-body buffering no longer applies to them. Application profiles. There is no universal payload. Each chain needs a decoder route, a live writer, a returned reader or another feedback path, a heap layout, and an application action. Every target needs a bespoke profile. The exploit is not a universal point-and-shoot. PoC Here is a self-contained proof of concept. It warms the Base64 decoder until the vulnerable intrinsic is used, then decodes the malformed 64 × "A" + "=" input into a 4096-byte array. On an affected JDK it prints REPRODUCED : the decoder rejects the input, but 62 bytes (offsets 50 to 111) past the decoded output have already been overwritten. Every write lands inside a real array, so the trigger is safe to run. Copy import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets; import java.util.Arrays; import java.util.Base64; /** Bounded standalone trigger: every write stays inside a real 4096-byte array. */ public final class Base64Trigger { private static volatile int sink; public static void main(String[] args) { Base64.Decoder decoder = Base64.getDecoder(); byte[] valid = "A".repeat(64).getBytes(StandardCharsets.US_ASCII); byte[] malformed = ("A".repeat(64) + "=").getBytes(StandardCharsets.US_ASCII); byte[] target = new byte[4096]; for (int i = 0; i < 200_000; i++) { sink += decoder.decode(valid, target); } Arrays.fill(target, (byte) 0x5a); boolean rejected = false; try { decoder.decode(malformed, target); } catch (IllegalArgumentException expected) { rejected = true; } int changed = 0; int first = -1; int last = -1; for (int i = 50; i < target.length; i++) { if (target[i] != (byte) 0x5a) { changed++; if (first < 0) first = i; last = i; } } System.out.println("runtime=" + System.getProperty("java.runtime.version")); System.out.println("vm=" + System.getProperty("java.vm.name")); System.out.printf("rejected=%s changed=%d first=%d last=%d%n", rejected, changed, first, last); if (!rejected || changed != 62 || first != 50 || last != 111) { System.err.println("NOT REPRODUCED"); System.exit(1); } System.out.println("REPRODUCED"); } } We are holding back the application-specific exploits for now. This write-up covers the vulnerability and the general exploitation technique. The weaponized chains for individual products stay private until everyone has had a chance to upgrade. We will publish them later. Affected products Java4Shell affects OpenJDK from version 17.0.6 or newer. Because they are built from OpenJDK, the following Java distributions are also vulnerable: Amazon Corretto Eclipse Temurin Microsoft Build of OpenJDK Azul Zulu BellSoft Liberica SAP SapMachine Red Hat OpenJDK Oracle OpenJDK Oracle Java SE Oracle GraalVM for JDK According to Oracle, the following Oracle Java SE versions are vulnerable: 8u511b33-perf, 17.0.21.0.3, 21.0.13.0.3, 25.0.5.0.3, 27.0.1.0.3. We thank Oracle for providing this information ahead of publication time. Because the vulnerable code is hardware-specific, Java4Shell also requires an x86-64 processor with AVX-512 VBMI support. ARM64 CPUs are not affected. These mainstream CPU families meet the hardware requirements: Intel Xeon: Ice Lake, Sapphire Rapids, Emerald Rapids, Granite Rapids AMD EPYC and Ryzen: Zen 4 or newer On Linux, you can check whether your CPU is vulnerable with this command: Copy grep -m1 '^flags' /proc/cpuinfo | tr ' ' '\n' | grep -E '^(avx512f|avx512bw|avx512vbmi|bmi2)$' The output must include all four flags. Recommendations OpenJDK released a security advisory and Oracle released a patch at 1:00pm PT on Nov 17, 2026. All Java users should update immediately. You can also mitigate Java4Shell by starting OpenJDK with either: -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics to disable hardware-accelerated Base64 encoding and decoding, or -XX:UseAVX=2 to disable AVX-512. Apply this flag only on x86-64 hosts. OpenJDK on ARM doesn't recognize it and will fail to start. Disclosure timeline This bug has an interesting history. The first public report of this bug came in June, more than four months before we independently discovered it with Codex. On October 24, our researcher Quang Luong asked Codex to audit Netty and the JVM for highly reachable vulnerabilities, with a focus on x64 intrinsics. Codex found the bug within an hour. We reviewed its tool calls in the agent transcripts and confirmed that it hadn’t looked up any existing bug reports. The bug is fairly easy to trigger. We wondered why it didn't cause more crashes in ordinary use. That question sent us looking through public bug reports. We found that sundarms had already hit the bug in the wild and reported it in June . In September, sundarms posted a proof of concept that reproduced the crash, and albertnetymk identified the root cause and proposed a fix in OpenJDK . The pull request saw no further activity and was eventually closed without being merged. Our team on October 26, finding the public report. By the time we found the public report, we had already reported the bug to Oracle with a PoC demonstrating post-auth remote code execution in Elasticsearch. When Oracle asked for more information, we shared two more PoCs demonstrating pre-authentication RCE in Jenkins and Keycloak. On November 9, we pointed Oracle to the public report and asked to begin coordinating disclosure. Java4Shell followed a pattern we'd seen with PHP2Shell. The bug had already been reported, but it was patched only after we showed it could be exploited. Here's the timeline as we understand it. All dates are in 2026, Pacific Time. Date Event June 9 sundarms hit the bug in the wild and opened an Adoptium support issue . September 8 sundarms posted a proof of concept that reproduced the crash . albertnetymk identified the root cause that same day. September 9 albertnetymk proposed a fix in openjdk/jdk#32781 . October 24 Quang Luong of Calif independently discovered the bug with Codex. October 24 Quang reported the bug to Oracle with a PoC demonstrating post-auth RCE in Elasticsearch. October 26 Dion Blazakis of Calif asked, “why doesn't it crash much under normal operation?” That same day, Quang found sundarms's original report . October 29 Oracle responded to Quang's report and asked for more information. October 31 Quang shared PoCs with Oracle demonstrating pre-auth RCE in Jenkins and Keycloak. November 9 Bruce Dang of Calif told Oracle, “Given this bug's criticality, impact, and the fact that it is actually public (although people do not realize it), we want to begin the disclosure coordination process.” November 13 Oracle notified Calif it had fixed the bug and would release the patch at 1 p.m. Pacific Time on November 17. November 14–17 Calif notified government agencies and industry partners. November 16 Calif and Oracle met for the first time to discuss the severity of the bug and the fix. November 17 Oracle released the fix and credited albertnetymk and Quang Luong. Calif published this write-up the same day. November 19 Calif added this timeline. Credits Research, write-up and exploits by Quang Luong of Calif. Original bug report by sundarms and albertnetymk. Exploit improvement by Jenish Rakholiya of Calif. Artwork by Michal Zalewski of Calif. Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938) was found and reported by Calif.io .   See also PHP2Shell and Squidbleed .

title: Ruby2ßhell: Pre-authentication RCE on stock Rails
body_text: Ruby2Shell (CVE-2026-132825) | Veria Labs Blog Sign in Get a demo ruby2Ãhell Ruby2Shell is a one-byte heap overflow to remote code execution in Ruby's string case conversion. Reachable without authentication in the default configuration of common Ruby web frameworks and self-hosted software. Severity Critical Fixed in 3.3.14, 3.4.13, 4.0.10 Access needed Network, no authentication CVE CVE-2026-132825 GHSA-34m4-m9fh-gqp5 Affected software Ruby versions Ruby series Affected Fixed in 4.0 4.0.0 to 4.0.9 4.0.10 3.4 3.4.0 to 3.4.12 3.4.13 3.3 3.3.0 to 3.3.13 3.3.14 3.2 and older All releases back to 2.4.0 EOL Frameworks The bug is reachable from the following frameworks in their default configuration . Other frameworks are not exposed by default, but application code that upcases strings received in a legacy encoding may also be vulnerable. Framework Status on an affected Ruby Rails Affected Sinatra (classic style) Affected Other frameworks and plain Rack Not exposed by default Self-hosted software These products bundle their own Ruby, so the fix has to come from the vendor. Products marked Vulnerable have no fixed release yet: every current version is vulnerable. Software Affected versions Fixed in Status GitHub Enterprise Server 3.22.5 and earlier None Vulnerable Chatwoot 4.20.0 and earlier 4.20.1 Patched GitLab 19.6.0 and earlier 19.6.1 , 19.5.8 , 19.4.10 Patched Mastodon 4.7.5 and earlier 4.7.6 , 4.6.12 , 4.5.22 , 4.4.29 Patched OpenProject 17.9.7 and earlier 17.9.8 , 17.8.3 Patched Discourse base image Before 2.0.20261119-0203 2.0.20261119-0203 Patched Updated 21 November 2026 at 03:52 UTC . Remediation Your deployment Upgrade Ruby to a fixed release: 3.3.14 , 3.4.13 or 4.0.10 . Self-hosted software Install the vendor's fixed release. See Self-hosted software for fixed versions of popular products. Technical details Root cause Most of Ruby's single-byte encodings have no capital Ã . Upcasing it writes two bytes, SS , but the loop only bounds-checks one ( to < to_end ). 1 while ( * pp < end && to < to_end) { /* room for one byte */ 2 code = * ( * pp) ++ ; 3 if (code == SHARP_s) { 4 if (flags & ONIGENC_CASE_UPCASE) { 5 * to ++ = 'S' ; /* first byte */ 6 code = 'S' ; 7 } 8 /* ... */ 9 } 10 /* ... */ 11 * to ++ = code; /* second byte, unchecked */ 12 } The output buffer is allocated as the input length plus 20 bytes. Each Ã adds one byte to the output, so an input with 21 of them overflows the buffer by one byte. The same loop is in several ISO-8859 and Windows-125x encodings and has been there since Ruby 2.4.0. It is reached by upcase , swapcase , downcase(:fold) and casecmp? . UTF-8 strings take a different code path and are not affected. Fixed upstream in ruby/ruby@d582f8f . Primitive A one-byte heap overflow. The byte written is S ( 0x53 ) when upcasing or s ( 0x73 ) when case-folding, and it lands directly after the output buffer. The attacker controls the size of the buffer through the input length. Copying the result out of the buffer then reads one byte out of bounds. Proof of concept We'll be publishing a proof of concept demonstrating remote code execution on stock Rails on 25 November 2026 , or later if major vendors have not shipped a fix by then. Credits Veria Labs found this vulnerability independently and was the first to demonstrate remote code execution. The Ruby security advisory also credits Stephan Lipp (Ada Logics) and Anthropic with reporting the underlying primitive. Additional discoverers include Moritz Sanft in collaboration with OpenAI.
