title: Pancreatic cancer halted by virus injection in three patients
body_text: Pancreatic cancer halted by virus injection in three patients | New Scientist Advertisement Sign In Sign In Curiosity Engine Events Tours Shop Subscribe now Explore by section News Features Newsletters Podcasts Video Comment Culture Games This week’s magazine Explore by subject Health Space Physics Technology Environment Mind Humans Life Mathematics Chemistry Earth Society Explore our products and services Curiosity Engine Events Tours Shop Subscribe now Manage your subscription Check your subscription status, update your details and more. Manage your subscription Activate your subscription Your account Check your subscription status, update your details and more. Manage your subscription Your newsletters Subscriber benefits Sign out Subscribe now Health Pancreatic cancer halted by virus injection in three patients A cancer-killing virus has stopped pancreatic tumours from growing and spreading in three people in an initial safety trial, raising hopes that it may help to beat the deadly condition By Alice Klein 29 May 2026 Facebook Threads X / Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Reddit Email Print A scanning electron micrograph of pancreatic cancer cells ANNE WESTON, EM STP, THE FRANCIS CRICK INSTITUTE/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY A virus has stopped pancreatic cancer in its tracks in three people in a clinical trial in the US. Further evaluation is needed in larger trials, but the early results are encouraging, especially since only small doses of the virus were administered for initial safety testing. “We only injected one-tenth of the dose we are eventually aiming at, so the efficacy is better than I expected, especially as this is pancreatic cancer,” says Masato Yamamoto at the University of Minnesota, who led the development of the viral treatment. Read more Woman in cancer remission without treatment in highly unusual case Pancreatic cancer is notorious for being the deadliest type of the condition. One reason is that symptoms tend to appear late, when the cancer has already spread and cannot be surgically removed. Once diagnosed, people usually live only around three to six months . Advertisement Another reason is that pancreatic tumours have tough, fibrous exteriors that block chemotherapy drugs from getting in. “They’re hard as hockey pucks,” says Yamamoto. Immunotherapies that boost immune activity against cancer are also ineffective, because pancreatic tumours can hide from the immune system . The first patient in the trial, who had a pancreatic tumour 7 centimetres across, was administered the treatment a year ago, and the other two have been since then. At the time, their tumours hadn’t spread beyond the pancreas. Since being treated, their tumours haven’t grown any further. “They are all still alive and have clinically stable disease,” says Yamamoto, who presented the results at the annual meeting of the American Society of Gene and Cell Therapy in Boston, Massachusetts, earlier this month. Another 15 patients will now be given higher doses to find the optimum level. “I think this is an interesting early signal, but as a pancreatic surgeon, I think it’s important to keep perspective,” says Kai Brown at Royal North Shore Hospital in Sydney. “The history of oncology is littered with promising early signals that vanished by the time rigorous phase III [late-stage] testing was done, so I think these preliminary conference results should probably just be seen as hypothesis-generating at this stage.” He also notes that the trial so far hasn’t included a control group, so it is hard to know whether the cancer-killing virus works better than other treatments or none at all. Free newsletter Sign up to Health Check Sign up to newsletter The virus is an adenovirus that has been genetically engineered to replicate only inside tumours and not healthy tissue. Its replication is specifically activated by an enzyme called cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2), which is present at much higher levels in cancer cells than in normal ones. After cancer cells become infected with the virus, they burst open and die, releasing more virus that can infect neighbouring cancer cells. In the trial, the virus was injected directly into the patients’ tumours through a thin tube that was guided down a patient’s throat to their pancreas. The tube had an ultrasound probe on the end to allow visualisation of the tumours. The reason the tumours have stopped growing but haven’t become any smaller may be due to the low treatment dose, says Yamamoto. He thinks they may start to shrink as the virus has more time to replicate. As the tumour cells start to break apart and leak their contents, the immune system may also be able to recognise and fight the cancer, says Yamamoto. “The patient’s immune system can realise something is wrong, and then go and attack the tumour,” he says. The hope is that the immune system will also recognise and destroy any tumour cells that have spread to other parts of the body. If so, the treatment could be effective against metastatic pancreatic cancer. mRNA covid vaccines spark immune response that may aid cancer survival An analysis of patient records suggests that mRNA covid-19 vaccines boost the immune response to cancerous tumours when given soon after people start a type of immunotherapy, extending their lives To try to supercharge this natural immune response, Yamamoto and his colleagues are now planning to combine the viral treatment with immunotherapies like checkpoint inhibitors – drugs that block proteins that stop the immune system from attacking the cancer cells – in future clinical trials. Adenoviruses, which cause cold- and flu-like symptoms in their unmodified forms, have a long history of being investigated as potential cancer treatments . In the 1950s, for instance, women with cervical cancer were injected with an unmodified adenovirus in a clinical trial , with partial success. However, it became clear that adenoviruses must be engineered to make them selectively target cancer cells, for safety and efficacy reasons. The only cancer-killing virus that has been approved by the Food and Drug Administration in the US is T-VEC , a genetically modified herpes simplex virus that is injected directly into melanoma tumours, causing the cells to rupture and die. title: Pete Warden on local AI, open models, voice interfaces, the future of hardware
body_text: Why AI Wants to Be Local - The Data Exchange Skip to content The Data Exchange Bluesky Linkedin RSS YouTube Reddit 🥇 One of the Top 0.5% most popular podcasts. Menu Home About Subscribe Contact Archive Gradient Flow Why AI Wants to Be Local Ben Lorica November 19, 2026 November 19, 2026 Uncategorized Post navigation Previous Pete Warden on Local AI, Open Models, Voice Interfaces, and the Future of Hardware. Subscribe: Apple • Spotify • Overcast • Pocket Casts • YouTube • AntennaPod • Podcast Addict • Amazon • RSS . Pete Warden , co-creator of Moonshine Voice and a longtime deep learning engineer, joins me to discuss why AI increasingly wants to run locally rather than in the cloud. We explore the rapid progress of open-weight models, what it takes to run AI on laptops and in browsers, and how low-latency speech models could make voice a more natural interface. We also discuss specialized versus end-to-end models, the economics of local AI, and emerging hardware approaches that could challenge today’s GPU-centric infrastructure. [This episode originally aired on Generative AI in the Real World , a podcast series I’m hosting for O’Reilly.] Subscribe to the Gradient Flow Newsletter Interview highlights – key sections from the video version: Local AI Is More Capable Than Most People Realize Open Models, Quantization, and Running LLMs on Laptops Can Local AI Replace Cloud Models for Knowledge Work? Privacy, Personal AI, and Models Built Into Operating Systems Voice as a Computing Interface Beyond Siri and Alexa Why Latency Matters for Voice AI and User Experience How Local AI Changes the Economics of Applications Designing Voice Interfaces for Failure and Human Feedback Compound AI Versus End-to-End Speech Models Multimodal Models Versus Specialized Speech Models Running AI Models Directly in the Browser Why AI Wants to Be Local and Why Enterprises Need Control Apple, NVIDIA, and Rethinking GPUs for AI Inference High-Bandwidth Flash and the Future of AI Hardware Jump to transcript Related content : A video version of this conversation is available on our YouTube channel . Hacker News thread for this episode The local AI question I had backwards I changed my mind about world models Previewing the Debate Over Frontier AI Regulation Your Model Is Not Your Moat Richard Ho → Inside OpenAI’s First Chip Joel Hron → Why Build Your Own AI Model When Frontier Models Already Exist? Pete Warden → TinyML, Sensor-Driven AI, and Advances in Large Language Models Support our work by subscribing to our newsletter📩 Transcript Below is a polished and edited transcript . Ben Lorica. All right. Today we have an old friend, Pete Warden of Useful Sensors, and their main website is actually at moonshine.ai. If you go to the website, you’ll see that they’re very much about voice on-device, and we will definitely talk to Pete about all things speech and all things edge computing. But I do want to take advantage of Pete being one of the OG deep learning engineers to get his sense of what’s going on these days. And with that, Pete, welcome back to the podcast. Pete Warden. Thanks for having me, Ben. Ben Lorica. All right. So I would say, Pete, I don’t know if this is a fair characterization, but one of the main thrusts of your work is the whole idea that local AI does not have to be compromised. In fact, it’s something that people should take more seriously. As I mentioned, we’ll definitely talk about your work on speech models on-device. But broadly speaking, Pete, for our audience that doesn’t really follow local models, where are we for someone who wants to run a model on a laptop, not a phone, just a laptop? What’s the state of ease of use? I guess one of the obstacles is that it’s always easier to use a cloud API, right? So where are we in terms of the tooling around local AI? Pete Warden. Yeah. So at the moment, it’s like many open-source projects. Every year is going to be the year of the Linux desktop. I think there’s always going to be a bit of a lag in usability for the average user with this stuff, but I think there’s an even bigger lag in marketing because it’s very hard to make money off local models. That means the big companies like Anthropic and OpenAI, and even the big tech companies generally, aren’t going to push that. If you give them a choice between a SaaS service that you can actually make money on and this other thing where you’re not even going to know that people are using it because they’re not contacting your service, every company is going to go for the one that has an easy subscription revenue model. That means you have a massive amount of marketing around all of these tools that are basically a little text box on a website. And so it means that most people have never heard of these local models. Now, if you use something like Ollama, which is probably the most well-known, I think people will be pleasantly surprised by how straightforward it is to use and by the quality of the models. I saw some news recently that Anthropic is actually a bit concerned because people are turning to more specialized models versus always going for the most sprawling, expensive model that’s available. Local models are actually doing very well in the benchmarks. They continue to be only a few months behind the capabilities of the big commercial Anthropic and OpenAI models. But I also believe that local models have gotten to the point where they can do the things that people want to use them for. What I’m really hoping is that it’s one of those situations, for those of us old enough to remember the dot-com boom, when people were paying thousands of dollars for SPARC servers or using Microsoft IIS and paying massive amounts of money because web servers were seen as such an arcane thing. Then, of course, Apache, Nginx, and all of these alternatives, once people actually had time to look around and the alternatives had a little bit of time to improve, just wiped the floor with the commercial alternatives. I don’t know if we’re going to quite get there, but that’s the pattern I’m seeing. Ben Lorica. Yeah, my sense is that open models, whatever your definition of open is, mainly open weights, I guess, will ultimately prevail. It just seems like that makes a lot more sense to me. As you mentioned, in the early days of Linux versus Solaris, or even Postgres and MySQL versus Oracle, it was far from clear that these open-source projects would ever get to the point of us having to take them seriously. But ultimately, I think they’re such important parts of the stack that the open alternatives are what people will opt for. Speaking of which, Pete, you mentioned Ollama, right? And obviously, there are other alternatives. Let’s say, for the sake of argument, that they are in fact easy to install and use. As far as the models are concerned, you have things like Gemma, I suppose, and other small models, right? What kind of hardware does someone need to have in order to run these models so that they don’t have to wait 20 minutes for each prompt? Pete Warden. So a lot of it comes down to your model choice. Ben Lorica. Yeah. Pete Warden. You can get very capable models that are like 9 billion parameters these days. Especially if you look around at the Qwen family of models, they tend to be doing very well, though there are a bunch of other alternatives. Ben Lorica. But translate that, Pete. To someone with a normal laptop, is 9 billion big or small? Pete Warden. So the key thing is whether you can fit that into your graphics card’s memory. With weight quantization, 9 billion, if it was eight bits, is like nine gigabytes. A lot of decent midrange laptops that are shipping now have more than that. But using Q4, and there are all sorts of schemes, you can actually get that down into a four-gigabyte graphics card, and that’s widely available. There are a lot of even older laptops that have that amount of GPU memory, VRAM, in them. So really, the hardware barriers are a lot lower than people think. And the other piece of good news is that all of the hardware manufacturers are looking at this. They’re slightly hobbled by the DRAM craziness, the price increases. But if you look at the new M5 Studio from Apple, they have a configuration that’s 256 gigabytes of system memory. Apple does a great job of actually making that available to the accelerators that they build into all of their Macs now, too. And with that, you’re looking at something like a model with hundreds of billions of parameters that you can actually run at a decent speed. Once you get up into those numbers, you’re really looking at something where it can be hard to tell if you’re using Claude or if you’re using an open-weights model at that point. They have different characteristics, but one isn’t clearly worse than the other. Ben Lorica. So as I mentioned, we’ll definitely dive deep into voice and speech in a second here. But sticking with this notion of local models, obviously privacy and IP security are arguments for it. Do you think, if we look ahead, let’s say 12 to 24 months, these local models are going to be capable enough that people doing knowledge work in an enterprise might even consider them here and there? For example, someone who travels a lot is on an airplane, not connected to the internet, and needs to keep writing a document or generating images or even coding, vibe coding, on a laptop. Do you think we’ll get to the point where, with these local models, you essentially feel like you’re not compromising when you’re doing your knowledge work? Pete Warden. I think you can actually get to that point right now, and I know that’s a fairly bold statement. Ben Lorica. But when you say you, does that mean Pete Warden, who’s going to compile all of these? We want normal people. We want civilians, Pete. Pete Warden. I think the biggest barriers are usability. If you look at the benchmarks, it really is no longer a question of model quality. Ben Lorica. Model quality. Pete Warden. Yeah, a question of model quality. There are still things around the edges where you might prefer some of the commercial online models, but it’s not clear-cut. And people are finding that some of the models actually work better, especially if you’re dealing with things like, I don’t want to call it censorship because I feel like that’s a loaded term, but a lot of commercial models have restrictions. They may be intended to prevent a bad use case, but pretty often they can also trip you up even if you’re trying to do something benign. I know a lot of people who work in cybersecurity, for example, who are white hats, but they’re having to work with a lot of stuff where they’re asking questions about malicious actions. With the commercial models, you’re going to keep tripping over the restrictions and the guardrails that are built in with good intentions, but they can really impact your work. Ben Lorica. Right, right, right. By the way, Pete, the model is one component, but then there are the things surrounding the model, the so-called harness, or even context, memory, knowledge. You can imagine someone, and this is actually something I’ve thought about. You know how people are starting to use these LLMs as therapists or friends, right? Pete Warden. Yes. Ben Lorica. Then if you’re going to do that, why not do that on a local model? Why do it on something connected to the cloud? I guess one argument against it is that if you do it locally, you’re responsible for model upgrades and things like that, right? Whereas if you use one of these digital or AI therapist services, they take care of all your history and all of this. Do you think it will become easier for consumers to use local models that are essentially something they trust 100% because they own it? Pete Warden. Yeah, I mean, these should be part of the OS. At this point, it’s really an operating system capability that should be available to apps, and I feel like Apple is moving in this direction. Ben Lorica. I see. Yeah, that makes a lot of sense. Pete Warden. Yeah, they’re getting the hardware capabilities. The other thing I would say is that local doesn’t have to mean on your laptop. Especially as an enterprise user, you can host on-prem or even spin up a cloud instance that your enterprise has control over, run these models there, and have the same experience. One thing I do want to emphasize is that people are finally having to pay something approaching the real cost of running these models through Anthropic and OpenAI, and hosting locally or hosting on-prem can cost a lot less, too. Ben Lorica. Although if you look at their consumer offerings, it’s still insanely cheap, right? So $20 a month. I mean, you probably blow through that in a day. Pete Warden. Yeah. Especially on the enterprise side, there are a bunch of options that don’t require high-end NVIDIA GPUs. You still need those for training, but for inference, for just running models, as an enterprise, you might already have the capacity lying around. Ben Lorica. So another important aspect of what you’ve been doing is getting people excited about voice and speech, right? This notion that speech could become a basic computing primitive. It doesn’t necessarily have to feel like some remote service. I still remember you demonstrating to me this voice transcription service in a loud coffee shop near Precita Park. Pete Warden. Yes. Right. Yeah. Ben Lorica. This was several years ago. The accuracy of this thing was insane, and it was running not even on a laptop. I think it was just running on a Raspberry Pi. Pete Warden. That’s right. Yeah. Ben Lorica. And so talk to us about the state of voice as an actual interface, similar to a mouse or a keyboard. Where are we? Pete Warden. I think a lot of people are skeptical of voice because they’ve used Siri and Alexa, and it’s a very stilted way of communicating. But the question I often ask people when I’m having a conversation about this stuff and I encounter that resistance is, when you’re sitting on the couch and you’re trying to decide what TV show to watch with your significant other next to you, do you text them or do you talk to them? Ben Lorica. Right. Pete Warden. Apart from a few Gen Z people, almost everybody says talk to them. And so following on from that, it’s like, okay, well, it’s not that people don’t like voice interfaces. It’s that people don’t like bad voice interfaces. So the problem becomes an engineering and user experience problem of how do we make voice interfaces that are pleasant and efficient to use? I think once we do that, voice can really take its place as maybe even a more frequent input medium than the keyboard or touchscreen. Ben Lorica. Yeah, because I think the general impression people have is that voice and speech are much less deterministic than a keyboard or a touchscreen, right? Although people now interact with their LLMs and misspell things right and left, and it doesn’t seem to matter. But the impression people have is that there’ll be problems with accents, background noise, phrasing, and so on and so forth. So where are we in terms of all of these things? Pete Warden. We have solutions available to most of those problems, or at least big improvements. But because there’s no commercial incentive to pull them all together, it really hasn’t hit the mainstream yet. I feel like we’re still dealing with interfaces that are from the previous generation. They haven’t taken on board the LLM era fully, and they’re still suffering from a lot of those problems you listed. And that’s why I think open source can be a really strong lever. Ben Lorica. So as you’ve been trying to solve a lot of these interface problems, what are some of the lessons that you’ve learned? In fact, maybe some of them might even apply to people who are not working with voice but are just building AI applications. I think one of the things you mentioned to me years ago is that with voice, you don’t have to wait until someone has finished talking to start doing work, right? So what are some of these interface lessons? Pete Warden. I think latency is a massive deal. That is something you just don’t get with cloud-based voice interfaces. You’re usually waiting at least a couple of seconds, and that’s long enough for people to wonder if they were actually heard. Ben Lorica. Yeah, it’s like being on a Zoom call or phone call with someone, and then there’s a pause. Pete Warden. Yeah, and they’re just sitting there. It feels like the other person is just sitting there, ignoring you. We know from general user experience research that you really want to be in that 200-millisecond or lower range to feel responsive. I often ask people to imagine that you press a key on the keyboard and it takes two seconds for the key to show up in the window. That would be very awkward. Ben Lorica. By the way, this is something that people who work with LLMs also have to deal with, but on the output side, right? They want to make sure that the response is not too long. Otherwise, people get impatient, right? Pete Warden. Yeah, absolutely. And I do want to mention another thing, which I think might be helpful to people thinking about local AI in general as well. When you’re no longer paying per token, when you’re no longer having to pay to use a voice interface, the way you can use these things, the world of possibilities, becomes so much wider. If you imagine that every app developer had to pay a few cents every time somebody touched an icon on the touchscreen in their app, you would design apps very differently, and a lot of apps wouldn’t exist because of that tax. So once LLMs are built into the OS and just generally available with no cost, and the same with voice, that is not just an incremental change going from a cent to zero. That massively increases the number of viable things that you can use those for. Ben Lorica. So I imagine, Pete, this is one thing where you’ve done a lot of work, which is basically designing for failure, right? Because in voice, a lot of things can go wrong. What are some of the lessons there in terms of designing your applications with failure in mind? Pete Warden. One of my favorite examples of designing for failure is the use of snippets in Google Search. Google Search, from the beginning, knew they couldn’t always get the number one result right. There’s a reason you didn’t just hit “I’m Feeling Lucky.” Ben Lorica. Yeah, exactly. “I’m Feeling Lucky.” Pete Warden. What was genius about their approach was that they actually let you browse, just scan with your eyes. They hoped to get the right result in the top three most of the time, and then you actually narrow it down by looking at the snippets, which tell you enough to click on the right one. And the same thing for voice. The more you can actually read the body language of somebody, as we’re talking, you’re nodding a little bit to indicate what’s happening. Ben Lorica. Wait a minute, I’m only voice, so you can’t see me. Pete Warden. No, I can see. Ben Lorica. No, no, but in general, right? In general. Pete Warden. Well, that’s actually a whole other part of this that I haven’t mentioned. I think having a little camera that’s completely local-only will be a massive part of this. But even without a camera, if you hear supportive noises, or if you start giving a response and somebody reacts, all of those things that we recognize as people, we respond to them and ask more questions versus assuming that we picked the right thing. So really trying to understand all of those cues that we use as people. Some of them are verbal, some of them are body language and visual, but really having them all understood locally. And ensuring that all of those recordings never get recorded, because you can verify that locally. You don’t know what happens to audio and video once you send it up to the cloud. It’s impossible to audit, basically. With local stuff, you can audit. So I’m hoping that opens up the chance to use cameras without increasing the risk to users around privacy. Ben Lorica. So there are the people who work on speech models, and there’s been a lot of work in that area. In fact, one thing that I think is vastly underappreciated is that people talk about deep learning having an ImageNet moment, but actually the first impressive deep learning models were in speech, before ImageNet, right? So there are people working on speech models. They’ve even talked about end-to-end models, but obviously we have LLMs. For the people who don’t follow this closely, Pete, what’s the relationship between the LLMs and the speech models, or do people not use LLMs? Do they just use speech models? Pete Warden. There’s been a massive debate, a split between what I think of as LLM maximalists, who expect everything to be an end-to-end model. Ben Lorica. “Machines of Loving Grace.” Pete Warden. Yes, exactly. And I see usually Anthropic, OpenAI, the big AI companies. Ben Lorica. Or, you know, the hype machine has to be fed, right? Pete Warden. Well, the hype machine has to be fed, and specifically, if the future is end-to-end models, then only the people with the most money can actually build and train them. Now, I’m very strongly in what Berkeley calls the compound AI camp, where you actually build your applications out of multiple models, each of which has a specialized task. So there, instead of having a model that takes speech in and outputs speech audio, you actually have a model that takes speech audio in, converts it to text, feeds that into an LLM, and the LLM then outputs text, which is converted into speech. Now, every time you convert the audio into text, you actually lose a bunch of expressiveness. It’s like a bottleneck of information. You can’t tell how somebody’s asking it, whether they’re asking it with a particular intonation and all of this other stuff. Ben Lorica. Can’t you, as you’re doing that translation, add metadata? Pete Warden. You kind of can, but the whole point of compound AI is that you can take models from different sources and plug them together. So you need some kind of common language, and at the moment, the only thing that all LLMs speak is text input and text output. But the advantages are that you can actually train all of the models independently. With a speech end-to-end model, if you have a new accent, then if it’s a true end-to-end model, you have to do a whole bunch of training. If you have a new input accent, if you have new output voices or new capabilities, if it’s a true end-to-end model, then you’re having to train the whole thing. If it’s not actually, if end-to-end is just a marketing term, then you can train individual components, individual modules separately. But then you’re always agreeing on some settled interface data, like some schema, some language. Even if it’s not text, even if it’s an embedding, you still have to have those fixed points. So yeah, I see end-to-end as much more of a marketing term and something to justify the insane amounts of money that are flowing into these companies. Ben Lorica. Pete, what about, for our listeners who’ve heard of the term multimodal, right? Gemini is supposed to be multimodal. And coincidentally, I just spoke to someone who works in the visual reasoning and understanding space, and they said actually Gemini is quite poor in terms of understanding video. So what is the state of these multimodal models for your domain, speech? Pete Warden. They’re actually often pretty good. Qwen, 1.7 billion, I think it is, actually does a better job than Whisper, a significantly better job on some languages like Mandarin. And the same goes for Gemma. The trouble is that, as general-purpose models, one of the failure cases with Gemma is that you upload audio of some speech, it transcribes it, but it then gets confused by the content of that speech and thinks you’re asking it a question, say, if there was a question in the transcribed speech. So it’s one of these things where you’re trying to use a Swiss Army knife, and it’s a lot easier to use an actual wood saw versus the thing that can do everything and has a little saw attachment with it. So that’s another drawback of the end-to-end models. Ben Lorica. By the way, obviously you’re the king on this topic. General-purpose models are dead on arrival on the edge, right? Pete Warden. I mean, right now, only… Ben Lorica. For the types of, I mean, some of the really small pieces of hardware that you work on. Pete Warden. One of the things I recently did was get a full voice interface where you could connect to Wi-Fi, set the password, and all of this sort of stuff, running on a Raspberry Pi Pico microcontroller that only has 500 kilobytes of RAM. Now, there, you’re never going to have a general-purpose model that’s going to work well for you. But as always… Ben Lorica. And by the way, one of the things that you’ve also worked on, which is interesting, and which I don’t see a lot of people working on, is taking the browser more seriously, right? So tell us, what’s the motivation behind that, and what has been the reception? Pete Warden. Yeah, so it’s tricky because I sometimes think of “We’ve done X, but in the browser” as Hacker News bait, because that always gets a lot of attention as a novelty. But it’s often hard to find practical uses for a lot of these things. With the voice capabilities, with voice input and voice output, what I’ve seen is that it makes it part of the browser operating system, or feel like part of the browser operating system. And once you’re able to transcribe fast and accurately in the browser, it’s a way for people to easily start experimenting with this stuff, and there aren’t any costs for this at the moment. I’ve tried to put a few examples. If you go to Moonshine AI… Ben Lorica. But the whole notion of using the browser as a point of inference, right? You can imagine other models doing that too, not just yours, which focuses on speech. You can imagine text, I mean, browser inference for text kinds of applications, right? Pete Warden. Well, if you’re running Chrome, you’ve already got a very capable model installed. You’ve got a 4-billion-parameter model. I actually did a blog post last year showing how you could just go through Chrome settings and start using it as a chatbot, just typing in the window and getting responses. I think that’s an example of the models becoming part of the operating system, because Chrome is essentially an operating system that sits on top of other operating systems. You can already access that built-in LLM, I think now from any website. It used to be just extensions, but now I think any website can access that from JavaScript. And again, we’re still figuring out what the best use cases are for that. But once it becomes free and you can rely on it being everywhere, I really feel like it’s an iPhone moment for a lot of these new LLM technologies. Ben Lorica. Or even what you mentioned earlier, which is for people on a laptop, it’ll be part of the OS somehow, right? So looking ahead, Pete, and again, for our listeners, you can follow Pete’s work at Moonshot AI. Moonshine. Ah, Moonshine. Moonshine.ai. And a lot of the work is open source, and you can take advantage of that. So looking ahead, Pete, 12 to 24 months. I hate to put you on the spot. Where are we in terms of, I guess, local or edge models, number one, and number two, just the state of open models in general? Pete Warden. Yeah, and I’m always terrible at predictions. Ben Lorica. But one thing Pete is super good at, for our listeners, is knowing what to work on. So that’s an indication. Just tell us what you’re working on. Pete Warden. Yes. So what I see from being deep in the technical side, most of what I end up working on is because I’ve been working on something, and it becomes blindingly obvious that the only reasonable technical solution is X, and so of course I want to work on X. And what I see, and what I’ve seen for the last few years, is the gravitational pull of running this stuff locally or on-prem, or however you want to call it. I often say, “AI wants to be local.” If you think about something like Google Search, you need massive databases, you need armies of servers, you need all of this stuff. If you look at what Claude and ChatGPT are doing, you can run that entirely on one laptop with no internet connectivity. So the shape of these models is perfect for running locally, unlike almost everything else we’ve seen over the last couple of decades, where the cloud has made more sense. So what I expect is all of these pressures: cost for enterprises especially, worries about privacy, worries about capabilities going away, worries about changes. If you built an application on top of a particular version of Claude, even if you’re using the same version in the dropdown, what’s actually happening behind the scenes can change from day to day. So if you want stability, you actually need to host your own, at least in your own cloud infrastructure, if not locally on users’ laptops. And I can keep going on and on. Ben Lorica. Yeah. And then the other thing, too, is I think a lot of enterprises are recognizing that the moat, or their moat, is really not the model. It’s that compounding loop around the model, right? As you use the model more, you learn more and things like that. So why in the world would you send that to a commercial proprietary model? Pete Warden. And why not do fine-tuning on your own model? Ben Lorica. Yeah, I mean, with that data. Pete Warden. Yeah, exactly. Ben Lorica. And then, as you point out, you actually control your timing and roadmap as well, because you have the model and you know when it’s safe to replace that model with something else. No one is going to replace that model underneath you, right? Pete Warden. Nobody’s going to start charging 10 times as much overnight. Ben Lorica. Right, right, right. And then also, even if they keep the cost the same, they may weaken the model for some reason, right? Pete Warden. Yep. Yeah, and it could even be pressure from outside. Ben Lorica. So by the way, one last question for you, Pete, because obviously you work in a space where you really care about hardware, right? Right now, we’re in a world where Jensen Huang seems to own everything. So what’s your prediction about the state of AI hardware? Are we going to get more diversification? Is AMD going to up its game, or what’s going on in hardware in general? Pete Warden. So watch Apple. And disclaimer, I worked at Apple for five years in the 2000s. My wife worked there for 13 years. But if you look at what they’re doing, they’re getting lots of RAM, increasing the RAM speed so that you can actually run models much faster, and they have their own inference-only accelerators. I think with those three, you don’t need a GPU. Ben Lorica. So you just run everything on a CPU? Pete Warden. Well, run everything on a different kind of accelerator. Ben Lorica. Oh, okay. That’s not a… Pete Warden. GPU. Ben Lorica. I see. I see. So CPU… Pete Warden. Could actually be pretty fast. Obviously, the… Ben Lorica. The NVIDIA answer is why we have all the HBM, high-bandwidth memory, on the GPU, right? Pete Warden. And I like to think of GPUs as being designed for large batches and training. I like to think of a GPU as trying to use an oil tanker to go and do your shopping. They’re fantastic for these large training jobs, but they’re complete overkill for inference. Inference has a very different shape to the workload that it places on hardware. Ben Lorica. One thing that I’ve started to pay attention to lately, and it’s very, very early, is high-bandwidth flash. Pete Warden. Absolutely. Ben Lorica. Right. So what’s your take? Pete Warden. So that’s another example. I see the massive amount of money that NVIDIA is pulling in, and that also has its own gravitational pull on all of these hardware companies, where they’re looking from a technical side. I don’t have any special insights. I’ve just worked with these things. I know what the workloads look like. Other people are looking at those too, and they’re like, “Oh, I see. We have to stream all of the weights. All of the weights have to be processed for every token.” So if you have something, even if you’re running on the CPU, if you have something that’s got high enough bandwidth to pull the 27 billion weights in a fraction of a second, then the rest of it is fairly easy in terms of actually doing the processing. It’s very much memory-bound, usually. So it’s been awesome seeing high-bandwidth flash, what Apple is doing, increasing the bandwidth on regular RAM. I think we’re going to see a lot of really imaginative solutions now that people understand what the workload looks like. Ben Lorica. Yeah, and with that, thank you, Pete. And again, the website is moonshine.ai. title: SSD prices may begin to decline in the latter half of 2027
body_text: When Will Hard Drive Prices Come Down? The 2026-2028 Outlook | DriveVault DriveVault Features Pricing Changelog Blog FAQ Download on the App Store Storage Market When Will Hard Drive Prices Come Down? The Honest 2026-2028 Outlook Published September 17, 2026 • 11 min read • Forecasts and price data checked September 2026 Photo: Sandisk on Unsplash . It is the question we get asked more than any other right now, and it is the most searched phrase that brings people to this blog. So here is the straight answer: SSD prices should start to ease in the second half of 2027. Hard drives will take longer, probably into 2028, because the factories that make them have already sold that output. That is not a guess. It comes from the analysts who track memory contract prices every quarter, and from what Seagate and Western Digital told their own investors this summer. Below we lay out the evidence, explain why spinning drives and SSDs are running on different clocks, and give you a realistic timeline with the signals to watch. We have been following this since the start. Our April explainer on the storage price surge covered why prices took off. This article is the follow-up everyone keeps asking for: when does it end? While you wait, the cheapest terabyte is the one you already own. DriveVault scans each of your external drives once and keeps a searchable catalogue of everything on them, so you can see free space, spot duplicate project folders and find old files without plugging anything in. For a lot of people that audit pushes the next drive purchase back by months, which is exactly what you want when prices are at a record. Waiting for prices to fall? Use what you have first. DriveVault catalogues every drive you own so you can search them offline, find free space and spot duplicates before you buy. Download Free The short answer SSDs and flash Second half of 2027 NAND supply is forecast to catch up with demand from mid-2027. Expect a gradual slide, not a crash. Hard drives 2028 at the earliest Capacity is contracted into 2028 and no new factories are planned. Relief comes via bigger drives, slowly. The Short Version Prices are still rising, just more slowly. A year into the crisis, hard drives cost 134% more than in September 2025 and SSDs 129% more, in ComputerBase's tracking. SSDs should turn first. TrendForce expects the NAND shortage to end in the second half of 2027. Hard drives are booked up. Seagate has most of its data centre capacity allocated into 2028, and neither it nor Western Digital is building new factories. 2024 prices are not coming back soon. Contracts now include pricing, and AI demand is still growing. Need storage for work? Buy it. Buying speculatively? Wait, and favour SSDs, which should get cheaper first. Where Prices Stand in September 2026 Before looking forward, it helps to be honest about where we are. The German tech site ComputerBase has priced the same dozen popular drives every month since mid-September 2025, which makes its tracker one of the cleanest before-and-after records of this crisis. Its one-year check, published today , shows hard drives averaging 134% above their pre-crisis prices, up from 129% a month earlier. SSDs are 129% higher, up from 126%. Both are new records. Drive Sept 2025 Sept 2026 Change Seagate IronWolf 4TB (HDD) €94 €195 +108% WD Red Plus 8TB (HDD) €170 €349 +105% Toshiba MG09 18TB (HDD) €288 €858 +198% Seagate BarraCuda 24TB (HDD) €308 €804 +161% Kingston NV3 1TB (SSD) €50 €144 +189% Samsung 990 Pro 4TB (SSD) €285 €609 +114% Source: ComputerBase price check , 16 September 2026. German retail prices, excluding eBay and Amazon Marketplace sellers. The pattern in that table matters. The biggest hard drives, the 18TB to 24TB models that data centres also buy, have risen fastest. The smaller desktop drives most creatives actually use have "only" doubled. If you are shopping for a budget external drive , you are feeling the mild end of this. The one encouraging detail: the monthly increases have shrunk to a few percentage points. Prices are still climbing, but the curve is flattening. That is usually the first stage before a market turns. Why Hard Drives and SSDs Will Recover at Different Times Most coverage lumps "storage prices" together. That hides the most useful part of the answer, because hard drives and SSDs are made by different companies, in different factories, and sold in different ways. SSDs follow the chip market SSDs are built from NAND flash chips made by Samsung, SK hynix, Kioxia, Micron, Sandisk and YMTC. Those chips are priced quarter by quarter in contract negotiations, and some trade on a spot market that moves weekly. When supply catches up, SSD prices can respond within a couple of quarters. They went up fast. They can come down reasonably fast too. Hard drives follow multi-year contracts Hard drives come from essentially two companies, Seagate and Western Digital, with Toshiba a distant third. Almost all of their output now goes to cloud providers on long-term agreements. Those agreements lock in volume and, crucially, price for years at a time. That is why hard drive prices rose later and more steadily than SSDs, and it is why they will be slower to fall. Portable SSDs are built on the same NAND flash that AI servers consume, so they are tied to the chip cycle. Photo: Samsung Memory on Unsplash . The SSD Timeline: What the Analysts Say TrendForce is the most widely cited memory pricing firm, and its forecasts have been the best guide through this cycle. Here is how its view has shifted during 2026. At the start of the year, it was forecasting NAND contract prices rising 33 to 38% in a single quarter , with client SSDs rising at least 40% as suppliers moved capacity to data centre drives. By July the tone had changed. Its third-quarter survey forecast a much smaller 10 to 15% rise for NAND , and said plainly that PC and smartphone makers had hit the limit of what they could afford to pay. Then came the forecast that actually answers the question. In its July NAND update, TrendForce said the market would run a 4 to 5% supply deficit through 2026, then move back into balance in the second half of 2027 . The reasons it gives are ordinary ones: manufacturers squeezing more bits out of existing fabs, steady output growth, and consumer demand staying weak because everything costs so much. It expects notebook shipments to fall around 10% this year and shrink again in 2027. New supply is also arriving from China. YMTC reached around 14% of global NAND shipments in the second quarter and has told investors it wants to be the world's largest NAND maker by the end of 2027, backed by a planned $4.9 billion share listing. Even if it falls short of that target, that much extra flash entering the market is exactly the kind of pressure that pushes SSD prices down. Balance is not the same as cheap. TrendForce also warns that memory contract prices will remain broadly elevated in 2027 , with cloud providers' spending projected to rise another 50% next year. And it flags that a breakthrough in agentic AI could soak up the extra supply. A market in balance means prices stop rising and start drifting down. It does not mean a return to 2024. You may also have seen SK hynix's chief executive say that 2027 will be the worst supply year in the industry's history . That sounds like it contradicts TrendForce, but it mostly does not. His comments are about memory overall, and the worst of the squeeze is in DRAM and the high-bandwidth memory used in AI accelerators. TrendForce itself now describes a diverging market in 2027 : DRAM staying tight while NAND eases. That is good news for SSDs and less good news for RAM, which is part of why Macs keep getting more expensive, as we covered in our piece on Apple's price rises . The Hard Drive Timeline: Booked Into 2028 For spinning drives, the most reliable evidence is what the two big manufacturers said on their earnings calls this summer. It is not encouraging for anyone hoping for a quick drop. Seagate reported its fiscal year results on 28 July , with a record 52.7% gross margin. On the call , management said data centres now take around 90% of the capacity it ships, and that the vast majority of its high-capacity drive output is now allocated into calendar 2028. Seagate also told investors it has contracts setting both product configuration and pricing for the whole of 2027, and that it is not adding drive manufacturing capacity . Its plan is to cram more data onto each disk instead. Western Digital tells the same story. Its fourth-quarter revenue rose 44% year on year , while the amount of storage it shipped rose only 22%. The gap is price. According to analysis of the earnings call , the company's average price per terabyte rose by a high-teens percentage, and its long-term agreements run through 2027 with two major customers and through 2028 with one, with price terms attached. Put simply: the companies are sold out, they are making record margins, their contracts fix prices into 2028, and they have chosen not to build more factories. None of those conditions produce falling retail prices. So where does hard drive relief come from? Density. Seagate's HAMR (heat-assisted magnetic recording) drives already make up around 40% of its data centre capacity shipments , and Western Digital plans full-scale HAMR production in 2027 . As the cloud giants move to 36TB, 40TB and larger drives, the cost per terabyte falls for everyone, and older production lines can eventually be freed up for the consumer and mid-capacity drives you and I buy. That is a slow, grinding process. It points to prices levelling off through 2027 and easing from 2028, rather than a sudden correction. Tip: if you need big-capacity archive storage today, our guide to high-capacity external drives from 16TB to 44TB compares the options on value as well as speed. A Realistic Timeline Pulling all of that together, here is our best reading of how the next two years should play out. Treat it as a forecast, not a promise. Every forecast in this cycle so far has been revised at least once. Rest of 2026 Still rising, but slowly Small monthly increases for both hard drives and SSDs. Black Friday may bring a handful of genuine deals on specific SSDs, but no broad drop. The NAND market stays in deficit. First half of 2027 The plateau SSD contract prices flatten as new flash supply builds. Hard drive prices hold at their peak under long-term contracts. DRAM remains very tight, so Macs and PCs stay expensive. Second half of 2027 SSDs start to ease NAND supply and demand move into balance. Portable and internal SSD prices begin a gradual decline, with the largest capacities, which rose most, likely to fall most. Hard drives stay broadly flat. 2028 onwards Hard drives follow As current contracts roll off and HAMR drives dominate data centres, hard drive cost per terabyte should improve. Prices should settle meaningfully below today's levels, but probably above 2024's. What Could Change the Timeline It could come sooner if AI infrastructure spending cools, Chinese NAND output ramps faster than expected, or consumer demand stays so weak that manufacturers start discounting to move stock. Module makers are already sitting on higher inventories because shoppers have stopped buying, which is the kind of pressure that eventually breaks prices. It could come later if agentic AI takes off and data centres start storing far more data per user, if more manufacturers follow Micron's Crucial brand out of the consumer market, or if trade restrictions tighten on Chinese memory makers. Signals worth watching A flat or falling quarter in TrendForce's NAND contract survey. That would be the first since the crisis began, and the clearest sign SSD relief is on its way. ComputerBase's monthly price check going negative for SSDs or hard drives. It publishes mid-month and is a good public scoreboard. New SSD launches at the same or lower prices than the models they replace. The recent Samsung P9 and P7 did the opposite. Seagate or Western Digital mentioning pricing pressure or customers delaying orders. So far, both say demand visibility is improving. The drives you already own are the cheapest storage you will have for the next two years. Photo: Samsung Memory on Unsplash . Should You Buy Now or Wait? That depends entirely on why you need the storage. Here is how we would think about it. You need storage for paid work this year Buy now Waiting has no clear end date, and a lost booking costs more than the price premium. Buy what the job needs, not more. Our 4TB drive roundup and rugged 4TB SSD guide focus on value at today's prices. Your backups are incomplete Buy now A failed drive with no second copy is far more expensive than any price spike, especially when a replacement costs double. A basic spinning drive is still the cheapest way to hold a second copy. Just make sure the backup is actually complete. Our guide to verifying a backup drive shows how. You want a fast SSD upgrade that can wait Wait if you can SSDs are the category most likely to get cheaper first. If your current setup works, holding off until the second half of 2027 is a reasonable bet. You are accepting the risk that prices plateau rather than fall. You are stockpiling "just in case" Don't Buying spare capacity at record prices, to sit empty on a shelf, is the worst trade in this market. You would be paying the peak for storage you might not need until prices have eased. Before You Buy Anything, Audit What You Have The most useful thing you can do while prices are this high is find out exactly what is on the drives you already own. Most creatives with a few years of work behind them have a drawer of drives, a few with duplicate project folders, and at least one nobody is quite sure about. DriveVault turns that pile into a catalogue you can search in seconds, even when the drives are unplugged. See real free space across every drive before assuming you need a new one. Find duplicate folders across drives with drive comparison , and reclaim the space safely. Confirm a backup is complete before you wipe and reuse the original drive. Search files on unplugged drives , so shelved archives stay useful. Here is how offline search works . Share the catalogue with your team so nobody buys a drive to hold footage that already exists. See sharing drive catalogues . If you want a system for keeping it that way, our guide to organising multiple external drives covers naming, folder templates and archiving. Every terabyte you recover now is one you do not have to buy at 2026 prices. Frequently Asked Questions When will hard drive prices come down? Probably not before 2028 in any meaningful way. Seagate says the vast majority of its data centre hard drive capacity is already allocated into calendar 2028, and Western Digital has long-term agreements with price terms running through 2027 and 2028. Neither company is adding factory capacity. Relief is more likely to come from higher-capacity HAMR drives lowering the cost per terabyte than from a sudden price cut. When will SSD prices come down? TrendForce expects the NAND flash market to stay in a 4 to 5 percent supply deficit through 2026 and to move back into balance in the second half of 2027. That makes late 2027 the earliest realistic window for SSD prices to start falling, with gradual easing rather than a sharp drop. Will hard drive and SSD prices go back to 2024 levels? Not within the next two years on current evidence. Manufacturers have signed multi-year contracts that include pricing, and AI data centres now account for most of their output. Prices should ease from their peak, but planning around a return to 2024 prices is not supported by any current forecast. Should I buy a hard drive now or wait? If you need the storage for paid work or your backups are incomplete, buy now, because waiting for hard drive prices has no clear end date. If you are buying extra capacity speculatively, SSDs are the category most likely to get cheaper first, from the second half of 2027. Either way, audit the drives you already own first, since duplicated files often free up more space than people expect. Why are hard drives so expensive in 2026? AI data centres are buying almost all of the high-capacity drives Seagate and Western Digital can build, under long-term contracts. Data centres now take around 90 percent of Seagate's shipped capacity. With consumer products a small slice of their business and no new factories planned, retail prices have more than doubled since September 2025 in ComputerBase's tracking. The Bottom Line Storage prices will come down. Just not yet, and not evenly. SSDs are on track to turn first, from the second half of 2027, as new flash supply catches up and consumer demand stays weak. Hard drives are locked into contracts that run into 2028, and their recovery will be slower and quieter, carried by bigger drives rather than price cuts. The practical move for the next year is simple. Buy what you genuinely need, skip the stockpile, and get every usable terabyte out of the drives already on your desk. We will update this article as the forecasts change. Get more from the drives you already own. Estonia’s Digital Nomad Bet Pays Off As E-Residents Generate €125M All stories → More Latest Issue Culture Fintech Profiles European Business Magazine Awards 2026 About Executive Education Daily News Feed Media OutReach ACCESS Newswire Search Search European Business Magazine Search Home Business AI Agents Ask Better Questions Than KPMG Accountants in Landmark Audit Trial Business AI News AI Agents Ask Better Questions Than KPMG Accountants in Landmark Audit Trial By EBM Newsdesk November 18, 2026 2,038 views 0 comments LONDON, November 18, 2026 — Artificial intelligence has taken another significant step into the world of professional services after KPMG revealed that AI agents examining the accounts of a major UK-listed company sometimes investigated financial issues more deeply and asked better questions than its human audit team. The experiment, conducted by KPMG UK using more than 100 AI agents, marks an important development in the application of artificial intelligence to one of the most labour-intensive areas of the financial services industry. It also raises an uncomfortable question for the accountancy profession: if machines can increasingly perform the analytical work traditionally undertaken by highly trained professionals, how quickly will the economics of auditing change? According to the Financial Times , the project, codenamed Project Exponential, examined the financial statements of an unnamed FTSE 250 company. The AI agents worked alongside a conventional audit team, undertaking tasks across the audit process rather than simply assisting with isolated administrative functions. Join The European Business Briefing New subscribers this quarter are entered into a draw to win a Rolex Submariner. Join 40,000+ founders, investors and executives who read EBM every day. Subscribe KPMG UK head of audit Cath Burnet said the technology had, in several instances, gone considerably deeper into issues than the regular audit team, identifying areas requiring further investigation and asking questions that human auditors had not necessarily raised. The findings suggest that AI’s potential in professional services may extend well beyond improving productivity. It could fundamentally change how complex financial information is examined, interpreted and challenged. From supporting accountants to conducting audits Project Exponential represents a shift from using AI as a supporting tool towards deploying autonomous agents across an entire audit workflow. The agents collected information, analysed and documented data, developed draft conclusions and observations, and suggested subsequent steps. They were also able to work alongside one another, effectively dividing responsibilities and coordinating elements of the investigation. The technology was developed over approximately four months. However, KPMG was careful to distinguish the experiment from a formally approved statutory audit. Although an audit partner signed off on the experimental exercise, its findings were not used as the basis for formally approving the company’s accounts. Human oversight remained essential. During the trial, an auditor had to intervene when one AI agent failed to correctly match regulatory requirements with the company’s documentation. The episode illustrates both the capabilities and limitations of current AI systems when dealing with complex regulatory frameworks. KPMG plans to expand the initiative to as many as 20 larger audits, although the firm acknowledges that the technology is not yet sufficiently mature to be deployed across thousands of engagements. Data quality also remains a significant obstacle, with some businesses lacking the clean, structured information required for AI agents to operate effectively. A challenge to the Big Four business model? The implications for the accountancy industry could be substantial. Traditional auditing relies on large teams of junior accountants undertaking detailed and repetitive work, supervised by experienced managers and partners. AI agents potentially offer a different operating model, automating significant portions of data collection, analysis and documentation while allowing senior professionals to concentrate on complex judgements and exceptions. For firms such as KPMG, Deloitte, PwC and EY, the attraction is clear: faster audits, potentially lower operating costs and the ability to analyse much larger volumes of financial information. However, whether those savings will ultimately be passed on to clients remains uncertain. KPMG has acknowledged the potential for significant time savings but has not confirmed whether AI-driven efficiencies will translate into lower audit fees. Human judgement remains the final safeguard The transition also presents regulatory and professional challenges. The UK’s Financial Reporting Council has warned that the use of AI must not undermine auditor independence, integrity or professional scepticism. There are also concerns about data security, over-reliance on automated conclusions and the possibility of AI generating inaccurate or fabricated information. The fundamental responsibility for an audit opinion remains with the human auditor, regardless of the technology used. The KPMG experiment does not establish that AI can replace accountants or independently deliver a reliable statutory audit. It does, however, demonstrate that AI agents are beginning to challenge professionals in areas that were once considered dependent on human expertise. For the accountancy profession, the question is no longer simply whether AI will become part of the audit process. It is how much of that process will eventually be performed by machines — and what role human accountants will play when it does. title: Why is Gemini 4 Carbon taking so long?
body_text: Why is Gemini 4 Carbon taking so long? · Kernel kernel Why is Gemini 4 Carbon taking so long? November 2026 Y Discussion on Hacker News ▲ 238 points 125 comments → While benchmarking Gemini 4 Carbon on one of our private evals, we found something surprising: it spent close to an hour completing tasks that routinely took Opus and Astra only a few minutes: Time and cost per trial Left is faster; lower is cheaper. API list price On a $200 plan, fully used Carbon is priced at its post-introductory rate. Subscription subsidization rates used: Opus 40×, Astra 13×, Carbon 3×, Hydrogen 17×. Turns out we weren't alone in noticing this. Theo - t3.gg @theo I don't really know how to properly emphasize this. Gemini 4 Carbon is unacceptably slow in real world usage. Gemini 4 Carbon low: 22m21s Opus 5.5 high: 9m33s Nov 11, 2026 828 104 replies Elliot Arledge @elliotarledge i really love gemini 4 carbon but its too slow. im losing my mind waiting just to stay focused and learn simple things Nov 12, 2026 36 5 replies Shayan @ImSh4yy dude why is carbon so fucking slow Nov 13, 2026 8 4 replies Simon Mahns @ CoRL @nautsimon_ carbon is nearly unusable because of how slow it is, but people are majorly sleeping on it Nov 16, 2026 30 3 replies To find out why, we traced every step of Carbon's runs and quantified what contributes to the slowness. The Task In each task, the agent gets a codebase from just before a bug was fixed, along with a report that describes the bug only by its symptoms. Its job is to diagnose the bug and fix it, without making any unrelated changes. Much of the task's difficulty comes from engineering judgment rather than raw intelligence: tracing the user's symptoms to the right code path, ruling out rival explanations, putting the fix in the right place, and knowing when to stop. Slow inference, or more work? The first (and easiest) factor to separate out was inference speed: queueing at the provider, network latency, prompt processing and generation speed. Together, these set how long each step takes: Seconds per step Slower inference accounts for part of the gap: 16–30% of Carbon’s extra time compared with Astra, and 45–49% compared with Opus. The rest comes from longer trajectories. Carbon simply does more work per task, as the step counts, tool calls and tokens below show: The workload GPT-6 Astra against Gemini 4 Carbon, mean per bug. GPT-6 Astra Gemini 4 Carbon lighter = lower effort Carbon takes about seven times as many steps as Astra, and eleven times as many actions such as reading a file or running a command. It writes seven times as much and, because every step re-sends a longer and longer conversation, it processes more than sixteen times as much input. Ruling out the obvious Before looking inside the runs, we checked two simpler explanations. The harness. We also ran Carbon inside two other coding agents, opencode and mini-SWE-agent, and saw no meaningful difference. Mismatched reasoning levels. Effort settings aren't standardized across providers, so Carbon's "high" may sit closer to the other models' maximum settings, and the fairer comparison might have been Carbon on low. But on low, Carbon often failed to produce a fix at all: it went in circles, re-reading code it had already read instead of making the fix. Reading the traces We labelled every step of the Astra and Carbon runs by what it was for, and then counted how many steps went to each kind of work: Semantic trace analysis Each model’s steps, grouped by what they were for. Leaves out the 20 steps Carbon spent re-reading code it had already read; the next section covers those. Half of Carbon’s steps went into work the ticket never asked for: Auditing code beyond the bug. Once it had found the cause, Carbon kept widening its search, checking every related path through the system and auditing code the fix never needed to touch. Closing loopholes the ticket had already ruled out. Carbon defended against cases the ticket's facts had already excluded, hardening the code against problems nobody had reported. Can Carbon identify its own overworking? Sample trial: time to find the cause vs. time to first edit Minutes from the start of each run. GPT-6 Astra at max effort, Gemini 4 Carbon at high. In this sample trial, both models identified the cause early, Astra within a minute and Carbon within about six. Astra had its fix written three minutes later; Carbon didn't write any code for another 25 minutes. Carbon might not have been sure it had the cause (a knowledge gap), or it might have known and kept going anyway (a general habit, learned from training that rewards right answers more than it penalises extra steps). To tell them apart, we re-ran one of the trials in a modified harness that automatically injects the same check-in every five turns: "do you already have enough to make the fix?" Sample trial with check-ins: time to find the cause vs. time to first edit The same bug and scale as above. Gemini 4 Carbon at high, with the check-in injected every five turns (circles). With check-ins, Carbon finished in 28 minutes instead of 37, and the wait between naming the cause and editing shrank from 25 minutes to about 10. This implies that the slowness seems to come from how Carbon behaves, not what it knows. Carbon's necessary work is also slower Even within the steps the fix needed, we found some additional low-hanging fruit: Carbon got less done with each step, and it kept re-reading code it had already seen. Astra made more than two tool calls per step, often reading several files at once — Carbon, on the other hand, made about one, usually reading a single file. Carbon also re-read far more: 39% of the lines it read were ones it had already seen, against 7% for Astra. We estimate that these two "mechanical" inefficiencies account for roughly 25% of Carbon's excess runtime. Conclusion On difficult bug-fixing tasks, Carbon took close to an hour where Opus and Astra took minutes. We traced that gap to three sources: Slower inference. Each step takes longer, which explains 16–30% of the gap against Astra and about half against Opus. Unnecessary work. About half of Carbon's steps went on work the tickets never asked for: auditing code the fix didn't need and closing loopholes the ticket had already ruled out. Mechanical inefficiencies. Fewer tool calls per step and frequent re-reading slow Carbon down; we estimate that fixing them alone would cut its runtime by roughly a quarter. new tab) X (opens in a new tab) Facebook (opens in a new tab) Article link Copy link Share At MAI, our mission is to build you the very best models in the world and keep every developer and every enterprise at the frontier of capability. But as token spend skyrockets, we know that you also want models at a price point that lets you run agents 24/7 doing real engineering work. That’s why today we’re releasing a family of seven new world class models at a truly exceptional price-performance. Here’s the lineup: MAI Cyber 2 Flash beats GPT-6 Astra’s quality at less than 2% of the cost per task on the CyberGym-E2E benchmark. MAI Code 2 reaches 98% of the coding quality of GPT-6.1 Sol at about 40% of the price. And against Opus 5.5, it reaches 96% performance for just 5% of the price. MAI Code 2 Flash shows comparable performance GPT-6 Luna at 65% of the price, and Haiku 5.5 at 20% of the price. MAI Image 2.7 is #1 on Artificial Analysis image editing, outperforming GPT Image 2.6 Sunburst (max) at just one-fifth of the price. MAI Realtime 1 outperforms GPT-Realtime 2.1 and starts at just $0.01 per audio minute. Dragon Copilot Transcribe is built on MAI Transcribe 2, the world’s fastest and most accurate multilingual transcription model, and already powers 10 million patient encounters a month with multilingual error rates halved. Decision 1.1 is the latest decision model from Microsoft, 50x faster and 79x cheaper than GPT-6.1 Sol. Maia 200 , Microsoft’s second-generation AI accelerator, is now in production running our largest models, achieving 1.7x more tokens per watt.  Frontier cyber defense built to run 24/7 Security, alignment and containment are the most important priorities for agent development in 2027 and beyond. That’s our top priority. We need to run monitoring and control agents defending and patching live production systems 24/7. That’s why MAI Cyber 2 Flash was designed to deliver frontier intelligence at a fraction of the cost. Built with Microsoft’s decades of proprietary data and world-class security expertise, our models help defenders stay safe in this new era where attackers have cheap and abundant offensive tools. MAI Cyber 2 Flash builds on earlier MAI Cyber models that defenders already rely on. MAI Cyber accounts for almost 40% of scans in MDASH, and 90% of scans that started with MAI continued to use it. Our latest model is now priced 86% lower on output tokens than MAI Cyber 1.1 Flash, giving existing MDASH customers a stronger model at a lower price. Incredible coding performance at a fraction of the cost MAI Code 2 is built for the best price-performance for everyday enterprise coding tasks. Averaged over four widely used benchmarks that target the everyday enterprise coding tasks we see in GitHub Copilot (DeepSWE 1.1, Terminal Bench 2.1, SWE-Atlas and FrontierCode v1.1), MAI Code 2 gives you 98% of the performance of GPT-6.1 Sol at 40% of the price, and 96% of Claude Opus 5.5’s performance at just 5% of the price. We’ve built these models to prioritize the coding work our customers do every day. They’re explicitly not yet tuned for harder problems, like fundamental science research and very long horizon agentic work. MAI Code 2 also been tuned to generate great dashboards and visualizations. In a blind, side-by-side evaluation of frontend work, developers preferred MAI Code 2 over GPT-6 Sol 64% of the time. Try MAI Code 2 in GitHub Copilot today. Read more here . MAI Code 2 Flash is designed for high-volume, everyday tasks like code explanations, targeted edits, routine fixes, and rapid iterations, while bringing quality at a much lower cost. It performs comparably to GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 at 65% and 20% of the price, respectively, across three coding benchmarks measuring day-to-day, high-volume routine coding tasks (DeepSWE 1.1, Terminal Bench 2.1 and SWE-Atlas). It’s available in GitHub Copilot and in a limited-access preview in Microsoft Foundry . The best image and transcription models in the world MAI Image 2.7 is the best image editing model in the world, taking the #1 spot on Artificial Analysis, outperforming GPT Image 2.6 Sunburst (max) at just one-fifth of the price. At text-to-image generation, our model is ranked #4, making us the second-best lab. And MAI Image 2.7 Flash brings world class image generation for high-volume scenarios at ~$10 per 1,000 images. Both are available in Microsoft Foundry here . MAI Realtime 1 is our first live speech-to-speech model, designed for natural, low-latency conversations. In our evaluations, it outperformed GPT-Realtime 2.1 across external and Dynamics 365 benchmarks. It’s priced for enterprise-scale use, starting at a budget-saving price of $0.01 per audio minute. You can try it out in MAI Labs and register your interest here . Dragon Copilot Transcribe , built on MAI Transcribe 2, is now live in Dragon Copilot, powering 100% of doctor–patient conversation transcriptions. It covers 10 million encounters a month, halves error rates in multilingual workflows, and is in the hands of a third of US physicians. The leading Decision model in the market Decision 1.1 provides model routing integrated right into your applications so that the bigger, pricier models are only used when you really need them. On the Artificial Analysis Decision Index Microsoft is ahead of Jev, Google and OpenAI, while being faster and cheaper. Used by 4,000 customers, it’s 50x faster and 79x cheaper than GPT-6.1 Sol. Customize models for your business We’ve heard again and again from leaders that no one wants to pour their IQ into someone else’s model. And if you build on open weights, can you really trust where they came from, or how they’ll behave when you use one as the foundation for your most valuable IP and data? We heard you. We started with Custom Models. AT&T developed an MAI custom model for 5G network operation analytics and it outperformed GPT-6.1 Sol at 1/50th of the cost. On complex scenarios, they found that Code 2 delivered frontier-level performance at a significantly lower price than alternatives. Today, we’re taking a big step forward with MAI Licensed Weights : models under your control. Take a frontier MAI model, customize it using your proprietary data if you want to. Then run it securely in your own Azure environment. You control who can access it. Your data and adaptations stay yours. And we’ll work with you through Frontier Company to deliver the custom model and embed it in your own products and agents. So that’s MAI, a family of world class models with exceptional price performance: the world’s best image editing model; the world’s best transcription model; frontier cyber defense at 2% of the cost; and world class everyday coding models at a price you can scale. And crucially all of it with Your IQ. Your agents. Your weights. All under your control. This is Frontier Intelligence you can trust, from the company you can trust. title: Making 8-page foldable zines from a single A4 sheet in the browser
body_text: Paper, folds, and what’s new in fanzines.app – Wilson Tovar (krthr) Wilson Tovar (krthr) home • blog • poesía • photography • say hi 👋 Paper, folds, and what’s new in fanzines.app 19 Nov, 2026 A few months ago, I wrote about how I started giving away zines to my friends, my family, and people at work. If you've never made one, the fold is simple. Take a single A4 sheet of paper, fold it in half three times, open it back up, and cut along the center crease with scissors. Fold the sheet into a cross and close it, and you have an 8-page booklet with no staples or glue. I fill mine with whatever I feel like printing: photos, poems, or notes. Why fanzines.app exists The part I never liked was laying out the flat sheet on the computer before printing. Because the A4 paper folds back on itself, the pages sit in a strange order and the top row has to be upside down: ┌─────────┬─────────┬─────────┬─────────┐ │ 6 │ 5 │ 4 │ 3 │ ← upside down (180°) ├─────────┼─────────┼─────────┼─────────┤ │ Back │ Cover │ 1 │ 2 │ ← right-side up └─────────┴─────────┴─────────┴─────────┘ I got tired of rotating pictures and double-checking columns in Photoshop every time I wanted to print a new zine, so I built fanzines.app . In the browser, you lay out each page right-side up with photos and text. When you export, the app places all 8 panels onto the A4 grid with the top row rotated 180 degrees and generates a 300 DPI PDF. Everything stays local in the browser; no photos are uploaded to a server. Over the last few days, I rebuilt the editor around the things that kept getting in my way when I sat down to make a zine. Fixing how pages are paired In the first version, the sidebar listed the 8 pages in a plain two-column grid. It paired the Front Cover with Page 1, Page 2 with Page 3, Page 4 with Page 5, and Page 6 with the Back Cover. It looked tidy on screen, but it didn't match the physical booklet. When you hold a folded zine, the front cover sits alone on the right. Open it and Page 1 faces Page 2 across the fold, then 3 faces 4, 5 faces 6, and the back cover ends up alone on the left. The sidebar now groups the page thumbnails into those real spreads, in reading order. I also added a Spread view on the canvas. While you're editing Page 1, Page 2 sits beside it at lower opacity so you can check how the two facing pages sit together before printing. Clicking the dimmed page switches straight to editing it. Smaller changes that make the editor less fussy When I make a photo zine, I usually start with a folder of 8 photos already picked out. Now you can drag the whole batch onto the editor window, and the sidebar highlights which pages will take each photo in reading order before you drop them. I changed the side panel too. Early on, clicking a photo opened four coordinate inputs ( X , Y , Width , Height ). I rarely needed to type coordinates; mostly I wanted a photo to fill the page, fit inside the margins, or sit centered. Fill, Fit, and Center now sit at the top of the inspector and in a small toolbar above the selection. The exact fields are still in a collapsible section at the bottom, now in millimeters (for the 74.25 × 105 mm folded panel) and points for text. Before downloading the PDF, a Review step shows the full unfolded A4 sheet with toggles for cut/fold lines and a 5 mm safe margin. Most home printers clip a few millimeters around the edge of an A4 sheet, so the safe margin scales the layout to about 95% to keep the covers intact. A couple of other additions: the editor now works on phone screens (one page at a time with a thumbnail strip along the bottom), and the site is available in English as well as Spanish . Changing the language keeps your current pages. Thanks for reading, Wil You can create your own zine in English or Spanish at fanzines.app #tech #zines Toast this post   Subscribe to my blog via email or RSS feed . Powered by Bear ʕ•ᴥ•ʔ
