How the European Commission rolled out Matrix to more than 40k staff
body_text: How the European Commission rolled out Matrix to more than 40,000 staff All Government Engineering Security Get Started All Government Engineering Security Get Started How the European Commission rolled out Matrix to more than 40,000 staff November 19, 2026 Digital sovereignty The European Commission went from a Matrix proof of concept in December 2025 to a sovereign communication tool rolled out to every Commission laptop by September 2026. That tool, built on Matrix by Element, and run by the Commission itself, now serves more than 40,000 users. At The Matrix Conference 2026, Diana Gheorghe, Head of Sector for Digital Workplace Communication and Collaboration Services, and Alexandru Vignide, Service Delivery Manager for the Commission's sovereign communication tool, told the story of how they got there. The pair were transparent about what got harder at scale, and how they dealt with it. Sovereignty means more than where the servers sit “Sovereignty” can have a different meaning for different people and organisations, so the Commission started by pinning down what it means for them. Their answer spans five dimensions: resilience and business continuity, vendor diversity, control over their data, ownership of the platform, and leverage in procurement - the ability to negotiate with, or walk away from, a supplier. That last one is easy to forget, and arguably the one that bites hardest when it's missing. For internal communications specifically, the priorities were resilience, data ownership and, crucially, interoperability. That's what led them to Matrix: an open protocol whose value lies in letting separate systems talk to each other. They chose Element Server Suite Pro (ESS Pro), Element's enterprise distribution of Matrix, as a mature implementation, and decided to host, operate and architect the service under their own control. Sovereign cloud hosting, familiar login, without federation (yet) With the building blocks chosen, Alexandru walked through three architecture decisions. Hosting. The service doesn't run in a Commission-owned data centre. Instead it runs with sovereign cloud providers selected through the sovereign hosting tender awarded earlier this year, in order to meet its sovereignty and hosting requirements. Sovereign doesn't have to mean building everything in-house; it means choosing who you depend on, and on what terms. Identity. The deployment is integrated with EU Login, the sign-in staff already use every day. A new tool is easier to adopt when logging in feels familiar. Federation. Connecting to Matrix servers outside the Commission is still under assessment. The technical side is being explored - there was a separate hands-on demo using non-production environments at the conference - but federation also needs governance, participation and structure, which takes longer to agree than a config change. Nine months from proof of concept to every Commission laptop The Commission started working with Matrix in summer 2025, or, as Alexandru put it, at last year's Matrix Conference. From there, things moved quickly: December 2025: the architecture and engineering team delivered a proof of concept showing Matrix and Element were viable for the Commission. It earned a green light for a Commission-wide service, which Alexandru described as a nice Christmas present. January to June 2026: the team built the production infrastructure, along with the hosting and operations needed to run it, and was ready by June. Pilots: a laptop pilot covering both the desktop and web clients, followed by a mobile pilot through the Commission's mobile device management (MDM) platform. July to September 2026: the laptop rollout to all Commission users, delivered in waves, was and completed in September. The Commission is now exploring a mobile rollout, and what federation could look like. Scaling to 40,000 users brought challenges Rolling out to 40,000 people surfaces problems no pilot will. Alexandru described the four main ones his team ran into, and how they tackled each. Finding colleagues across servers. The Commission runs several Synapse homeservers, and early on, people on different servers couldn't always find each other. The Commission's teams worked with Element to fix this, and now a plain user search finds anyone in the Commission, whichever server they're on. Accounts that only appear after sign-up. The Commission chose user-led account creation rather than pre-provisioning every account. The catch is that you can't find a colleague who hasn't registered yet, which made the discovery problem above feel worse while adoption was still ramping up. Live presence was switched off. As more users came on board, the load from live presence (the real-time “online/away” indicator) started to affect performance, so the team disabled it. They're now looking at a user status feature being developed with Element as the replacement. Infrastructure had to learn to scale itself. Rolling out in waves over three months meant uneven, shifting demand, so the team tuned the infrastructure to adjust automatically. Running through all of this was the balance between security and usability. Most of the hardening work was done with the Commission's security teams before the rollout, and continues through regular security reviews and continuous improvements. The team made sure that hardening didn't get in the way of everyday tasks like creating an account, recovering it or verifying a new device, and documented those steps clearly for staff. Feedback from tickets, internal forums and public channels is consolidated into prioritised goals for the Commission's own roadmap. Element complements the Commission's toolset The most common question, Diana said, is whether Element is meant to replace Microsoft Teams, or consumer apps like Signal and WhatsApp. The short answer: neither, directly. Element is positioned as an internal communication tool for specific use cases - secure communication among them - where the Commission's existing stack doesn't fully meet its needs. Teams bundles communication, collaboration and a whole platform behind it, so there's no one-to-one swap to be had. That makes expectation-setting part of the job. People naturally compare workplace tools with the apps they use at home and go looking for feature-for-feature matches. Diana's view is that this mindset is something to address head-on in any organisational change: Element is a tool in its own right, with its own feature set, that the Commission and Element can evolve together. Part of the goal is to bring work conversations onto a tool the Commission controls.  Federation goes beyond tech The Commission has been interested in federation for a long time. The obvious starting point is other EU institutions, but it wouldn't stop there: the Commission also works closely with member states, governments and non-governmental organisations. No decision has been made yet, and the Commission is taking it one step at a time. First comes the technical question of what the technology can actually do, because, as Diana put it, there's no point writing policies technology can't deliver. Then comes governance: who the partners would be, on what terms, with what scope, and how security and privacy are handled. The Commission's Takeaways Alexandru ended the talk by sharing what the deployment had taught the Commission. Sovereignty is operational. It depends on operational control and the trustworthiness of the whole chain of partners, not just on where the service is hosted. Adoption depends on everyday usability. Discoverability, onboarding support and everything around the product shape whether people use it. Interoperability needs more than technology. It also needs clear structure, participation and governance. He also noted that introducing a new communication tool has been a journey, and still is. Along the way, the Commission has relied on trustworthy service providers, and he described the collaboration with Element as a success. Thibault Martin Senior Technical Marketing Engineer Related Posts Government “Matrix, come here.” The world’s first cross-border government federation demo Five public sector organisations, five sovereign run deployments, one conversation, spanning three countries and two international institutions. The live demo was a proof point of what governments can do with the Matrix open standard. Thibault Martin 21/10/2026 Government Making sovereignty standard for European governments Element is thrilled to be sponsoring the public sector track at The Matrix Conference again, running from October 20th to 23rd, 2026, in Malmö, Sweden. Steve Loynes 17/09/2026 Interoperability We’re interoperable, so you can be sovereign Interoperability is the foundation of digital sovereignty; it’s the key ingredient to ensure that end-users stay in control, rather than the vendor. This help j Next menu item k Previous menu item g p Previous man page g n Next man page G Scroll to bottom g g Scroll to top g h Goto homepage g s Goto search (current page) / Focus search box Released November 19, 2026 Faster, Safer, More Powerful. PHP 8.6 is a major update of the PHP language , with new features including Partial Function Application , a new Duration class, a Polling API , and a new clamp() function What's new in 8.6 Upgrade to PHP 8.6 Key Features in PHP 8.6 More expressive code , stronger types , and scalable I/O . Partial Function Application Allows some of a function's arguments to be provided in advance, returning a Closure that accepts the rest. New \Time\Duration Class The Duration class represents elapsed time as measured by a stopwatch. Polling API Scalable I/O multiplexing using epoll, kqueue, and other native mechanisms, available to event loop libraries like ReactPHP and AMPHP. New clamp() Function Ensures that a given value (numeric or otherwise) falls within a specified range. New SortDirection Enum A standard, type-safe way to express sort order that can be shared across libraries. Readonly Property Defaults Allows readonly properties to declare default values, so fixed values no longer have to be assigned in the constructor. Partial Function Application Allows some of a function's arguments to be provided in advance, using ? and ... placeholders for the rest. The result is a Closure, and the function is only called once the remaining arguments are passed to it. PHP 8.5 and older $versions = [ '8.4' , '8.5' , '8.6' , '8.7' , '9.0' ]; $supportsPfa = array_filter ( $versions , fn ( $version ) => version_compare ( $version , '8.6' , '>=' ), ); PHP 8.6 NEW RFC ↗ Doc ↗ $versions = [ '8.4' , '8.5' , '8.6' , '8.7' , '9.0' ]; $supportsPfa = array_filter ( $versions , version_compare (?, '8.6' , '>=' ), ); New \Time\Duration Class The Duration class represents elapsed time as measured by a stopwatch. Its representation is independent of any time and timezone and can represent a range of more than 250 years with nanosecond precision. This makes it well-suited to represent timeouts or benchmark timings in an expressive way. PHP 8.5 and older /** * All delays are in microseconds. */ function backoff ( int $baseDelay , int $step , int $attempt , ): void { $delay = $baseDelay + ( $step * ( 2 ** $attempt )); // Wait at most 30 seconds. usleep ( min ( $delay , 30_000_000 )); } // 1 second base delay, plus 100 milliseconds // doubling with each attempt. backoff ( 1_000_000 , 100_000 , $attempt ); PHP 8.6 NEW RFC ↗ Doc ↗ use Time\Duration ; function backoff ( Duration $baseDelay , Duration $step , int $attempt , ): void { $delay = $baseDelay -> add ( $step -> multiplyBy ( 2 ** $attempt )); // Durations are comparable, so min() works directly. $delay = min ( $delay , Duration :: fromSeconds ( 30 )); time_nanosleep ( $delay -> seconds , $delay -> nanoseconds ); } backoff ( Duration :: fromSeconds ( 1 ), Duration :: fromMilliseconds ( 100 ), $attempt , ); // Preconfigure the delays using Partial Function Application. $waitBeforeRetry = backoff ( Duration :: fromSeconds ( 1 ), Duration :: fromMilliseconds ( 100 ), attempt : ?, ); $waitBeforeRetry ( $attempt ); Polling API The new Io\Poll API efficiently monitors many streams at once using the best mechanism available on each platform (epoll, kqueue, event ports, or WSAPoll), without the scalability limits of stream_select() . It is designed as a common foundation that event loop libraries such as ReactPHP and AMPHP can build on. PHP 8.5 and older $server = stream_socket_server ( 'tcp://0.0.0.0:8080' ); $clients = []; while ( true ) { $read = [ $server , ... $clients ]; $write = $except = null ; // Based on select(), which typically can't handle // more than 1024 connections stream_select ( $read , $write , $except , null ); foreach ( $read as $stream ) { if ( $stream === $server ) { $clients [] = stream_socket_accept ( $server ); continue; } $data = fread ( $stream , 8192 ); if ( $data === '' || $data === false ) { $key = array_search ( $stream , $clients , true ); unset( $clients [ $key ]); fclose ( $stream ); } else { fwrite ( $stream , $data ); } } } PHP 8.6 NEW RFC ↗ use Io\Poll \{ Context , Event }; $server = stream_socket_server ( 'tcp://0.0.0.0:8080' ); // Automatically uses epoll, kqueue, event ports, or WSAPoll $poll = new Context (); $poll -> add (new StreamPollHandle ( $server ), [ Event :: Read ]); while ( true ) { foreach ( $poll -> wait () as $watcher ) { $stream = $watcher -> getHandle ()-> getStream (); if ( $stream === $server ) { $client = stream_socket_accept ( $server ); $poll -> add ( new StreamPollHandle ( $client ), [ Event :: Read ], ); continue; } $data = fread ( $stream , 8192 ); if ( $data === '' || $data === false ) { $watcher -> remove (); fclose ( $stream ); } else { fwrite ( $stream , $data ); } } } Stream Error Handling Stream operations can now be configured to throw a StreamException or to fail silently instead of emitting warnings. Errors are reported as structured StreamError objects with a StreamErrorCode enum case, the wrapper name, and the affected path or URL, and can also be retrieved later with stream_last_errors() or passed to a custom error handler. PHP 8.5 and older $config = @ file_get_contents ( '/etc/app/config.json' ); if ( $config === false ) { // Only an unstructured message string is available $error = error_get_last (); log_error ( $error [ 'message' ]); } PHP 8.6 NEW RFC ↗ Doc ↗ $context = stream_context_create ([ 'stream' => [ 'error_mode' => StreamErrorMode :: Exception , ], ]); try { $config = file_get_contents ( '/etc/app/config.json' , context : $context , ); } catch ( StreamException $e ) { foreach ( $e -> getErrors () as $error ) { // $error->code is a StreamErrorCode enum case log_error ( $error -> code -> name , $error -> message , $error -> wrapperName , ); } } New clamp() Function Ensures that a given value (numeric or otherwise) falls within a specified range. Otherwise, the nearest boundary value is returned. PHP 8.5 and older var_dump ( max ( 0 , min (- 10 , 100 ))); // int(0) var_dump ( max ( 0 , min ( 50 , 100 ))); // int(50) var_dump ( max ( 0 , min ( 110 , 100 ))); // int(100) PHP 8.6 NEW RFC ↗ Doc ↗ var_dump ( clamp (- 10 , 0 , 100 )); // int(0) var_dump ( clamp ( 50 , 0 , 100 )); // int(50) var_dump ( clamp ( 110 , 0 , 100 )); // int(100) // Any comparable value works with clamp(). This // includes the new Duration class. var_dump ( clamp ( \Time\Duration :: fromSeconds ( 30 ), min : \Time\Duration :: fromMinutes ( 1 ), max : \Time\Duration :: fromMinutes ( 10 ), )-> seconds ); // int(60) New SortDirection Enum The SortDirection enum provides a shared, type-safe way to express sort order with its Ascending and Descending cases. Previously, every library had to define its own way of representing sort direction, resulting in a mix of incompatible integers, strings, booleans, and custom enums. Since SortDirection is built into PHP, libraries can accept it in their public APIs without needing adapter code. Learn more about this feature in The PHP Foundation’s blog . PHP 8.5 and older class QueryBuilder { private array $orderBy = []; public function orderBy ( string $column , int $direction = SORT_ASC , ): static { $this -> orderBy [] = $column . ' ' . match ( $direction ) { SORT_ASC => 'ASC' , SORT_DESC => 'DESC' , }; return $this ; } } $qb -> orderBy ( 'name' , SORT_DESC ); $qb -> orderBy ( 'name' , SORT_STRING ); // Accepted by the signature, then fails inside the method: // UnhandledMatchError: Unhandled match case 2 PHP 8.6 NEW RFC ↗ Doc ↗ class QueryBuilder { private array $orderBy = []; public function orderBy ( string $column , SortDirection $direction = SortDirection :: Ascending , ): static { $this -> orderBy [] = $column . ' ' . match ( $direction ) { SortDirection :: Ascending => 'ASC' , SortDirection :: Descending => 'DESC' , }; return $this ; } } $qb -> orderBy ( 'name' , SortDirection :: Descending ); $qb -> orderBy ( 'name' , SORT_STRING ); // TypeError: QueryBuilder::orderBy(): Argument #2 ($direction) // must be of type SortDirection, int given DocComments for Function Parameters Function and method parameters can now have their own DocComments, which are available via the new ReflectionParameter::getDocComment() method. This allows each parameter to be documented right next to its declaration, without repeating its name and type in a @param tag. PHP 8.5 and older class DB { /** * Returns up to $limit items matching the $query. * * @param string $query Terms to search * @param int $limit Maximum number of results */ public function search ( string $query , int $limit = 10 ): array { return []; } } // Parameter descriptions can only be extracted // by parsing the function's DocComment. PHP 8.6 NEW RFC ↗ class DB { /** * Returns up to $limit items matching the $query. */ public function search ( /** Terms to search */ string $query , /** Maximum number of results */ int $limit = 10 , ): array { return []; } } var_dump ( new ReflectionParameter ([ DB ::class, 'search' ], 'query' ) -> getDocComment (), ); // string(22) "/** Terms to search */" New ReflectionProperty::isReadable() and ReflectionProperty::isWritable() Methods With readonly properties, asymmetric visibility, and property hooks, checking whether a property is public is no longer enough to know whether it can be read or written. The new methods answer this directly for a given scope, and optionally for a specific object, taking into account visibility, initialization state, hooks, and magic methods. PHP 8.6 NEW RFC ↗ Doc ↗ class NewsEntry { public string $title = 'PHP 8.6 released!' ; public private(set) string $slug = 'php-86-released' ; } $entry = new NewsEntry (); foreach ([ 'title' , 'slug' ] as $item ) { $property = new ReflectionProperty ( NewsEntry ::class, $item ); printf ( "%s: isReadable=%s isWritable=%s\n" , $item , $property -> isReadable ( null , $entry ) ? 'yes' : 'no' , $property -> isWritable ( null , $entry ) ? 'yes' : 'no' , ); } // title: isReadable=yes isWritable=yes // slug: isReadable=yes isWritable=no Readonly Property Defaults Instance readonly properties, including those in readonly classes, can now declare a default value. This makes it simple to implement get-only interface properties with fixed values, which previously required assigning them in a constructor. The default counts as the property's initialization, so the constructor cannot overwrite it. PHP 8.5 and older interface Rule { public string $parser { get ; } } final readonly class SlugRule implements Rule { public string $parser ; public function __construct () { $this -> parser = SlugParser ::class; } } PHP 8.6 NEW RFC ↗ Doc ↗ interface Rule { public string $parser { get ; } } final readonly class SlugRule implements Rule { public string $parser = SlugParser ::class; } Additional Features and Improvements The #[\Override] attribute can now be applied to class constants and enum cases. Enums can now implement the __debugInfo() magic method. Properties of objects stored in constants can now be modified directly, e.g. Config::DEFAULTS->timeout = 30 . New Uri\Rfc3986\UriBuilder and Uri\WhatWg\UrlBuilder classes build URIs from their components, along with new methods for detecting URI and host types and a Uri\WhatWg\url_percent_encode() function. The Sodium extension adds post-quantum key encapsulation (X-Wing and ML-KEM-768), IP address encryption, and the SHAKE and TurboSHAKE extendable-output functions. TLS streams now support session resumption, external pre-shared keys, and TLS 1.3 early data (0-RTT). New mysqli::quote_string() method escapes a string and wraps it in quotes, matching PDO::quote() . pack() and unpack() now accept the < and > endianness modifiers on integer and float format codes. JSON error messages now include the location of the error in the input. The new error_include_args INI setting consistently includes function arguments in error messages. New grapheme_strrev() function reverses strings by grapheme cluster, and the new IntlNumberRangeFormatter class formats ranges of numbers. New ZipArchive::openString() and ZipArchive::closeString() methods work with in-memory archives. Performance improvements include compiling array_map() with first-class callable or partial application callbacks into loops, faster printf() calls, caching of stateless closures, and faster JSON encoding. Deprecations and Backward Compatibility Breaks Using return inside a finally block is now deprecated, as it silently discards exceptions and overrides values returned from the try or catch block. Returning a value from __construct() or __destruct() is now deprecated, as is making them generators. Declaring a nullable return type for __debugInfo() is also deprecated. Using let or is as the name of a class, function, or constant is now deprecated. Using _ as a constant name, namespace as a class constant name, or readonly as a function name is also deprecated. The mbstring regular expression functions such as mb_ereg() and mb_split() have been deprecated, as the underlying Oniguruma library is no longer maintained. PCRE functions with the u modifier can be used instead. The is_double() , is_long() , is_integer() , and doubleval() aliases have been deprecated. Use is_float() , is_int() , and floatval() instead. spl_object_hash() has been deprecated in favor of spl_object_id() , and spl_classes() in favor of ReflectionExtension::getClassNames() . Passing an object where an array is expected to array_walk() , array_walk_recursive() , http_build_query() , mb_convert_variables() , and compression functions and filters is now deprecated. Use get_object_vars() to convert the object first. strcoll() and the SORT_LOCALE_STRING sort flag have been deprecated. Use the Collator class from the intl extension instead. Passing a third argument to define() is now deprecated, as is calling is_a() or is_subclass_of() with a class name string when $allow_string is false . Using more than 16 filters in a php://filter URL without setting the filter.max_filter_count context option is now deprecated. Sessions are now more secure by default: session.use_strict_mode and session.cookie_httponly are enabled, and session.cookie_samesite is set to Lax . Custom session handlers that do not implement both create_sid() and validateId() are now deprecated. The metaphone() , mysqli_get_charset() , and mysqli_stmt_init() functions are now deprecated, along with the CSV methods of SplFileObject and the sorting, flag, and serialization methods of ArrayIterator . trim() , ltrim() , and rtrim() now also strip form feed ( \f ) characters by default. fclose() , file_put_contents() , and copy() now return false when flushing or closing the stream fails, instead of silently ignoring the failure. Many functions now throw a ValueError for out-of-range values, invalid flags, or strings containing NUL bytes, instead of silently truncating or ignoring them. Better syntax, improved performance and type safety. Upgrade to PHP 8.6 The full list of changes is recorded in the ChangeLog . Please consult the migration guide for a detailed list of new features and backward-incompatible changes. PHP is developed and maintained by a global community of contributors.
